### Pattern 2 — Gherkin v39: Comments Inside Descriptions and Korean Rule Keyword

Gherkin v39 (March 2026, bundled in playwright-bdd v9 via `@cucumber/gherkin 39.x`) added
two features relevant to BDD documentation quality:

1. **Comments inside descriptions**: `#`-prefixed lines are now valid anywhere in Feature,
   Rule, Scenario, and Background description blocks (the free-text between keyword line and
   first step). Previously, comments in descriptions caused parse errors in some implementations.

2. **Korean `Rule` keyword translation**: Expands Gherkin's international accessibility to
   Korean-language teams.

**Why it matters**: Comments inside descriptions unlock a documentation pattern that was
previously impossible: inline rationale text adjacent to scenario definitions, without
creating a new Scenario that pollutes the test count.

```gherkin
# features/pricing/bulk-discounts.feature
Feature: Bulk discount pricing
  # Source: Product team requirement doc PRD-2024-117, approved 2025-11-01
  # Business rule: discounts apply to the subtotal before tax, after coupons.
  # Edge case: discounts do NOT stack with promotional pricing (see Rule below).

  Rule: Standard bulk discount tiers
    # Discount schedule: 0-9 units = 0%, 10-24 = 5%, 25-99 = 10%, 100+ = 15%
    # Reviewed by Finance: 2026-02-14. Do not change tiers without Finance sign-off.

    Scenario: No discount for fewer than 10 items
      Given a customer has 9 units of "widget" in their cart
      When the order total is calculated
      Then the discount applied should be 0 percent

    Scenario: 5% discount for 10-24 items
      Given a customer has 15 units of "widget" in their cart
      When the order total is calculated
      Then the discount applied should be 5 percent

  Rule: Promotional price exclusion
    # Promotional SKUs flagged with promo_price=true bypass all bulk rules.
    # Combining promo + bulk was causing revenue leakage — see incident INC-2025-0441.

    Scenario: Bulk discount does not apply to promotional items
      Given a customer has 50 units of "widget-promo" in their cart
      And "widget-promo" is marked as a promotional item
      When the order total is calculated
      Then the discount applied should be 0 percent
```

**[community] Comments inside descriptions do not appear in HTML reports or the Cucumber Messages stream**: The description-level comment is a documentation artifact only — it is parsed and discarded by the Gherkin parser before the test run. Teams that add rationale comments expecting them to show in Allure or Cucumber HTML reports will not find them there. For rationale that must appear in living documentation, use a non-step `Background` description (no `#` prefix) or a `@description:"..."` custom tag processed by a formatter plugin. [community]

### Pattern 3 — Cucumber Expressions v19: `StepMatchArgument.Group.children` Now Optional

Cucumber Expressions v19 (January 2026) made `StepMatchArgument.Group.children` optional in
the TypeScript and Java types. This is a **data model change** that matters to anyone who
has written a custom Cucumber formatter or reporter that traverses step match arguments.

**Why it matters**: Prior to v19, `Group.children` was typed as `Group[]` (always an array,
possibly empty). In v19, it is `Group[] | undefined`. Code that previously did
`group.children.length === 0` now needs a null-guard, otherwise it throws at runtime on
simple (non-capturing-group) step matches. This is a silent breaking change: TypeScript type
errors only surface if you have strict null checks enabled.

```typescript
// BEFORE v19 — works, but potentially incorrect on v19 runtime:
function extractMatchGroups(groups: Group[]): string[] {
  return groups.flatMap(g => [
    g.value ?? '',
    ...extractMatchGroups(g.children),  // TypeError if children is undefined in v19
  ]);
}

// AFTER v19 — correct pattern:
function extractMatchGroups(groups: Group[] | undefined): string[] {
  if (!groups || groups.length === 0) return [];
  return groups.flatMap(g => [
    g.value ?? '',
    ...extractMatchGroups(g.children),  // children is Group[] | undefined in v19
  ]);
}

// Custom formatter using the match argument safely (v19+):
import type { IFormatterOptions } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { Group } from '@cucumber/cucumber-expressions';

function formatStepArguments(stepMatchArguments: Array<{ group: Group }>): string {
  return stepMatchArguments
    .map(({ group }) => {
      const children = group.children ?? [];  // Safe: ?? [] handles undefined
      return children.length > 0
        ? children.map(c => c.value ?? '<no value>').join(', ')
        : group.value ?? '<matched>';
    })
    .join(' | ');
}
```

**[community] Strict null checks (`"strictNullChecks": true`) are required to catch v19 Group.children migration issues at compile time**: Teams with `strict: false` or `strictNullChecks: false` in their TypeScript config will not see the type error when upgrading to Cucumber Expressions v19 — the runtime will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'length')` only during test execution when a step with no capture groups is matched. The fix takes 5 minutes but is invisible without strict null checks. Always enable `"strict": true` in formatter and plugin packages. [community]

---

### Pattern 4 — Declarative-Only Step Writing: The "Will It Change If Implementation Changes?" Test

The Cucumber documentation's "better Gherkin" guide (updated May 2026) articulates a precise
heuristic for choosing between declarative and imperative step writing that is more actionable
than "be declarative": **ask "Will this wording need to change if the implementation changes?"**
If yes, the step is too implementation-specific; rewrite it.

**Why it matters**: This test operationalizes the declarative principle into a reviewable,
mechanical check during Three Amigos sessions and PR reviews — it does not require aesthetic
judgment, just a specific question.

```gherkin
# IMPERATIVE (fails the test — all three steps would change if the UI changed):
Scenario: User logs in
  Given I am on the login page at /auth/login
  When I type "alice@example.com" in the input with id "email-field"
  And I type "s3cr3t" in the input with id "password-field"
  And I click the button with text "Sign In"
  Then I should see the text "Welcome back, Alice" in the h1 element

# DECLARATIVE (passes the test — none would change if the URL, selectors, or copy changed):
Scenario: User logs in
  Given Alice has a registered account
  When Alice logs in with her valid credentials
  Then she should be taken to her personal dashboard
```

```typescript
// src/steps/auth/login.steps.ts — declarative step implementations hide UI details
import { Given, When, Then } from '../world';

// Implementation detail: "valid credentials" means username+password from fixtures
// If we switch to SSO tomorrow, only this step implementation changes — not the feature file
Given('Alice has a registered account', async ({ page, fixtures }) => {
  // Seed or retrieve Alice's account via API — not via UI
  await fixtures.ensureUser({ email: 'alice@example.com', role: 'customer' });
});

When('Alice logs in with her valid credentials', async ({ page }) => {
  // Encapsulates the entire login flow — UI details hidden from Gherkin
  await page.goto('/auth/login');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('alice@example.com');
  await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard/**');
});

Then('she should be taken to her personal dashboard', async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard/);
  // Assert business outcome, not UI implementation: dashboard loaded, not "h1 text"
  await expect(page.getByRole('main')).toBeVisible();
});
```

**[community] The declarative heuristic has a second side that teams miss: steps that are TOO declarative become untestable**: A step like "the system works correctly" or "all business rules are satisfied" is so abstract it provides no actionable test condition. The sweet spot is: declarative enough that implementation changes don't break the Gherkin, specific enough that a developer can implement the step without asking the product owner what to assert. If writing the step definition requires a follow-up question about what "correctly" means, the Gherkin is not declarative enough to be specific — it is abstract. [community]

---

### Pattern 5 — Example Mapping Color-Card Workflow in Remote Teams

The official Example Mapping format (Cucumber documentation, updated May 2026) specifies a
four-color index card system. Adapting this for remote teams — where physical cards are
unavailable — requires deliberate tooling choices to preserve the visual separation that makes
the session work.

**Why the colors matter**: The color coding enforces cognitive discipline: yellow (story) at
the top keeps everyone anchored on scope; blue (rules) forces explicit articulation of
business logic before examples are written; green (examples) ground abstract rules in
concrete behavior; red (questions) externalizes uncertainty rather than silently deferring it.
Without the color separation, Example Mapping sessions drift into unstructured discussions
that produce no artifacts.

```yaml
# example-mapping-template.yaml — digital equivalent of index cards
# Use with a collaboration tool (Miro/FigJam/GitHub Issues) — one YAML per story

story:
  id: STORY-441
  title: "Bulk discount pricing for B2B customers"
  acceptance_criteria_owner: "product@myorg.com"

rules:
  - id: R1
    text: "Discounts apply to the subtotal before tax, after coupons"
    examples:
      - id: E1-1
        title: "Standard 10% discount for 25+ units"
        given: "A B2B customer has 30 units of SKU-001 in cart"
        when: "The order total is calculated"
        then: "A 10% discount is applied to the subtotal"
      - id: E1-2
        title: "No discount for fewer than 10 units"
        given: "A B2B customer has 9 units of SKU-001 in cart"
        when: "The order total is calculated"
        then: "No discount is applied"

  - id: R2
    text: "Bulk discounts do not stack with promotional pricing"
    examples:
      - id: E2-1
        title: "Promotional SKU bypasses bulk discount"
        given: "A B2B customer has 50 units of promo SKU-PROMO in cart"
        when: "The order total is calculated"
        then: "No bulk discount is applied (promo price already reduced)"

questions:
  - id: Q1
    text: "Do B2C customers get bulk discounts or only B2B?"
    owner: "product@myorg.com"
    status: "open"
    raised_by: "qa"
    raised_at: "2026-05-10"
  - id: Q2
    text: "What is the discount tier for 100+ units?"
    owner: "finance@myorg.com"
    status: "open"
    raised_by: "dev"
    raised_at: "2026-05-10"

new_stories_discovered:
  - "Discount audit logging for Finance reporting"
  - "B2B account tier management UI"
```

**[community] Red-card questions are the most valuable output of Example Mapping — but teams routinely skip them**: The questions (red cards) surface ambiguities that would otherwise become defects. In remote sessions, teams tend to skip red cards because the discussion already resolved the question verbally. The key practice: write down every question that was asked, even if it was immediately answered in the session, because (a) it confirms the answer is documented somewhere, and (b) future team members reading the session output understand why the rule was shaped as it is. A session with zero questions almost always means the team stopped challenging assumptions too early. [community]

---

### Pattern 6 — Cucumber.js v12.6.0 Color Output Migration: `colorsEnabled` → `FORCE_COLOR`

Cucumber.js v12.6.0 (January 2026) deprecated the `colorsEnabled` format option in favor of
the standard `FORCE_COLOR` environment variable used by most Node.js CLIs. The transition
aligns Cucumber with the Node.js ecosystem convention established by `chalk`, `kleur`, and
`supports-color`.

**Why it matters**: Teams that set `colorsEnabled: false` in their format options to suppress
ANSI escape sequences in CI logs will now get a deprecation warning on every run — and after
Cucumber.js v13 (when `colorsEnabled` is removed), their color suppression will silently
break. `FORCE_COLOR=0` is the correct v12.6+ pattern.

```bash
# CI configuration — BEFORE (deprecated in v12.6.0, breaks in v13):
# npx cucumber-js --format-options '{"colorsEnabled":false}'

# CI configuration — AFTER (v12.6.0+ correct pattern):
FORCE_COLOR=0 npx cucumber-js --profile ci

# GitHub Actions workflow — correct environment setup:
# env:
#   FORCE_COLOR: "0"   # Suppress ANSI in GitHub Actions log output
#   CI: "true"

# Local development — let terminal auto-detect (no FORCE_COLOR needed):
npx cucumber-js --profile default
```

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — BEFORE (generates deprecation warning in v12.6.0):
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

export default {
  paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
  require: ['src/steps/**/*.steps.ts'],
  format: ['html:reports/cucumber.html'],
  formatOptions: {
    colorsEnabled: false,  // DEPRECATED — use FORCE_COLOR=0 env var instead
  },
} satisfies Partial<IConfiguration>;

// cucumber.config.ts — AFTER (v12.6.0+ clean config):
export default {
  paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
  require: ['src/steps/**/*.steps.ts'],
  format: ['html:reports/cucumber.html'],
  // No formatOptions.colorsEnabled — handled by FORCE_COLOR env var
} satisfies Partial<IConfiguration>;
```

**[community] `FORCE_COLOR=1` in CI can cause garbled output in log aggregation systems that don't understand ANSI**: Some log aggregation services (Splunk, CloudWatch without ANSI stripping) will ingest the raw ANSI escape sequences as visible characters in log lines (e.g., `[32mPASSED[0m`). The default behavior — letting the terminal auto-detect (no `FORCE_COLOR`) — is correct for most environments. Only set `FORCE_COLOR=1` if your CI display explicitly supports it (GitHub Actions with `::group::` annotations, GitLab CI with `--ansi` flag). Default to `FORCE_COLOR=0` in CI unless you have confirmed end-to-end ANSI support. [community]

---

### Pattern 7 — Fail-Fast BDD Suites: Combining `process.exitCode` Plugin with CI Retry Strategy

In large BDD suites with hundreds of scenarios, a single infrastructure failure (database
unavailable, auth service down) can cause cascading failures across all scenarios. A fail-fast
plugin combined with a targeted CI retry strategy reduces wasted CI minutes and provides
faster signal on infrastructure vs. application failures.

```typescript
// src/support/fail-fast-plugin.ts — Cucumber.js Plugin API fail-fast implementation
import type { Plugin } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

interface FailFastOptions {
  /** Maximum allowed failures before stopping the run. Default: 1 */
  maxFailures?: number;
  /** If true, infrastructure errors (Given step failures) count double */
  escalateGivenFailures?: boolean;
}

export const failFastPlugin: Plugin<FailFastOptions> = (
  { on },
  options = {}
) => {
  const max = options.maxFailures ?? 1;
  const escalate = options.escalateGivenFailures ?? false;
  let failureCount = 0;

  on('test-case-finished', ({ result, testCase }) => {
    if (result.status !== 'FAILED') return;

    // Escalate Given-step failures (infrastructure) if configured:
    const isInfraFailure = escalate && testCase.pickleSteps
      .some(s => s.astNodeIds.length > 0 && s.text.startsWith('Given '));

    failureCount += isInfraFailure ? 2 : 1;

    if (failureCount >= max) {
      console.error(
        `[fail-fast] ${failureCount} failure(s) reached threshold of ${max} — stopping.`
      );
      process.exitCode = 1;
      // Note: Cucumber.js does not have a programmatic abort signal in v12.
      // Setting process.exitCode causes orderly shutdown after current workers finish.
    }
  });
};
```

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — with fail-fast plugin in CI profile
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';
import { failFastPlugin } from './src/support/fail-fast-plugin';

export const ci: Partial<IConfiguration> = {
  paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
  require: ['src/support/world.ts', 'src/steps/**/*.steps.ts'],
  tags: 'not @wip',
  parallel: 4,
  format: ['json:reports/cucumber-ci.json', 'progress'],
  plugins: [
    [failFastPlugin, { maxFailures: 5, escalateGivenFailures: true }],
  ],
};
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/bdd.yml — CI retry strategy: retry only failed scenarios, not the full suite
jobs:
  bdd:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Run BDD suite (first attempt)
        run: npx cucumber-js --profile ci 2>&1 | tee reports/run1.log
        continue-on-error: true
      - name: Retry failed scenarios only (using rerun formatter output)
        if: failure()
        run: |
          # rerun formatter writes failed scenario URIs to reports/rerun.txt
          # Format: features/checkout.feature:42\nfeatures/checkout.feature:67
          npx cucumber-js @reports/rerun.txt --profile ci
        # Note: add --format rerun:reports/rerun.txt to the first run's format list
```

**[community] The `rerun` formatter is the correct retry mechanism for BDD suites — not `jest --retryTimes` or `retry` in Playwright config**: `playwright-bdd` runs inside Playwright Test, so Playwright's `retries` config applies per-scenario. But Cucumber.js standalone uses the `rerun` formatter, which writes the URI+line of each failed scenario to a file. Re-running that file retries only genuinely failed scenarios, not the entire suite. Teams that restart the full suite on failure waste CI minutes and mask infrastructure flakiness vs. application defects. Use `rerun` for targeted retry; use fail-fast for infrastructure signal. [community]

---

### Pattern 8 — Gherkin Scenario Outline with `Rule`-Scoped `Examples`: Data-Driven Rules

A documented but underused Gherkin combination: `Scenario Outline` nested inside a `Rule`
block with `Examples` that are tagged specifically for that rule. This structures data-driven
testing around business rules rather than around technical test cases.

```gherkin
# features/shipping/delivery-sla.feature
Feature: Delivery SLA calculation

  Rule: Standard delivery tiers apply to domestic orders
    # SLA table from logistics contract LGS-2025-007, effective 2025-01-01
    Scenario Outline: Domestic delivery SLA for <service> service
      Given a domestic order placed at <order_time>
      When the delivery SLA is calculated for "<service>" service level
      Then the estimated delivery date should be <expected_days> business days later

      @smoke
      Examples: Standard domestic tiers
        | service    | order_time | expected_days |
        | economy    | 09:00      | 7             |
        | standard   | 09:00      | 5             |
        | express    | 09:00      | 2             |
        | next-day   | 14:00      | 1             |

      @regression
      Examples: Cutoff time edge cases
        | service    | order_time | expected_days |
        | next-day   | 13:59      | 1             |
        | next-day   | 14:01      | 2             |
        | express    | 23:59      | 3             |

  Rule: International orders use a separate SLA matrix
    Scenario Outline: International delivery SLA for <region>
      Given an international order to region "<region>"
      When the delivery SLA is calculated for "standard" service level
      Then the estimated delivery date should be <expected_days> business days later

      @regression
      Examples: International regions
        | region   | expected_days |
        | EU       | 10            |
        | APAC     | 14            |
        | Americas | 7             |
```

**[community] Multiple `Examples` blocks on a single `Scenario Outline` have independent tag inheritance, which creates unexpected CI behavior with tag filters**: When you run `npx cucumber-js --tags @smoke`, only `Examples: Standard domestic tiers` runs — the `@regression` Examples block is excluded. This is correct behavior, but teams often discover it after a `@smoke` CI run passes while regression edge cases have not run. A common mistake: tagging the `Scenario Outline` with `@smoke @regression` and assuming all Examples blocks will run in both profiles. Tag the Examples blocks individually, and document in your profile README which tags cover which blocks. [community]

---

### Pattern 9 — BDD Living Documentation via Cucumber HTML Report with GitHub Pages

The Cucumber HTML formatter (`html:reports/cucumber.html`, built into Cucumber.js v12) produces
a self-contained single-file HTML report that can be published to GitHub Pages after every
main-branch BDD run. This creates publicly accessible living documentation that non-technical
stakeholders can read without access to CI tooling.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/bdd-docs.yml — publish living documentation on main-branch pushes
name: BDD Living Documentation

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  bdd-docs:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.page_url }}

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci

      - name: Run BDD suite and generate HTML report
        run: |
          FORCE_COLOR=0 npx cucumber-js --profile ci \
            --format html:docs/cucumber-report.html \
            --format json:reports/cucumber-results.json
        continue-on-error: true  # Always publish, even if tests fail (shows red in report)

      - name: Add index.html redirect
        run: |
          echo '<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=cucumber-report.html">' > docs/index.html

      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v4
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: docs/
      - id: deploy
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
```

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — HTML report with test-case-centric view (v12.3.0+)
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

export const ci: Partial<IConfiguration> = {
  paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
  require: ['src/support/world.ts', 'src/steps/**/*.steps.ts'],
  tags: 'not @wip',
  parallel: 4,
  format: [
    // Test-case-centric HTML (v12.3.0+) — named hooks appear in the report
    'html:reports/cucumber.html',
    'json:reports/cucumber-results.json',
    // Rerun file for targeted retry on failure:
    'rerun:reports/rerun.txt',
  ],
  // gzip compression for publish (v12.4.0+):
  publish: { url: process.env.CUCUMBER_PUBLISH_TOKEN ? undefined : undefined },
};
```

**[community] The Cucumber HTML report's "test-case-centric" view added in v12.3.0 is a major stakeholder communication improvement over the previous feature-centric view**: The old format showed scenarios as children of Feature files — forcing stakeholders to navigate a file hierarchy. The new test-case-centric view shows each scenario as a first-class item with its full path, tags, and named hook statuses. Teams that upgraded from Cucumber.js v11 and have not regenerated their HTML report template are still producing the legacy format. Re-run `npx cucumber-js` with v12.3.0+ to pick up the new renderer automatically. [community]

---

### Pattern 10 — Background vs. `BeforeAll` vs. Tagged `Before`: When to Use Each

One of the most common BDD architectural mistakes is using the wrong setup mechanism for
shared test state. The three mechanisms serve distinct purposes and mixing them up causes
either test isolation failures or excessive duplication.

```typescript
// DECISION GUIDE — which setup mechanism to use:
//
// Background:  Gherkin-level, runs before EVERY scenario, VISIBLE in feature files,
//              meant for domain setup that is PART OF THE STORY (business-relevant context)
//
// Before hook: Code-level, runs before each scenario, NOT visible in Gherkin,
//              meant for infrastructure setup NOT relevant to business stakeholders
//              (e.g., browser state, auth headers, test data cleanup)
//
// BeforeAll:   Runs once per worker, NOT per scenario,
//              meant for EXPENSIVE one-time setup (DB connections, seeded reference data)
//              Use when setup cost is > 100ms and the state is safely SHARED across scenarios

// CORRECT: Background for business-relevant context visible to stakeholders:
// Feature: Shopping cart
//   Background:
//     Given Alice has a registered account
//     And Alice's cart is empty
```

```typescript
// src/support/hooks.ts — Before vs BeforeAll usage pattern
import { Before, BeforeAll, After, AfterAll, setWorldConstructor } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { chromium, Browser, BrowserContext, Page } from 'playwright';

let sharedBrowser: Browser;  // One browser per worker — expensive to start

// BeforeAll: expensive one-time setup (browser launch = ~500ms)
BeforeAll({ name: 'browser:launch' }, async () => {
  sharedBrowser = await chromium.launch({ headless: true });
});

AfterAll({ name: 'browser:close' }, async () => {
  await sharedBrowser?.close();
});

// Before hook: cheap per-scenario context (new context = ~30ms, ensures isolation)
Before({ name: 'context:create' }, async function () {
  this.context = await sharedBrowser.newContext({
    storageState: undefined,  // Clean state for every scenario
  });
  this.page = await this.context.newPage();
});

After({ name: 'context:close' }, async function () {
  // Attach screenshot on failure before closing context
  if (this.result?.status === 'FAILED') {
    const screenshot = await this.page?.screenshot();
    if (screenshot) {
      await this.attach(screenshot, 'image/png');
    }
  }
  await this.context?.close();
});
```

**[community] `Background` steps that perform database writes violate scenario isolation when running in parallel**: Each Cucumber.js parallel worker runs in a separate process, so `Background` steps execute once per scenario per worker. If two workers both execute a `Background` that inserts a user with the same email (`Given a user with email "test@example.com" exists`), the second insert throws a unique-constraint violation. The correct pattern: use random or worker-indexed identifiers in `Background` steps that write data (`"test-worker-#{process.env.CUCUMBER_WORKER_ID}@example.com"`), or use idempotent upsert operations. [community]

---

### Pattern 11 — Step Definition Naming Convention: Verb-First, Business Domain, No UI Verbs

A concrete naming convention for step definitions that eliminates the most common source of
step proliferation: multiple near-identical steps for the same business action written by
different team members.

The official Cucumber anti-patterns guide and "better Gherkin" documentation both emphasize
domain language, but neither specifies a naming convention for the steps themselves. This
pattern closes that gap.

```typescript
// ANTI-PATTERN: UI-verb steps that proliferate and are hard to share
// (each member writes a slightly different version)
// "I click the 'Submit' button"
// "I press the Submit button"
// "I tap Submit"
// "I select Submit from the form"

// CORRECT PATTERN: business-verb steps that describe the action's business meaning:
// VERB: business domain verb (buy, submit, cancel, approve, reject, refund)
// SUBJECT: domain entity (order, account, subscription, invoice)
// QUALIFIER: optional specifics as {string} or {int} parameters

// Convention:
// Given: "[entity] [state descriptor]" — e.g., "an order with [status]"
// When:  "[actor] [business action] [object]" — e.g., "the buyer cancels the order"
// Then:  "[observable outcome] [should/has/is] [value]" — e.g., "the order status should be"

import { Given, When, Then } from '../world';

// Given — state setup using domain entity language:
Given('an order {string} is in {string} status', async ({ fixtures }, orderId, status) => {
  await fixtures.createOrder({ id: orderId, status });
});

// When — business action using domain verbs:
When('the buyer cancels the order {string}', async ({ page }, orderId: string) => {
  await page.goto(`/orders/${orderId}`);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel Order' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('dialog').getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm Cancellation' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toContainText('Order cancelled');
});

// Then — observable outcome using domain state language:
Then(
  'the order {string} status should be {string}',
  async ({ request }, orderId: string, expectedStatus: string) => {
    const resp = await request.get(`/api/orders/${orderId}`);
    const order = await resp.json();
    expect(order.status).toBe(expectedStatus);
  }
);
```

**[community] Step proliferation is the single most common cause of BDD suite abandonment at scale**: Teams that do not enforce a naming convention accumulate 3-5 variations of every common step within 6 months. The variations are rarely obviously duplicates — `"I click the submit button"` vs `"I press Submit"` vs `"I activate the submit action"` — so they all pass linting. The only sustainable remediation is a naming convention enforced at Three Amigos sessions (verbal review of proposed step names before writing the feature file) and at PR review (check new step text against the existing step registry). Automated orphan detection catches dead steps; naming conventions prevent duplicate living ones. [community]

---

### Pattern 12 — BDD Scenario Tagging Taxonomy for Multi-Speed CI Pipelines

A consistent tag taxonomy enables multi-speed CI pipelines where fast feedback runs in
pre-commit hooks and full regression runs in merge gates — without duplicating feature files
or maintaining separate test suites.

```gherkin
# features/checkout/payment.feature
# Tag taxonomy:
# @smoke      — critical path, runs in <60s, executes on every commit
# @regression — full suite, runs on PR + nightly, includes edge cases
# @slow       — tests requiring >30s (data migration, bulk operations)
# @wip        — in development, never runs in CI (tagged on scenario, not feature)
# @manual     — human-only: cognitive, visual, exploratory verification
# @api        — API-layer scenarios, no browser needed
# @ui         — browser-required scenarios
# @flaky      — known intermittent; quarantined, tracked, not blocking

@regression @ui
Feature: Payment processing

  @smoke
  Scenario: Successful credit card payment
    Given Alice has items in her cart worth $45.00
    When she pays with a valid Visa card
    Then her order should be confirmed
    And she should receive a confirmation email

  @regression
  Scenario: Payment rejected for expired card
    Given Alice has items in her cart worth $45.00
    When she pays with an expired Visa card
    Then her payment should be declined
    And she should see the error "Your card has expired"

  @slow @regression
  Scenario: Bulk order payment with 500 line items
    Given Alice has 500 items in her cart
    When she pays with a valid Visa card
    Then her order should be confirmed within 10 seconds

  @wip
  Scenario: Split payment across two cards
    Given Alice has items worth $100 in her cart
    When she pays $50 from card A and $50 from card B
    Then both cards should be charged successfully
```

```bash
# CI pipeline tag-based execution:

# Pre-commit hook (fast, critical path only):
npx cucumber-js --tags "@smoke and not @wip" --profile smoke

# PR merge gate (full non-slow regression):
npx cucumber-js --tags "@regression and not @slow and not @wip" --profile ci

# Nightly full suite (all non-wip, including slow):
npx cucumber-js --tags "not @wip" --profile ci --parallel 8

# Quarantined flaky (monitored, non-blocking):
npx cucumber-js --tags "@flaky" --profile ci 2>&1 | tee reports/flaky-$(date +%F).log
```

**[community] `@wip` scenarios that stay tagged for more than 2 sprints become permanent dead weight**: The `@wip` tag is an escape hatch intended for scenarios that are in active development. Teams that use `@wip` as a long-term quarantine mechanism for broken or deferred scenarios end up with a growing dark matter of untested behavior. Enforce a `@wip` time-box: any scenario tagged `@wip` for more than 14 days triggers a backlog item to either complete it or delete it. The easiest enforcement is a CI step that fails if any `@wip` scenario's Git blame is older than 14 days. [community]

---

### Pattern 13 — `@cucumber/cucumber-expressions` Async Transformer: Domain Object Hydration

A step parameter that requires an async lookup (database query, API call, feature flag check)
cannot use the synchronous `transformer` function in `defineParameterType`. The `transformer`
option accepts a function returning a `Promise`, enabling full async domain object hydration
directly in the parameter type definition.

```typescript
// src/support/parameter-types.ts — async transformer for domain object hydration
import { defineParameterType } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { prisma } from '../db/client';

// Define a domain parameter type that loads a full Order from DB by ID
// Usage in steps: Given the order {order} is in processing
//                 When I cancel the order {order}
defineParameterType({
  name: 'order',
  // Matches UUID format or short IDs like "ORD-12345"
  regexp: /ORD-\d{5}|[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}/,
  transformer: async (id: string) => {
    // Async is fully supported — transformer returns Promise<Order>
    const order = await prisma.order.findUnique({
      where: { id },
      include: { items: true, customer: true },
    });
    if (!order) {
      throw new Error(
        `Order "${id}" not found. Did you create it in a Given step first?`
      );
    }
    return order;
  },
  useForSnippets: false,  // Don't generate snippets for complex types
});

// Define a parameter type for Money values — parses "$45.00" into { amount, currency }
defineParameterType({
  name: 'money',
  regexp: /\$(\d+\.\d{2})/,
  transformer: (matched: string) => {
    const amount = parseFloat(matched.replace('$', ''));
    return { amount, currency: 'USD' };
  },
});
```

```typescript
// src/steps/orders/cancellation.steps.ts — using async parameter types
import { Given, When, Then } from '../world';
import type { Order } from '@prisma/client';

// The {order} parameter is automatically hydrated from the DB via the async transformer:
Given('the order {order} is in {string} status', async (_, order: Order, expectedStatus: string) => {
  expect(order.status).toBe(expectedStatus);
});

When('a customer cancels the order {order}', async ({ page }, order: Order) => {
  await page.goto(`/orders/${order.id}`);
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Cancel Order' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('dialog').getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm' }).click();
});

Then('the order {order} should have status {string}', async (_, order: Order, expected: string) => {
  const refreshed = await prisma.order.findUniqueOrThrow({ where: { id: order.id } });
  expect(refreshed.status).toBe(expected);
});
```

**[community] Async parameter transformers run before the step function body — failures appear as "undefined step" errors in some reporters**: When an async transformer throws (e.g., the order does not exist), the error is thrown during argument binding, not inside the step function. Some reporters log this as "Step definition not found" or show a cryptic "undefined" error rather than the actual thrown message. The workaround: catch in the transformer and re-throw with a clear message that identifies the parameter name and expected format, as shown in the example above. The Cucumber.js team tracks this reporting gap in their issue tracker. [community]

---

### Pattern 14 — BDD Scenario Pruning: Removing Low-Value Scenarios Without Losing Coverage

BDD suites accumulated over years develop "scenario bloat" — a large number of scenarios that
test the same behavior from slightly different angles. Regular pruning sessions improve
execution time and reduce maintenance burden without sacrificing coverage.

**The pruning criteria (from Cucumber.io's better-gherkin guidance and community practice):**

1. **Duplicate scenarios**: Two scenarios that produce the same executable outcome — keep the
   one with more descriptive Gherkin, delete the other.
2. **Happy-path scenarios made redundant by Scenario Outline**: If a `Scenario Outline` row
   covers the same case as a standalone `Scenario`, delete the standalone.
3. **Implementation-detail scenarios**: Scenarios asserting internal state (database records,
   log entries, queue messages) rather than observable user outcomes — migrate to unit tests.
4. **Superseded behavior**: Scenarios for removed features or changed business rules — delete
   them, they make the living documentation a lie.

```typescript
// scripts/audit-scenarios.ts — detect scenario duplication candidates
// Run: npx ts-node scripts/audit-scenarios.ts
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';
import { glob } from 'glob';

// Normalizes a scenario title for fuzzy similarity detection
function normalizeTitle(title: string): string {
  return title
    .toLowerCase()
    .replace(/["'`]/g, '')           // Remove quotes
    .replace(/\b(the|a|an|my|i|am|is|are|be)\b/g, '')  // Remove articles/copula
    .replace(/\s+/g, ' ')
    .trim();
}

async function auditScenarios() {
  const featureFiles = await glob('features/**/*.feature');
  const scenarioTitles: Map<string, string[]> = new Map();  // normalized → [file:line, ...]

  for (const file of featureFiles) {
    const content = fs.readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
    const lines = content.split('\n');
    lines.forEach((line, idx) => {
      const match = line.match(/^\s*(Scenario|Scenario Outline):\s*(.+)/);
      if (match) {
        const normalized = normalizeTitle(match[2]);
        const existing = scenarioTitles.get(normalized) ?? [];
        scenarioTitles.set(normalized, [...existing, `${file}:${idx + 1}`]);
      }
    });
  }

  console.log('\n[Duplicate Scenario Candidates]');
  let dupeCount = 0;
  for (const [normalized, locations] of scenarioTitles) {
    if (locations.length > 1) {
      console.warn(`  POSSIBLE DUPLICATE: "${normalized}"`);
      locations.forEach(loc => console.warn(`    → ${loc}`));
      dupeCount++;
    }
  }
  console.log(dupeCount > 0
    ? `\n${dupeCount} duplicate candidate(s) found — review manually before deleting.`
    : '\nNo duplicate scenarios detected.'
  );
}

auditScenarios().catch(console.error);
```

**[community] Pruning sessions are more effective when led by the product owner, not the QA engineer**: The product owner knows which scenarios represent behavior that is still in production and still matters to users. QA engineers tend to keep scenarios "just in case" and developers tend to delete too aggressively. The correct process: schedule a 30-minute scenario audit with the product owner every quarter, go through the candidate list from the audit script, and make deletion decisions collaboratively. Each deleted scenario should have a comment in the git commit body explaining the pruning rationale — it prevents "why did we delete this?" questions in future reviews. [community]

---

### Pattern 15 — Gherkin `*` (Asterisk) Keyword for List-Style Steps

The `*` keyword in Gherkin acts as a wildcard for any step type (Given/When/Then/And/But)
and is most useful in Background and setup steps where a list of preconditions reads more
naturally as bullet items than as repetitive `And` chains.

```gherkin
# features/inventory/stock-management.feature
Feature: Inventory stock management

  Background:
    # Using * for list-style precondition blocks — reads as a bulleted list
    * the warehouse "WH-01" has 100 units of "widget-a" in stock
    * the warehouse "WH-01" has 50 units of "widget-b" in stock
    * the warehouse "WH-02" has 200 units of "widget-a" in stock
    * all automated restocking rules are disabled for this test

  Scenario: Transfer stock between warehouses
    When 30 units of "widget-a" are transferred from "WH-01" to "WH-02"
    Then "WH-01" should have 70 units of "widget-a"
    And "WH-02" should have 230 units of "widget-a"

  Scenario Outline: Low stock alerts trigger at correct thresholds
    Given "WH-01" has <current_stock> units of "widget-a"
    When the stock manager checks for low-stock alerts
    Then a low-stock alert <should_alert> be triggered for "widget-a"

    Examples:
      | current_stock | should_alert |
      | 11            | should not   |
      | 10            | should       |
      | 5             | should       |
      | 0             | should       |
```

```typescript
// src/steps/inventory/stock.steps.ts — step definitions for * wildcard steps
import { Given, When, Then } from '../world';

// The * keyword maps to Given/When/Then/And/But depending on position in the scenario.
// For Background * steps, they are treated as Given steps by Cucumber's parser.
// Use the same Given() binding — no special handler needed for *:
Given(
  'the warehouse {string} has {int} units of {string} in stock',
  async ({ fixtures }, warehouseId: string, qty: number, sku: string) => {
    await fixtures.setStock({ warehouseId, sku, quantity: qty });
  }
);

Given(
  'all automated restocking rules are disabled for this test',
  async ({ fixtures }) => {
    await fixtures.disableRestockingRules();
  }
);

When(
  '{int} units of {string} are transferred from {string} to {string}',
  async ({ request }, qty: number, sku: string, from: string, to: string) => {
    const resp = await request.post('/api/inventory/transfer', {
      data: { sku, quantity: qty, fromWarehouse: from, toWarehouse: to },
    });
    expect(resp.status()).toBe(200);
  }
);

Then(
  '{string} should have {int} units of {string}',
  async ({ request }, warehouseId: string, expectedQty: number, sku: string) => {
    const resp = await request.get(`/api/inventory/${warehouseId}/${sku}`);
    const stock = await resp.json();
    expect(stock.quantity).toBe(expectedQty);
  }
);
```

**[community] `*` keyword in non-Background positions reduces readability when Given/When/Then have distinct meanings**: The `*` keyword is readable in Background (list of preconditions) and in purely procedural setup sequences where the keyword type is obvious from context. In the Scenario body, replacing `Given/When/Then` with `*` removes the linguistic signal that tells readers whether a step is context (Given), action (When), or assertion (Then). Reserve `*` for lists of parallel preconditions in Background. Use the named keywords in Scenario bodies — the extra verbosity is a feature, not overhead. [community]

---

### Pattern 16 — BDD World Object: Lazy-Init Pattern for Expensive Resources

The Cucumber.js World object is instantiated once per scenario. World constructor functions
must be synchronous in Cucumber.js, but step definitions often need async-initialized resources
(database connections, authenticated API clients, browser pages). The **lazy-init pattern**
defers async setup to the first step that needs the resource, avoiding `BeforeAll` coupling.

```typescript
// src/support/world.ts — lazy-init World pattern for expensive resources
import { World, IWorldOptions, setWorldConstructor } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { APIRequestContext, Browser, Page } from 'playwright';

export class AppWorld extends World {
  // Lazy-init: resources initialized on first access, not in constructor
  private _apiClient?: APIRequestContext;
  private _page?: Page;
  private _authToken?: string;

  constructor(options: IWorldOptions) {
    super(options);
    // Constructor MUST be synchronous — only assign cheap values here
    this._authToken = process.env.TEST_AUTH_TOKEN;
  }

  // Lazy getter — initializes on first access in a step definition
  async getApiClient(): Promise<APIRequestContext> {
    if (!this._apiClient) {
      const { request } = await import('@playwright/test');
      this._apiClient = await request.newContext({
        baseURL: process.env.API_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
        extraHTTPHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${this._authToken}` },
      });
    }
    return this._apiClient;
  }

  async getPage(): Promise<Page> {
    if (!this._page) {
      // Access shared browser from global (set in BeforeAll)
      const browser = (global as any).__sharedBrowser as Browser;
      const context = await browser.newContext();
      this._page = await context.newPage();
    }
    return this._page;
  }

  // Cleanup called by After hook — only disposes what was actually initialized
  async cleanup(): Promise<void> {
    await this._apiClient?.dispose();
    await this._page?.context()?.close();
  }
}

setWorldConstructor(AppWorld);

// src/support/hooks.ts — After hook calls cleanup on AppWorld
import { After } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

After({ name: 'world:cleanup' }, async function (this: AppWorld) {
  if (this.result?.status === 'FAILED') {
    const page = await this.getPage().catch(() => null);
    if (page) {
      await this.attach(await page.screenshot(), 'image/png');
    }
  }
  await this.cleanup();
});
```

**[community] Lazy-init World resources that are never cleaned up silently accumulate across scenarios in `--parallel` runs and exhaust file descriptors**: The Cucumber.js World is garbage-collected after each scenario, but resources like `APIRequestContext` and browser contexts hold OS-level handles (TCP connections, file descriptors) that are not released by GC. In `--parallel 8` runs with 200 scenarios, a World that creates but never disposes an `APIRequestContext` per scenario opens ~200 TCP connections. This causes `EMFILE` or `ECONNRESET` errors in the last 20-30% of scenarios. Always call `dispose()`/`close()` in an `After` hook, even for resources that are "just an HTTP client". [community]

---

### Pattern 17 — Cucumber.js v12.8.0 `externalise` Plugin Option: Cross-Package Step Validation

In addition to its use in step sharing (Pattern 1), the v12.8.0 `externalise` option has a
validation use case: it allows a plugin to fail the build if any scenario step text does not
match an available step definition. This is the "undefined steps fail CI" pattern, but
implemented at the plugin level rather than relying on Cucumber's default behavior.

```typescript
// src/support/strict-step-validation-plugin.ts
// Ensures ALL steps in feature files are defined — fails CI on missing definitions
import type { Plugin } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

interface StrictValidationOptions {
  /** If true, treat 'pending' steps as failures (default: false) */
  pendingAsFail?: boolean;
}

export const strictStepValidationPlugin: Plugin<StrictValidationOptions> = (
  { on },
  options = {}
) => {
  const pendingAsFail = options.pendingAsFail ?? false;
  const undefinedSteps: string[] = [];
  const pendingSteps: string[] = [];

  on('test-step-finished', ({ testStep, result, pickle }) => {
    if (result.status === 'UNDEFINED') {
      undefinedSteps.push(`  [UNDEFINED] ${pickle.name}: "${testStep.text}"`);
    }
    if (pendingAsFail && result.status === 'PENDING') {
      pendingSteps.push(`  [PENDING] ${pickle.name}: "${testStep.text}"`);
    }
  });

  on('test-run-finished', ({ success }) => {
    const failures = [...undefinedSteps, ...pendingSteps];
    if (failures.length > 0) {
      console.error('\n[strict-step-validation] Unimplemented steps found:');
      failures.forEach(f => console.error(f));
      console.error(
        `\n${failures.length} unimplemented step(s). Add step definitions before merging.\n`
      );
      process.exitCode = 1;
    }
  });
};
```

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — strict validation in CI, permissive in local development
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';
import { strictStepValidationPlugin } from './src/support/strict-step-validation-plugin';

const isCI = process.env.CI === 'true';

export default {
  paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
  require: ['src/support/world.ts', 'src/steps/**/*.steps.ts'],
  tags: 'not @wip',
  plugins: isCI
    ? [[strictStepValidationPlugin, { pendingAsFail: true }]]
    : [],  // Local dev: undefined steps show as yellow, don't block
} satisfies Partial<IConfiguration>;
```

**[community] Cucumber.js already fails with exit code 1 on undefined steps by default — the plugin adds value only when you need step-level reporting without a full test run**: The built-in `--dry-run` flag surfaces undefined steps without executing any scenarios. The plugin pattern adds value when you want to (a) surface undefined steps alongside other test results in CI, (b) distinguish undefined (no binding at all) from pending (binding exists but throws `'pending'`) for different team workflows, or (c) send undefined step counts to a metrics dashboard. For most teams, `npx cucumber-js --dry-run` in a pre-commit hook is sufficient. [community]
