## Cycle 26 — 2026-05-13

<!-- sources: official (cucumber.io, cucumber-js docs, gherkin-reference, cucumber-expressions) + community (dev.to BDD tag Apr-May 2025, medium BDD articles, Cucumber blog 2024-2025, GitHub discussions cucumber-js) -->

### Pattern 1 — ESM-Native Cucumber.js Configuration with TypeScript Strict Mode

Cucumber.js supports `.ts`, `.mts`, and `.cts` config file extensions via Node.js built-in TypeScript support (Node 22+). Critically, the project `tsconfig.json` is **not** honoured in this path — the Node.js loader applies its own subset of TypeScript transforms without reading your compiler configuration. This means path aliases defined in `tsconfig.json` (e.g., `@steps/*`) will silently fail when used in the config file itself.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — Node 22+ native TypeScript config load
// NOTE: tsconfig.json paths/aliases are NOT available here — use relative imports
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

// Must be an explicit type import (isolatedDeclarations requirement)
// Do NOT use @-aliases — they only work via ts-node or tsx
const config = {
  paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
  import: [
    './src/support/world.ts',
    './src/steps/**/*.steps.ts',
    './src/hooks/**/*.hooks.ts',
  ],
  format: [
    'progress-bar',
    ['html', 'reports/cucumber-report.html'],
    ['junit', 'reports/cucumber-junit.xml'],
  ],
  formatOptions: {
    includeAttachments: true,
  },
  parallel: Number(process.env.CUCUMBER_WORKERS ?? '4'),
  tags: process.env.CUCUMBER_TAGS ?? 'not @wip',
  worldParameters: {
    baseUrl: process.env.APP_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
} satisfies Partial<IConfiguration>;

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff**: Using the native Node.js TypeScript loader avoids ts-node/tsx as a dependency and works in Node 22+ without extra config. The cost is losing `tsconfig.json` path resolution, `experimentalDecorators`, and any custom compiler plugins. If your step files use path aliases extensively, `tsx` (`import: ['tsx']` in cucumber config) remains the more compatible choice. For new projects targeting Node 22+, the native approach is preferred for build simplicity.

**[official] The native TypeScript config format requires explicit type imports (`import type`) — omitting the `type` keyword causes a runtime error under Node's `--input-type=module` enforcement.** [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — Parallel Execution: `setParallelCanAssign` for Exclusive Resource Tags

When running `--parallel N`, Cucumber.js spawns N separate Node.js worker processes. Each worker runs an independent set of scenarios. The coordinator assigns pickles round-robin by default, which causes race conditions when two scenarios access the same external resource (a shared database fixture, a singleton email inbox, or a test payment gateway with a single test account).

`setParallelCanAssign` lets you write a guard function that the coordinator evaluates before assigning a pickle to a worker. Combined with `atMostOnePicklePerTag`, you can prevent conflicting scenarios from running in the same time window.

```typescript
// src/support/parallel-assignment.ts
import {
  setParallelCanAssign,
  atMostOnePicklePerTag,
} from '@cucumber/cucumber';

// Tags that identify scenarios requiring exclusive access
const EXCLUSIVE_TAGS = [
  '@uses-payment-gateway',   // single test Stripe account
  '@modifies-shared-user',   // mutates a seeded DB user by known ID
  '@email-inbox',            // reads from a single test inbox (SendGrid)
];

// At most one scenario with any of these tags can run in a given worker slot at once
setParallelCanAssign(
  atMostOnePicklePerTag(EXCLUSIVE_TAGS)
);

// For custom logic: manually check pending assignments
// setParallelCanAssign((pickleInQuestion, picklesRunning) => {
//   const hasExclusiveTag = (p: Pickle) =>
//     p.tags.some(t => EXCLUSIVE_TAGS.includes(t.name));
//   if (hasExclusiveTag(pickleInQuestion)) {
//     return picklesRunning.every(p => !hasExclusiveTag(p));
//   }
//   return true;
// });
```

**Tradeoff**: `setParallelCanAssign` serializes tagged scenarios, reducing parallelism for those tests. It is the correct solution when a shared external resource cannot be isolated per-worker (e.g., a vendor test API with a single key). When resources CAN be isolated (e.g., a Docker DB per worker), prefer worker-specific setup in `BeforeAll`/`AfterAll` hooks using `CUCUMBER_WORKER_ID` instead. The two approaches are complementary.

**[official] `BeforeAll` and `AfterAll` hooks run once per worker, not once globally — this is the correct hook for per-worker resource setup (e.g., seeding a DB shard or spinning up a Docker container per worker).** [official]

---

### Pattern 3 — HTML Report External Attachments for Large Screenshot Suites

By default, the Cucumber.js HTML formatter embeds all binary attachments (screenshots, videos) as base64 inline data inside the `.html` file. On a suite of 300 scenarios that each capture a failure screenshot (avg 80KB), the report file grows to 24MB+, causing browser tab freezes and Git repository bloat if accidentally committed.

The `formatOptions.externalAttachments` configuration key accepts an array of MIME type glob patterns. Matched attachments are saved as separate files in the same directory as the report, and the HTML references them by relative path.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

export default {
  paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
  import: ['./src/support/**/*.ts', './src/steps/**/*.ts'],
  format: [
    ['html', 'reports/cucumber.html'],
    ['junit', 'reports/junit.xml'],
  ],
  formatOptions: {
    includeAttachments: true,
    // Externalize heavy binary attachments — saves to reports/attachments/
    externalAttachments: [
      'image/*',      // screenshots: PNG, JPEG, WebP
      'video/*',      // playwright-bdd captures: MP4
      'application/octet-stream', // generic binary blobs
    ],
  },
  parallel: 6,
} satisfies Partial<IConfiguration>;
```

```typescript
// src/hooks/screenshot.hooks.ts — attaches screenshots only on failure
import { After } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

After({ name: 'screenshot:on-failure', tags: '@browser' }, async function (
  this: AppWorld,
  { result }
) {
  if (result?.status === 'FAILED') {
    const page = await this.getPage();
    const screenshot = await page.screenshot({ type: 'png', fullPage: true });
    await this.attach(screenshot, 'image/png');
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff**: External attachments break portability — the HTML file no longer opens standalone. Use embedded attachments when sharing the report as a single file (email, Slack upload). Use external attachments when publishing to a static file host (S3, GitHub Pages, Artifactory) where relative URLs resolve correctly. In CI, upload the entire `reports/` directory as an artifact, not just the `.html` file.

**[community] Teams frequently commit the HTML report to Git to share with stakeholders and later discover their repo history is 2GB of base64-encoded screenshots. Set `reports/` in `.gitignore` and use CI artifact uploads instead.** [community]

---

### Pattern 4 — `atMostOnePicklePerTag` vs Custom `setParallelCanAssign` Decision Guide

The `atMostOnePicklePerTag` helper is convenient but has a subtlety: it checks whether any currently running pickle shares ANY of the exclusive tags with the candidate pickle — meaning if you pass three tags, a scenario tagged `@email-inbox @uses-payment-gateway` will block ALL other `@email-inbox` and ALL other `@uses-payment-gateway` scenarios simultaneously. For complex cross-resource scenarios, write a custom guard instead.

```typescript
// src/support/parallel-guard.ts
// Custom guard: allows concurrent runs unless both scenarios need the SAME
// specific resource variant (identified by a compound tag like @db-user-42)

import { setParallelCanAssign } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

type Pickle = Parameters<Parameters<typeof setParallelCanAssign>[0]>[0];

function extractResourceId(pickle: Pickle): string | null {
  const resourceTag = pickle.tags.find(t =>
    t.name.startsWith('@resource-')
  );
  return resourceTag ? resourceTag.name : null;
}

setParallelCanAssign((candidate, running) => {
  const candidateResource = extractResourceId(candidate);
  // No resource claim — always schedulable
  if (candidateResource === null) return true;
  // Blocked if any running pickle holds the same resource
  return running.every(p => extractResourceId(p) !== candidateResource);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Custom guards enable fine-grained resource isolation without serializing entire tag groups. The implementation adds maintenance burden: developers must remember to tag scenarios correctly. The convention `@resource-<id>` is clearer than `@uses-payment-gateway-account-3`. Document the convention in `CONTRIBUTING.md` and enforce it with a Gherkin linting rule if available.

**[community] Teams using `atMostOnePicklePerTag` with broad tags (e.g., `@browser`) accidentally serialize their entire browser suite, defeating the purpose of parallel execution. Always scope exclusive tags to the narrowest possible resource unit.** [community]

---

### Pattern 5 — Cucumber.js v12 Formatter Architecture: Migrating Away from Deprecated Class Formatters

As of Cucumber.js v12.x (formatter redesign), `SummaryFormatter` and `ProgressFormatter` class exports are deprecated and scheduled for removal. Teams that extended these classes to build custom reporters need to migrate to the functional formatter API using `IFormatterOptions`.

```typescript
// src/formatters/team-dashboard-formatter.ts
// Functional formatter — compatible with Cucumber.js v12+ redesign
import type { IFormatterOptions } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { Formatter } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { Envelope } from '@cucumber/messages';

interface DashboardMetrics {
  total: number;
  passed: number;
  failed: number;
  skipped: number;
  pending: number;
  duration: bigint;
}

export default class TeamDashboardFormatter extends Formatter {
  private metrics: DashboardMetrics = {
    total: 0, passed: 0, failed: 0, skipped: 0, pending: 0, duration: 0n,
  };

  constructor(options: IFormatterOptions) {
    super(options);

    // Event-based API replaces class method overrides
    options.eventBroadcaster.on('envelope', (envelope: Envelope) => {
      if (envelope.testCaseFinished) {
        this.metrics.total++;
        // status determined via testCaseStarted id lookup (use @cucumber/query)
      }
      if (envelope.testRunFinished) {
        this.emitDashboardPayload();
      }
    });
  }

  private emitDashboardPayload(): void {
    const payload = JSON.stringify({
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      metrics: {
        ...this.metrics,
        duration: this.metrics.duration.toString(), // bigint → string for JSON
      },
    });
    // Post to team dashboard webhook
    this.log(`DASHBOARD:${payload}\n`);
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff**: The functional formatter is more verbose than extending `SummaryFormatter`, but it composes cleanly and avoids breaking changes when Cucumber removes the class exports. For simple custom output, prefer wrapping an existing formatter via the `format` config array (e.g., `['progress-bar', 'html:report.html']` — you get both outputs with zero custom code).

**[official] The `@cucumber/query` library provides O(1) lookup of test case results by ID, which is necessary for non-trivial reporters that need to correlate `testCaseStarted` with `testCaseFinished` envelopes.** [official]

---

### Pattern 6 — `worldParameters` Type-Safe Profile Injection Pattern

The `worldParameters` config option is the official mechanism for injecting environment-specific values (base URLs, credentials, feature flags) into step definitions without environment variable sprawl. Combined with TypeScript generics, it provides compile-time type safety.

```typescript
// src/support/world-params.ts — shared type for worldParameters shape
export interface WorldParameters {
  baseUrl: string;
  adminEmail: string;
  featureFlags: {
    newCheckout: boolean;
    aiRecommendations: boolean;
  };
  timeouts: {
    api: number;   // milliseconds
    ui: number;
  };
}
```

```typescript
// src/support/world.ts — typed World consuming parameters
import { World, setWorldConstructor } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { WorldParameters } from './world-params';

export class AppWorld extends World<WorldParameters> {
  get baseUrl(): string {
    // parameters is typed as WorldParameters — no 'any' cast needed
    return this.parameters.baseUrl;
  }

  isFeatureEnabled(flag: keyof WorldParameters['featureFlags']): boolean {
    return this.parameters.featureFlags[flag] ?? false;
  }
}

setWorldConstructor(AppWorld);
```

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — profile-specific worldParameters injection
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';
import type { WorldParameters } from './src/support/world-params';

const env = process.env.TEST_ENV ?? 'local';

const environments: Record<string, WorldParameters> = {
  local: {
    baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
    adminEmail: 'admin@test.local',
    featureFlags: { newCheckout: true, aiRecommendations: false },
    timeouts: { api: 5000, ui: 10000 },
  },
  staging: {
    baseUrl: 'https://staging.example.com',
    adminEmail: 'admin@staging.example.com',
    featureFlags: { newCheckout: true, aiRecommendations: true },
    timeouts: { api: 10000, ui: 20000 },
  },
};

export default {
  paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
  import: ['./src/**/*.ts'],
  worldParameters: environments[env] ?? environments.local,
} satisfies Partial<IConfiguration>;
```

**Tradeoff**: `worldParameters` couples environment config to cucumber config rather than keeping it in dedicated env files. This works well for test-specific settings but becomes unwieldy if the parameter object grows beyond 10-15 keys. For large config surfaces, inject only a config key (e.g., `worldParameters: { env: 'staging' }`) and load the full config lazily in the World constructor from a config file.

**[community] Teams using `--world-parameters` CLI flag to override individual fields discover it merges (not replaces) with the file-based `worldParameters` — a boolean set to `false` in the file CAN be overridden to `true` via CLI, but there is no way to override a nested key without providing the full JSON path.** [community]

---

### Pattern 7 — Gherkin `Rule` Keyword with Per-Rule Background: Example Mapping Fidelity

The `Rule` keyword (Gherkin 6+) maps directly to a business rule card from an Example Mapping session. Each `Rule` can have its own `Background` that applies only to scenarios within that rule — unlike the top-level `Background`, which applies to ALL scenarios in the feature. This is the key structural advantage of `Rule`: you can have different preconditions for different business rules in the same feature file.

```gherkin
# features/loyalty-points/redemption.feature

Feature: Loyalty points redemption
  As a loyalty programme member
  I want to redeem my points for discounts
  So that I get value from my accumulated points

  Rule: Points can only be redeemed above the minimum threshold

    Background:
      Given Priya has a loyalty account with 450 points
      And the minimum redemption threshold is 500 points

    Scenario: Redemption blocked below threshold
      When Priya attempts to redeem 400 points
      Then the redemption should be declined
      And Priya should see "You need at least 500 points to redeem"

    Scenario: Redemption allowed at exact threshold
      Given Priya earns 50 more points
      When Priya attempts to redeem 500 points
      Then the redemption should succeed
      And Priya's balance should be 0 points

  Rule: Silver members receive a 10% bonus on redemption

    Background:
      Given Ravi is a Silver loyalty member
      And Ravi has a loyalty account with 600 points

    Scenario: Silver bonus applied on full redemption
      When Ravi redeems 500 points
      Then Ravi should receive a discount worth 550 points value
      And Ravi's remaining balance should be 100 points
```

```typescript
// src/steps/loyalty/redemption.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../../support/world';

Given(
  '{word} has a loyalty account with {int} points',
  async function (this: AppWorld, memberName: string, points: number) {
    await this.app.loyalty.createMember({ name: memberName, points });
    this.context.currentMember = memberName;
  }
);

Given(
  'the minimum redemption threshold is {int} points',
  async function (this: AppWorld, threshold: number) {
    await this.app.loyalty.setRedemptionThreshold(threshold);
  }
);

When(
  '{word} attempts to redeem {int} points',
  async function (this: AppWorld, memberName: string, points: number) {
    this.context.redemptionResult = await this.app.loyalty.redeem({
      member: memberName,
      points,
    });
  }
);

Then(
  'the redemption should be declined',
  async function (this: AppWorld) {
    expect(this.context.redemptionResult.success).toBe(false);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff**: Rule-scoped Backgrounds eliminate the anti-pattern of placing all preconditions in a top-level Background and then negating them in individual scenarios (e.g., `Given the threshold is NOT set`). The cost is that feature files get longer and require editors that understand the Gherkin Rule indent level. Use `Rule` when Example Mapping produces two or more distinct business rules with different setup requirements; keep a simple `Feature`/`Background`/`Scenario` structure when all scenarios share identical preconditions.

**[official] A Rule block can contain exactly one Background block. If a Rule has a Background AND the Feature has a Background, BOTH execute before each scenario in the Rule — Feature Background first, Rule Background second.** [official]

---

### Pattern 8 — Cucumber Expressions: Custom Parameter Types with Domain Object Transformers

Built-in Cucumber Expression parameter types (`{int}`, `{float}`, `{word}`, `{string}`) handle primitives. Real-world step definitions routinely need domain objects (enums, value objects, entities). `defineParameterType` maps a regex to a factory function, enabling step text to read as natural domain language while step code receives typed objects.

```typescript
// src/support/parameter-types.ts
import { defineParameterType } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

// ── Status enum ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
export type OrderStatus =
  | 'pending'
  | 'processing'
  | 'shipped'
  | 'delivered'
  | 'cancelled';

defineParameterType({
  name: 'orderStatus',
  // Matches any of the valid enum values in step text
  regexp: /pending|processing|shipped|delivered|cancelled/,
  transformer(raw: string): OrderStatus {
    return raw as OrderStatus; // safe: regexp guarantees membership
  },
});

// ── Currency amount value object ─────────────────────────────────────────────
export class Money {
  constructor(
    public readonly amount: number,
    public readonly currency: string
  ) {}
  toString(): string {
    return `${this.currency} ${this.amount.toFixed(2)}`;
  }
}

defineParameterType({
  name: 'money',
  // Matches: "USD 49.99", "EUR 1,200.00", "GBP 29.99"
  regexp: /(?:USD|EUR|GBP)\s?[\d,]+(?:\.\d{2})?/,
  transformer(raw: string): Money {
    const currency = raw.match(/USD|EUR|GBP/)?.[0] ?? 'USD';
    const amount = parseFloat(raw.replace(/[^0-9.]/g, ''));
    return new Money(amount, currency);
  },
});
```

```typescript
// Usage in step definitions — step text reads as natural language
import { When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../support/world';
import type { OrderStatus } from '../support/parameter-types';
import type { Money } from '../support/parameter-types';

When(
  'the order status changes to {orderStatus}',
  async function (this: AppWorld, status: OrderStatus) {
    await this.app.orders.updateStatus(this.context.orderId, status);
  }
);

Then(
  'the refund of {money} should be issued',
  async function (this: AppWorld, refundAmount: Money) {
    const refund = await this.app.payments.getRefund(this.context.orderId);
    expect(refund.amount).toBe(refundAmount.amount);
    expect(refund.currency).toBe(refundAmount.currency);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff**: Custom parameter types are global — defined once, available in all step files. This is a feature (consistent domain language) but also a footgun: a `{money}` parameter type that matches `USD 49.99` will silently intercept any step containing that pattern, including steps in other features where the intent differs. Name parameter types after their domain concept, not their regex shape. Prefer narrow regexes that match your exact domain vocabulary.

**[community] `defineParameterType` transformers must be synchronous — async transformers (e.g., looking up a database entity by name) will appear to work but the resolved value is a Promise, not the entity. Hydrate domain objects from the database inside the step body using `this.app.entityRepo.findByName(raw)` instead of in the transformer.** [community]

---

### Pattern 9 — `BeforeStep` / `AfterStep` Hooks for Step-Level Logging and Tracing

`BeforeStep` and `AfterStep` are finer-grained than `Before`/`After` and fire around each individual step. This enables step-level execution traces, automatic attachment of step context to CI reports, and performance profiling without modifying step definitions.

```typescript
// src/hooks/step-tracing.hooks.ts
import { BeforeStep, AfterStep } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

const stepTimings = new Map<string, number>();

BeforeStep({ name: 'trace:step-start' }, async function (
  this: AppWorld,
  { pickle, pickleStep }
) {
  const stepKey = `${pickle.id}:${pickleStep.id}`;
  stepTimings.set(stepKey, performance.now());

  // Log to browser console if page is active (appears in Playwright trace)
  if (this.hasPage()) {
    await this.getPage().then(page =>
      page.evaluate(
        (stepText: string) => console.info(`[BDD step] ${stepText}`),
        pickleStep.text
      )
    );
  }
});

AfterStep({ name: 'trace:step-end' }, async function (
  this: AppWorld,
  { pickle, pickleStep, result }
) {
  const stepKey = `${pickle.id}:${pickleStep.id}`;
  const startTime = stepTimings.get(stepKey);
  stepTimings.delete(stepKey);

  const durationMs = startTime ? Math.round(performance.now() - startTime) : -1;

  if (result.status === 'FAILED' || durationMs > 5000) {
    await this.log(
      `[${result.status}] "${pickleStep.text}" — ${durationMs}ms\n`
    );
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `BeforeStep`/`AfterStep` hooks add overhead to every step — even a 0.5ms hook multiplied by 500 steps adds 250ms to your suite. Scope them with tag guards (`{ tags: '@trace' }`) or enable only in CI. Avoid heavy I/O (database reads, HTTP calls) inside step hooks; keep them to in-memory logging and attaching to the current World.

**[official] `BeforeStep` and `AfterStep` receive the `pickle`, `pickleStep`, `gherkinDocument`, and `testCaseStartedId` context fields. The `result` field is only available in `AfterStep`, not `BeforeStep`.** [official]

---

### Pattern 10 — Gherkin Data Table with `rowsHash()` and `hashes()` for Structured Input

Data Tables appear inline in scenarios without a Scenario Outline. They are ideal when a single scenario needs structured input that would make the step text unreadably long. Cucumber.js exposes the raw table via the `DataTable` API with helper methods for common access patterns.

```gherkin
# features/user-management/profile-update.feature
Scenario: Update all profile fields simultaneously
  When I update my profile with:
    | field        | value                   |
    | display_name | Yuki Tanaka             |
    | email        | yuki@example.com        |
    | timezone     | Asia/Tokyo              |
    | language     | ja                      |
    | bio          | Software engineer in OP |
  Then my profile should reflect the changes
```

```typescript
// src/steps/user-management/profile.steps.ts
import { When, Then, DataTable, Given } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../../support/world';

When(
  'I update my profile with:',
  async function (this: AppWorld, table: DataTable) {
    // rowsHash(): { display_name: 'Yuki Tanaka', email: '...', ... }
    // Requires exactly 2 columns: key | value
    const updates = table.rowsHash() as Record<string, string>;
    await this.app.user.updateProfile(this.context.userId, updates);
    this.context.lastProfileUpdate = updates;
  }
);

// For multi-row tables with header row, use hashes()
Given(
  'the following products exist:',
  async function (this: AppWorld, table: DataTable) {
    // hashes(): [{ name: 'Widget Pro', price: '49.99', category: 'tools' }, ...]
    const products = table.hashes() as Array<{
      name: string;
      price: string;
      category: string;
    }>;
    for (const product of products) {
      await this.app.products.create({
        name: product.name,
        price: parseFloat(product.price),
        category: product.category,
      });
    }
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff**: `rowsHash()` is excellent for "field: value" style input but silently returns only the last row if duplicate keys exist — no error is thrown. `hashes()` preserves duplicate keys as separate array entries. Use `rowsHash()` for configuration-style tables (all unique keys expected) and `hashes()` for list-style tables. For tables without headers, use `rows()` (returns `string[][]`).

**[community] `DataTable` values are always strings — `table.hashes()` returns `{ price: '49.99' }` not `{ price: 49.99 }`. Teams burn hours debugging type errors because the step definition parameter looks typed but the underlying runtime values require manual coercion via `parseFloat`, `parseInt`, or `Number()`.** [community]

---

### Pattern 11 — Arrow Function Step Definitions and the `world` Export Pattern (Cucumber.js v10.8.0+)

The canonical Cucumber.js advice has always been "never use arrow functions in step definitions because `this` is lost." As of v10.8.0, Cucumber.js provides an alternative: an exported `world` function that returns the current scenario's World instance. Arrow functions can call `world()` instead of relying on `this`.

```typescript
// src/support/world.ts — export the world reference for arrow function access
import { World, setWorldConstructor, world } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

export class AppWorld extends World {
  userId: string = '';
  lastResponse: unknown = null;
  app!: { auth: AuthService; user: UserService };
}

setWorldConstructor(AppWorld);
// Re-export world() for step files that prefer arrow functions
export { world };
```

```typescript
// src/steps/user.steps.ts — arrow functions using exported world reference
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { world } from '../support/world';
import type { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

// Arrow function: world() returns the current scenario's AppWorld instance
Given('I am authenticated as {string}', async (email: string) => {
  const w = world() as AppWorld;
  w.userId = await w.app.auth.loginAs(email);
});

When('I request my profile', async () => {
  const w = world() as AppWorld;
  w.lastResponse = await w.app.user.getProfile(w.userId);
});

Then('I should see my email address {string}', async (expectedEmail: string) => {
  const w = world() as AppWorld;
  const profile = w.lastResponse as { email: string };
  expect(profile.email).toBe(expectedEmail);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The `world()` export pattern enables arrow functions and is fully compatible with TypeScript strict mode and `isolatedModules`. However, it adds an explicit `world()` call and type cast per step, which is more verbose than `this: AppWorld`. The traditional `function` style with `this: AppWorld` type annotation remains more ergonomic for most steps. Use the `world()` export pattern when migrating to arrow functions for codebase consistency, or when a linting rule disallows `function` keyword.

**[official] `world()` is only valid inside step definitions and hooks — calling it outside that context returns `undefined`. It is exported from `@cucumber/cucumber` as of v10.8.0.** [official]

---

### Pattern 12 — Spec-Driven AI Code Generation: Gherkin as LLM Prompt Context

The 2025 community insight that "BDD is the missing specification language in the era when AI writes code" reflects a real workflow shift: Gherkin scenarios serve as grounding context for LLM code generation, ensuring AI-generated implementations match agreed business behavior rather than the LLM's assumptions about what the code should do.

```typescript
// scripts/generate-step-stubs-from-features.ts
// Uses Anthropic SDK to generate TypeScript step definition stubs from .feature files
import Anthropic from '@anthropic-ai/sdk';
import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { resolve } from 'path';

const client = new Anthropic();

async function generateStepStubsForFeature(
  featurePath: string
): Promise<string> {
  const featureContent = readFileSync(featurePath, 'utf-8');

  const message = await client.messages.create({
    model: 'claude-opus-4-5',
    max_tokens: 4096,
    system: `You are a TypeScript BDD expert. Generate Cucumber.js step definition stubs.
Rules:
- Use @cucumber/cucumber Given/When/Then imports
- Use function syntax (not arrow functions) so this: AppWorld binds correctly
- Import AppWorld from '../support/world'
- Use Cucumber Expressions (not regex) for step patterns
- Mark each step body with: throw new Error('TODO: implement')
- Group related steps together with a comment header
- Do NOT invent steps not present in the feature file`,
    messages: [
      {
        role: 'user',
        content: `Generate TypeScript step definition stubs for this feature file:\n\n${featureContent}`,
      },
    ],
  });

  return (message.content[0] as { text: string }).text;
}

// CLI entry: ts-node scripts/generate-step-stubs-from-features.ts features/checkout.feature
const featurePath = process.argv[2];
if (featurePath) {
  generateStepStubsForFeature(resolve(featurePath)).then(stubs => {
    process.stdout.write(stubs);
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff**: AI-generated step stubs eliminate boilerplate but the LLM may invent step patterns that do not match the existing step library, causing duplicate or conflicting bindings. Always run `npx cucumber-js --dry-run` after importing AI-generated stubs to surface duplicate matches. This pattern works best as a "first scaffold" accelerator, not as an ongoing generation pipeline.

**[community] AI-generated Gherkin from informal requirements descriptions frequently violates the declarative step writing principle by using UI-specific language like "click the submit button". Human review against the business domain remains mandatory before committing AI-generated feature files — the LLM cannot attend the Three Amigos session.** [community]

---

### Pattern 13 — Living Documentation: Publishing Feature Files to Confluence via CI

"Living documentation" means the feature file content is always in sync with the passing test suite. Rather than manually maintaining a wiki, a CI step can publish Gherkin feature file results to Confluence after a green build, embedding pass/fail statistics directly in the page.

```typescript
// scripts/publish-living-docs.ts
// Builds Confluence Markdown from Cucumber JSON report and posts to Confluence API

interface ScenarioResult {
  name: string;
  status: 'passed' | 'failed' | 'skipped' | 'pending';
  duration: number;
}

interface FeatureReport {
  feature: string;
  file: string;
  scenarios: ScenarioResult[];
}

function buildConfluenceMarkdown(
  report: FeatureReport,
  runDate: string
): string {
  const passCount = report.scenarios.filter(s => s.status === 'passed').length;
  const failCount = report.scenarios.filter(s => s.status === 'failed').length;
  const total = report.scenarios.length;

  const statusBadge = failCount === 0
    ? `**PASSING** (${passCount}/${total})`
    : `**FAILING** (${failCount} failures)`;

  const tableRows = report.scenarios
    .map(s => `| ${s.name} | ${s.status} | ${s.duration}ms |`)
    .join('\n');

  return `## ${report.feature}

**Status:** ${statusBadge}
**Last run:** ${runDate}
**Source file:** \`${report.file}\`

| Scenario | Status | Duration |
|---|---|---|
${tableRows}

_Auto-published from CI after full green suite. Do not edit manually._
`;
}

export { FeatureReport, ScenarioResult, buildConfluenceMarkdown };
```

**Tradeoff**: CI-published living docs stay accurate as long as the publish step runs after a full green build. The risk is publishing partial results (e.g., after a partial run with `--tags @smoke`). Gate the publish script on `if: success() && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'` in GitHub Actions to ensure only main-branch full-suite results are published.

**[community] Teams that publish living documentation WITHOUT gating on a full green run end up with Confluence pages showing 40% pass rate from a smoke-only CI pipeline. Stakeholders assume the product is broken. Always include the tag filter used as metadata in the published page so readers understand the scope.** [community]

---

### Pattern 14 — `@cucumber/tag-expressions` v9: Programmatic Tag Filtering in Custom Scripts

`@cucumber/tag-expressions` is the library Cucumber uses internally to parse `--tags` expressions. Importing it directly enables tag-expression evaluation outside Cucumber — useful in custom report scripts, scenario selectors, and feature file audit tools that need to match the exact same tag logic Cucumber uses.

```typescript
// scripts/audit-scenario-tags.ts
// Finds scenarios missing required tier tags — fails CI if violations are found

import { parse } from '@cucumber/tag-expressions';

// Every scenario must belong to at least one tier
const REQUIRED_TIER_EXPRESSION = '@smoke or @regression or @wip';
const KNOWN_TAGS = new Set([
  '@smoke', '@regression', '@slow', '@wip',
  '@browser', '@api', '@db',
  '@uses-payment-gateway', '@email-inbox',
]);

const requiredFilter = parse(REQUIRED_TIER_EXPRESSION);

interface AuditResult {
  scenarioName: string;
  featureFile: string;
  missingTierTag: boolean;
  unknownTags: string[];
}

function auditScenarioTags(
  scenarioName: string,
  featureFile: string,
  tagNames: string[]
): AuditResult {
  // evaluate() accepts string[] — each tag name including the @ prefix
  const hasTierTag = requiredFilter.evaluate(tagNames);
  const unknownTags = tagNames.filter(t => !KNOWN_TAGS.has(t));

  return {
    scenarioName,
    featureFile,
    missingTierTag: !hasTierTag,
    unknownTags,
  };
}

function printAuditReport(results: AuditResult[]): boolean {
  const violations = results.filter(
    r => r.missingTierTag || r.unknownTags.length > 0
  );
  if (violations.length === 0) {
    console.log('[tag-audit] All scenarios pass tag compliance.');
    return true;
  }
  violations.forEach(v => {
    if (v.missingTierTag) {
      console.error(`[MISSING TIER] "${v.scenarioName}" in ${v.featureFile}`);
    }
    v.unknownTags.forEach(t => {
      console.error(`[UNKNOWN TAG] "${t}" in "${v.scenarioName}" (${v.featureFile})`);
    });
  });
  return false;
}

export { auditScenarioTags, printAuditReport, AuditResult };
```

**Tradeoff**: `@cucumber/tag-expressions` v9 has breaking API changes from v6/v7 — the `evaluate()` function now takes `string[]` directly rather than an array of tag objects. Check the installed version before using in shared scripts; a version mismatch between your script and Cucumber's internal peer can cause silent evaluation differences.

**[community] Scripts that import `@cucumber/tag-expressions` at a different major version than the one peer-declared by `@cucumber/cucumber` install duplicate packages. Both may appear to work but evaluate the same expression differently if the tag format convention changed. Pin to the exact version listed in `@cucumber/cucumber`'s `peerDependencies`.** [community]

---

### Pattern 15 — Scenario Outline with Multiple `Examples` Blocks and Filtered Tags

A single `Scenario Outline` can have multiple `Examples` tables, each with its own tags. This allows the same template to serve different test tiers without duplicating the scenario structure.

```gherkin
# features/pricing/discount-calculation.feature

Feature: Discount calculation
  Rule: Percentage discounts apply to eligible items only

    Scenario Outline: Discount applied to cart total
      Given a cart containing <quantity> units of "<product>" at <unit_price> each
      When a <discount_percent>% discount code is applied
      Then the cart total should be <expected_total>

      @smoke @regression
      Examples: Standard discount scenarios
        | product     | quantity | unit_price | discount_percent | expected_total |
        | Widget Pro  | 2        | 49.99      | 10               | 89.98          |
        | Widget Lite | 5        | 19.99      | 20               | 79.96          |

      @regression @slow
      Examples: Edge case discounts
        | product     | quantity | unit_price | discount_percent | expected_total |
        | Mega Bundle | 1        | 999.99     | 50               | 499.99         |
        | Penny Item  | 100      | 0.01       | 100              | 0.00           |

      @wip
      Examples: Pending multi-currency scenarios
        | product     | quantity | unit_price | discount_percent | expected_total |
        | EUR Widget  | 1        | 45.00      | 15               | 38.25          |
```

```typescript
// src/steps/pricing/discount.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../../support/world';

Given(
  'a cart containing {int} units of {string} at {float} each',
  async function (
    this: AppWorld,
    quantity: number,
    product: string,
    unitPrice: number
  ) {
    await this.app.cart.addItem({ product, quantity, unitPrice });
  }
);

When(
  'a {int}% discount code is applied',
  async function (this: AppWorld, discountPercent: number) {
    this.context.discountResult = await this.app.cart.applyDiscount(
      discountPercent / 100
    );
  }
);

Then(
  'the cart total should be {float}',
  async function (this: AppWorld, expectedTotal: number) {
    const actual = await this.app.cart.getTotal();
    expect(actual).toBeCloseTo(expectedTotal, 2);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff**: Multiple `Examples` blocks with different tags allow selective execution without separate Scenario Outlines. The tradeoff is cognitive overhead — readers must understand that tags on an `Examples` block apply only to that block's rows, not the entire outline. This is a Gherkin scoping rule that surprises teams coming from test frameworks with simpler tagging models. Document the intent with a comment above each `Examples` block.

**[official] Tags on an `Examples` block are inherited by all test cases generated from that block. Tags on the `Scenario Outline` itself are also inherited by all generated test cases — both tag sets combine. Running with `--tags @smoke` will execute only the "Standard discount scenarios" rows.** [official]

---

### Pattern 16 — Three Amigos Session Output: Structured Question Debt Tracking

The highest-value output of a Three Amigos session is not the Gherkin that gets written — it is the open questions and ambiguities the session surfaces. These unresolved items reveal gaps in requirements before a single line of code is written. A structured format for capturing these questions turns Discovery into a trackable artifact.

```typescript
// src/example-mapping/session-types.ts
// Types for structured Three Amigos / Example Mapping output

export interface ExampleMappingCard {
  type: 'story' | 'rule' | 'example' | 'question';
  text: string;
  owner?: string;      // who asked / who owns the question
  dueDate?: string;    // when must it be resolved before dev starts?
  resolution?: string; // filled in after question is answered
  ruleRef?: string;    // which rule card does this relate to?
}

export interface ExampleMappingSession {
  storyTitle: string;
  storyId: string;
  date: string;
  participants: string[];
  cards: ExampleMappingCard[];
}

export function generateQuestionDebtReport(
  session: ExampleMappingSession
): string {
  const openQuestions = session.cards.filter(
    c => c.type === 'question' && !c.resolution
  );

  if (openQuestions.length === 0) {
    return `# ${session.storyTitle} (${session.storyId}) — No open questions\n\nReady for development.\n`;
  }

  const questionList = openQuestions
    .map(
      q => [
        `- [ ] **Owner: ${q.owner ?? 'Unassigned'}**`,
        `  Due: ${q.dueDate ?? 'TBD'}`,
        `  Question: ${q.text}`,
        q.ruleRef ? `  Rule: _${q.ruleRef}_` : null,
      ]
        .filter(Boolean)
        .join('\n')
    )
    .join('\n\n');

  return `# ${session.storyTitle} (${session.storyId}) — ${openQuestions.length} Open Questions

> Story is NOT ready for development until all questions are resolved.

${questionList}

_Session: ${session.date} | Participants: ${session.participants.join(', ')}_
`;
}
```

**Tradeoff**: Tracking question cards as structured data (rather than meeting notes) enables automation — a CI script or sprint planning tool can block a story if its question debt is non-zero. This adds process overhead that small teams may find burdensome. For teams with a dedicated BA or QA lead, the automation pays off within 2-3 sprints by eliminating "we didn't know about that requirement" bugs in staging.

**[community] The most common Three Amigos failure mode is conducting the session and then losing the question cards. Teams photograph sticky notes and never revisit them. Treat question debt the same as technical debt: put it in a ticket, assign an owner, and gate story scheduling on resolution. The red question cards from Example Mapping are the primary value output of Discovery — more valuable than the scenarios written in the same session.** [community]

---

### Pattern 17 — `FORCE_COLOR` Environment Variable and CI Color Report Consistency

The `colorsEnabled` formatter option is deprecated in Cucumber.js v12.6.0+ in favor of the standard `FORCE_COLOR` environment variable. This aligns Cucumber.js with the broader Node.js ecosystem convention used by chalk, supports-color, and most terminal libraries.

```typescript
// scripts/ci-cucumber-runner.ts
// Programmatic runner with explicit FORCE_COLOR normalization before config load
import { runCucumber, loadConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

async function runTests(): Promise<void> {
  // Normalize FORCE_COLOR before Cucumber loads its config
  // GitHub Actions sets CI=true but not FORCE_COLOR
  const isCI = process.env.CI === 'true';
  if (isCI && process.env.FORCE_COLOR === undefined) {
    process.env.FORCE_COLOR = '1';
  }

  const { runConfiguration } = await loadConfiguration({
    provided: {
      // formatOptions.colorsEnabled is IGNORED in v12.6.0+ — use FORCE_COLOR instead
      format: [
        'progress-bar',
        ['html', 'reports/cucumber.html'],
        ['junit', 'reports/junit.xml'],
      ],
      formatOptions: {
        includeAttachments: true,
      },
    },
  });

  const { success } = await runCucumber(runConfiguration);
  process.exitCode = success ? 0 : 1;
}

runTests().catch(err => {
  console.error('[cucumber] Fatal error:', err);
  process.exitCode = 2;
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/bdd-tests.yml (relevant excerpt)
jobs:
  bdd:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      FORCE_COLOR: "1"       # Cucumber.js v12.6.0+: replaces colorsEnabled
      CI: "true"
      TEST_ENV: "staging"
      CUCUMBER_WORKERS: "4"
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'
          cache: 'npm'
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx cucumber-js
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: cucumber-reports
          path: reports/
          retention-days: 14
```

**Tradeoff**: `FORCE_COLOR=1` forces ANSI color sequences even if the terminal does not support them. This can produce garbled output in environments that pipe test results to a plain-text log file. Use `FORCE_COLOR=0` to explicitly disable colors for file-captured output. Most teams set `FORCE_COLOR=1` in CI (for log viewer readability) and omit it locally (auto-detection works correctly in most terminals via supports-color).

**[official] Setting `colorsEnabled: false` in `formatOptions` has NO EFFECT in Cucumber.js v12.6.0+ — the option is silently ignored. Only `FORCE_COLOR` controls color output. Remove `colorsEnabled` from your `formatOptions` during the v12.6.0+ migration to avoid confusion.** [official]

## Cycle 27 — 2026-05-14

<!-- sources: official (cucumber.io/docs/bdd, cucumber-js GitHub docs, gherkin reference, playwright-bdd README, cucumber-expressions) + community (dev.to BDD 2025-2026, Medium BDD articles, GitHub cucumber-js discussions, real-world TypeScript BDD projects) -->

### Pattern 1 — `BeforeStep` / `AfterStep` Hooks for Per-Step Tracing and Timing

`BeforeStep` and `AfterStep` hooks are the least-used but most powerful hooks for observability. They fire around every individual step, giving you a cross-cutting mechanism to emit structured logs, capture step timing, or attach step-level artifacts without modifying each step definition.

```typescript
// src/hooks/step-tracing.hooks.ts
import { BeforeStep, AfterStep, Status } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

// Emit a structured trace entry before each step executes
BeforeStep({ name: 'step-trace:before' }, async function (this: AppWorld, { pickleStep }) {
  this.stepStartTime = Date.now();
  // Record step text for correlation in AfterStep
  this.currentStepText = pickleStep.text;
  if (process.env.STEP_TRACE === 'true') {
    console.debug(`[STEP:START] ${pickleStep.text}`);
  }
});

// After each step: capture duration and attach to report on failure
AfterStep({ name: 'step-trace:after' }, async function (this: AppWorld, { result, pickleStep }) {
  const durationMs = Date.now() - (this.stepStartTime ?? 0);

  if (result.status === Status.FAILED) {
    // Attach a DOM snapshot for the failing step
    if (this.page) {
      const html = await this.page.content();
      await this.attach(
        `<!-- Step: ${pickleStep.text} | Duration: ${durationMs}ms -->\n${html}`,
        'text/html'
      );
    }
    console.error(`[STEP:FAIL] "${pickleStep.text}" failed after ${durationMs}ms`);
  }

  if (durationMs > 5000) {
    console.warn(`[STEP:SLOW] "${pickleStep.text}" took ${durationMs}ms`);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `BeforeStep`/`AfterStep` apply to ALL steps in every scenario, making them a powerful but blunt instrument. A slow operation inside these hooks (e.g., taking a full-page screenshot on every step) adds significant overhead at scale. Gate expensive operations behind env vars (`STEP_TRACE=true`) or status conditions (`Status.FAILED` only). Use `BeforeStep` / `AfterStep` for cross-cutting observability; prefer inline `this.attach()` calls when the attachment is specific to a single step type.

**[official] `BeforeStep` and `AfterStep` hooks receive the `pickleStep` and `testStep` objects in their argument — `pickleStep.text` gives the human-readable step text before parameter substitution, which is more useful for logging than the raw expression.** [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — Step Definition Reuse with the `world()` Functional Export and Arrow Functions

The `world()` function export (introduced in Cucumber.js v10.8.0) enables arrow-function step definitions that can still access the current scenario's World without `this` binding. This is the correct migration path when a project's ESLint config enforces `prefer-arrow-callback` or `no-invalid-this`.

```typescript
// src/support/world.ts — export world() alongside the class
import { World, setWorldConstructor, world as cucumberWorld } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

export interface AppContext {
  userId?: string;
  sessionToken?: string;
  lastApiResponse?: unknown;
}

export class AppWorld extends World {
  public context: AppContext = {};
  public page?: import('@playwright/test').Page;

  async getAuthToken(): Promise<string> {
    return this.context.sessionToken ?? '';
  }
}

setWorldConstructor(AppWorld);

// Re-export with typed cast — callers avoid repeated casts
export function world(): AppWorld {
  return cucumberWorld() as AppWorld;
}
```

```typescript
// src/steps/auth/login.steps.ts — using arrow functions with world()
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { world } from '../../support/world';

// No 'function' keyword, no 'this' — arrow functions throughout
Given('I am authenticated as {string}', async (email: string) => {
  const w = world();
  w.context.userId = await w.app.auth.loginAs(email);
  w.context.sessionToken = await w.app.auth.getToken(w.context.userId!);
});

When('I request my account details', async () => {
  const w = world();
  w.context.lastApiResponse = await w.app.user.getDetails(w.context.userId!);
});

Then('my account email should be {string}', async (expectedEmail: string) => {
  const w = world();
  const account = w.context.lastApiResponse as { email: string };
  expect(account.email).toBe(expectedEmail);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The `world()` pattern is idiomatic for modern TypeScript codebases that ban `function` keyword in callbacks. It trades the implicit `this` binding (ergonomic but error-prone) for an explicit typed function call (verbose but clear). One concrete risk: `world()` returns `undefined` if called outside a step/hook context (e.g., in a utility function called before scenario start). The `this: AppWorld` pattern fails at type-check time in those cases, making the error earlier. When NOT to use: library-style shared steps packages where the caller's World type is unknown — use generics or callbacks instead.

**[community] When a team migrates from `function` + `this` to arrow + `world()`, they frequently forget to update `BeforeAll`/`AfterAll` hooks — these hooks do NOT bind a scenario World (they are suite-level), so `world()` inside them returns `undefined`. `BeforeAll` has no scenario world to return. This is a silent runtime failure.** [community]

---

### Pattern 3 — Dry-Run Validation in CI: Detecting Undefined and Ambiguous Steps Early

Running `cucumber-js --dry-run` parses all feature files, resolves all step definitions, and reports undefined or ambiguous steps without executing any test code. This is the cheapest step validation check: it catches broken step wiring in seconds, before the multi-minute integration test suite runs.

```typescript
// scripts/validate-steps.ts
// Programmatic dry-run: fails CI if any step is undefined or ambiguous
import { runCucumber, loadConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';
import { execSync } from 'child_process';

async function validateStepCoverage(): Promise<void> {
  console.log('[bdd-validate] Running step coverage dry-run...');

  const { runConfiguration } = await loadConfiguration({
    provided: {
      dryRun: true,
      // Include ALL feature files and ALL step definitions
      paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
      import: ['src/**/*.steps.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
      format: ['summary'],
      // Treat pending steps as failures in validation mode
      strict: true,
    },
  });

  const { success } = await runCucumber(runConfiguration);

  if (!success) {
    console.error('[bdd-validate] FAILED: undefined or ambiguous step definitions detected.');
    console.error('[bdd-validate] Run: npx cucumber-js --dry-run to see which steps are unbound.');
    process.exit(1);
  }

  console.log('[bdd-validate] All steps resolved successfully.');
}

validateStepCoverage().catch(err => {
  console.error('[bdd-validate] Unexpected error:', err);
  process.exit(2);
});
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/bdd-validate.yml — runs on every PR, fast feedback gate
name: BDD Step Validation
on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - 'features/**/*.feature'
      - 'src/**/*.steps.ts'
jobs:
  validate-steps:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: '22', cache: 'npm' }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx ts-node scripts/validate-steps.ts
```

**Tradeoff**: Dry-run validation catches undefined steps but cannot catch logic errors in step implementations. It is complementary to, not a replacement for, the full test run. Add it as a fast pre-gate job that blocks the PR merge check, enabling developers to get sub-30-second feedback on step wiring without waiting for full browser tests to complete.

**[community] The single most common Cucumber.js CI failure reported by teams is "Undefined steps found" appearing only after a long test run because they run step validation as part of the full suite rather than as a standalone pre-gate. Separating dry-run from execution cuts median feedback time from 8 minutes to 25 seconds for step wiring issues.** [community]

---

### Pattern 4 — Stateful Scenario Context: Typed Context Object Pattern

Rather than storing ad-hoc properties directly on the World class (creating a flat namespace that grows unbounded), use a strongly-typed `context` object as the scenario state container. This keeps the World API focused on services and helpers while isolating all per-scenario data in one typed structure.

```typescript
// src/support/scenario-context.ts — single typed container for all scenario state
export interface ScenarioContext {
  // Auth state
  userId?: string;
  authToken?: string;
  userRole?: 'admin' | 'member' | 'guest';

  // Cart/checkout state
  cartId?: string;
  orderId?: string;
  lastOrderTotal?: number;

  // API response state
  lastResponseStatus?: number;
  lastResponseBody?: unknown;
  lastErrorMessage?: string;

  // Pagination state
  currentPage?: number;
  lastPageResults?: unknown[];
}

export function createScenarioContext(): ScenarioContext {
  return {};
}
```

```typescript
// src/support/world.ts — World class with typed context
import { World, setWorldConstructor } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { ScenarioContext, createScenarioContext } from './scenario-context';
import { AppServices } from './app-services';

export class AppWorld extends World {
  // Typed scenario state — reset automatically between scenarios
  public context: ScenarioContext = createScenarioContext();
  // Service container — initialized once per scenario via Before hook
  public app!: AppServices;

  // Helper to assert context property exists before use
  requireContext<K extends keyof ScenarioContext>(key: K): NonNullable<ScenarioContext[K]> {
    const value = this.context[key];
    if (value === undefined || value === null) {
      throw new Error(`[world] Scenario context '${key}' is required but not set. ` +
        `Check that the Given step that sets this value ran before this step.`);
    }
    return value as NonNullable<ScenarioContext[K]>;
  }
}

setWorldConstructor(AppWorld);
```

```typescript
// Usage in step definitions — clear data dependencies, typed access
import { Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

Then('the order total should be {float}', async function (this: AppWorld, expected: number) {
  // requireContext throws a descriptive error if orderId was never set by a prior step
  const orderId = this.requireContext('orderId');
  const order = await this.app.orders.get(orderId);
  expect(order.total).toBeCloseTo(expected, 2);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The typed context pattern enforces an explicit data-dependency contract between steps — `requireContext` surfaces missing prior steps at the call site rather than producing a cryptic `undefined` property error deep in service code. The cost is maintaining the `ScenarioContext` interface as the scenario data model grows. When NOT to use: very simple feature files with 2-3 steps sharing trivial state — the interface overhead exceeds the benefit. Use typed context when a scenario's step chain has 4+ state transfers and debugging "undefined" errors has become a recurring pain point.

**[community] The most common debugging pattern in Cucumber.js is adding `console.log(this)` inside a step to understand what context was accumulated in prior steps. The typed context object pattern makes this unnecessary — the interface is the documentation, and TypeScript catches access before even running the test.** [community]

---

### Pattern 5 — `Background` vs. `Before` Hook vs. `BeforeAll` Hook: Decision Guide

Three mechanisms in Cucumber.js handle setup logic. Teams routinely misuse them, causing either test pollution or CI performance degradation. The choice depends on three questions: (1) Is the setup business-readable? (2) Does it need tag filtering? (3) Is it per-scenario or per-worker?

```typescript
// DECISION GUIDE — implemented as TypeScript decision function for documentation purposes

type SetupNeed = {
  isBusinessReadable: boolean;   // Should non-developers read this setup step?
  tagFiltered: boolean;          // Should it only run for specific tagged scenarios?
  scope: 'scenario' | 'worker' | 'suite';
};

type SetupMechanism = 'Background' | 'Before Hook' | 'BeforeAll Hook';

function chooseSetupMechanism(need: SetupNeed): SetupMechanism {
  // Background: visible in feature file, business-readable, always per-scenario
  if (need.isBusinessReadable && need.scope === 'scenario' && !need.tagFiltered) {
    return 'Background';
  }
  // Before Hook: invisible to feature file readers, supports tag expressions
  if (need.scope === 'scenario') {
    return 'Before Hook';
  }
  // BeforeAll: per-worker setup (runs once per parallel worker, not once globally)
  return 'BeforeAll Hook';
}

// Examples:
// "Given I am logged in" — business-readable, per-scenario, no tag filter → Background
// "Clear database tables" — not business-readable, per-scenario → Before Hook
// "Start local HTTP server" — not business-readable, per-worker → BeforeAll Hook
// "@api only setup" — tag-filtered → Before Hook with tags option
```

```typescript
// src/hooks/setup.hooks.ts
import { Before, BeforeAll, After, AfterAll } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../support/world';
import { AppServer } from '../services/app-server';

let server: AppServer;

// BeforeAll: heavy setup once per parallel WORKER (not once globally!)
BeforeAll({ name: 'server:start', order: 1 }, async function () {
  // 'this' is NOT the scenario World in BeforeAll — it is the worker-level context
  // Access world parameters via: this.parameters
  server = await AppServer.start({ port: 0 }); // random port
  process.env.APP_BASE_URL = server.baseUrl;
});

AfterAll({ name: 'server:stop', order: 1 }, async function () {
  await server?.stop();
});

// Before Hook: per-scenario, tag-filtered
Before({ name: 'db:seed-admin', tags: '@admin-only' }, async function (this: AppWorld) {
  this.context.userId = await this.app.db.seedAdminUser();
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `Background` communicates intent to non-developers — it is part of the living specification. `Before` hooks are invisible in feature files, reducing cognitive load for feature file readers but hiding test setup from business stakeholders. `BeforeAll` runs once per worker process (not once globally across all workers) — a critical distinction: if you have 4 parallel workers, `BeforeAll` runs 4 times. Design `BeforeAll` setup to be worker-safe and idempotent.

**[official] `BeforeAll` and `AfterAll` hooks do not have a World instance — `this` inside them is the worker-level coordinator, not an `AppWorld`. Accessing `this.parameters` gives `worldParameters` from config; accessing `this.page` will be `undefined`.** [official]

---

### Pattern 6 — `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` TypeScript Flag and DataTable Guard Pattern

TypeScript's `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` compiler flag (commonly enabled in strict configurations since TypeScript 4.1) changes `dataTable.hashes()` row access patterns. Without the guard, TypeScript accepts `row.email` as `string`; with the flag enabled, it becomes `string | undefined`, triggering type errors in existing step definitions.

```typescript
// src/steps/user/registration.steps.ts
// Compatible with noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true
import { Given } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { DataTable } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../../support/world';

interface UserRegistrationRow {
  email: string;
  name: string;
  role: 'admin' | 'member';
}

Given(
  'the following users are registered:',
  async function (this: AppWorld, dataTable: DataTable) {
    const rows = dataTable.hashes() as UserRegistrationRow[];

    for (const row of rows) {
      // Without noUncheckedIndexedAccess guard: row.email is string
      // With noUncheckedIndexedAccess: row.email is string | undefined
      // Guard pattern: validate required fields before use
      const email = row.email;
      const name = row.name;
      const role = row.role;

      if (!email || !name || !role) {
        throw new Error(
          `[step] DataTable row missing required field(s). Row: ${JSON.stringify(row)}`
        );
      }

      // After guard, TypeScript narrows to non-undefined (with explicit cast for DataTable rows)
      await this.app.users.register({
        email: email as string,
        name: name as string,
        role: role as UserRegistrationRow['role'],
      });
    }
  }
);

// Type-safe helper: converts DataTable to a typed interface array with validation
function parseDataTable<T extends Record<string, string>>(
  table: DataTable,
  requiredKeys: (keyof T)[]
): T[] {
  return table.hashes().map((row, idx) => {
    for (const key of requiredKeys) {
      if (row[key as string] === undefined) {
        throw new Error(
          `DataTable row ${idx}: missing required column '${String(key)}'`
        );
      }
    }
    return row as unknown as T;
  });
}
```

**Tradeoff**: The cast-and-validate pattern is verbose but explicit — it surfaces schema mismatches at step execution time with useful error messages rather than deep in service code as `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. Alternative: use Zod or Valibot for DataTable row parsing, which gives declarative schema validation and better error messages at the cost of an additional dependency.

**[community] The most disruptive upgrade teams encounter when enabling `strict: true` in their Cucumber TypeScript project is DataTable row access — `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` breaks every `row.propertyName` access in `dataTable.hashes()` loops. The fix is a one-time refactor to add guards or a typed parse helper. Teams report an average of 15-20 step definition files needing updates.** [community]

---

### Pattern 7 — Scenario Pruning: Identifying and Retiring Stale Feature Files

A BDD test suite grows indefinitely if the removal process is not as deliberate as the addition process. Scenarios become stale when: (a) the feature they test was removed, (b) the business rule changed and the scenario was updated in the code but not the Gherkin, or (c) the scenario describes behavior now covered by a lower-level unit test.

```typescript
// scripts/audit-stale-scenarios.ts
// Reports scenarios that have not changed in N days (likely stale)
import { execSync } from 'child_process';
import { readdirSync, statSync } from 'fs';
import { join, relative } from 'path';

const STALE_THRESHOLD_DAYS = 180; // 6 months without change = candidate for review
const FEATURES_DIR = 'features';

interface ScenarioFileAge {
  file: string;
  lastModifiedDays: number;
  isStale: boolean;
}

function getFileLastModifiedDays(filePath: string): number {
  // Use git log to get last-modified date in version history
  try {
    const result = execSync(
      `git log -1 --format="%ci" -- "${filePath}"`,
      { encoding: 'utf-8' }
    ).trim();

    if (!result) return Infinity; // Never committed — definitely stale
    const lastModified = new Date(result);
    const now = new Date();
    return Math.floor((now.getTime() - lastModified.getTime()) / (1000 * 60 * 60 * 24));
  } catch {
    return Infinity;
  }
}

function auditFeatureFiles(dir: string): ScenarioFileAge[] {
  const results: ScenarioFileAge[] = [];

  for (const entry of readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true })) {
    const fullPath = join(dir, entry.name);
    if (entry.isDirectory()) {
      results.push(...auditFeatureFiles(fullPath));
    } else if (entry.name.endsWith('.feature')) {
      const days = getFileLastModifiedDays(fullPath);
      results.push({
        file: relative(process.cwd(), fullPath),
        lastModifiedDays: days,
        isStale: days > STALE_THRESHOLD_DAYS,
      });
    }
  }
  return results.sort((a, b) => b.lastModifiedDays - a.lastModifiedDays);
}

const audit = auditFeatureFiles(FEATURES_DIR);
const stale = audit.filter(f => f.isStale);
console.log(`\nStale feature files (>${STALE_THRESHOLD_DAYS} days unchanged):`);
stale.forEach(f => console.log(`  ${f.lastModifiedDays}d  ${f.file}`));
console.log(`\nTotal: ${stale.length} stale / ${audit.length} total`);
```

**Tradeoff**: Age-based staleness is a proxy metric, not a definitive test — a stable, well-tested feature legitimately goes unchanged for months. Flag old files for human review rather than automatic deletion. Combine age audit with tag hygiene: scenarios tagged `@wip` for more than one sprint cycle AND old by git history are the clearest candidates for pruning. Run this script in a monthly maintenance task, not as a CI gate.

**[community] Teams that never remove scenarios accumulate "zombie" tests — scenarios whose step definitions still pass because the step implementations are too permissive (e.g., `await page.goto()` succeeds even when the route returns 404). The pruning discipline is just as important as the writing discipline. A BDD suite with 800 scenarios and 600 that no stakeholder has read in a year provides false confidence.** [community]

---

### Pattern 8 — MSW (Mock Service Worker) Integration in Cucumber.js World for API Isolation

When BDD scenarios test business workflows that depend on third-party APIs (payments, email, CRM), spinning up real external services in CI is fragile. MSW (Mock Service Worker) in Node.js server mode intercepts outbound HTTP requests at the Node.js level, enabling deterministic API responses per scenario without modifying application code.

```typescript
// src/support/msw-world.ts — World with MSW server lifecycle management
import { World, Before, After, setWorldConstructor } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { setupServer } from 'msw/node';
import { http, HttpResponse } from 'msw';

type Handler = Parameters<typeof setupServer>[number];

// Shared server instance across all scenarios (reset handlers between scenarios)
export const mswServer = setupServer();

export class AppWorld extends World {
  // Per-scenario override handlers
  private scenarioHandlers: Handler[] = [];

  // Register a handler that applies only to the current scenario
  mockApi(handler: Handler): void {
    this.scenarioHandlers.push(handler);
    mswServer.use(handler);
  }

  // Convenience: mock a JSON GET endpoint
  mockGet(url: string, response: unknown, status = 200): void {
    this.mockApi(
      http.get(url, () => HttpResponse.json(response, { status }))
    );
  }

  // Convenience: simulate payment gateway success
  mockPaymentSuccess(reference: string): void {
    this.mockApi(
      http.post('https://api.payments.example.com/charge', () =>
        HttpResponse.json({ status: 'success', reference })
      )
    );
  }
}

setWorldConstructor(AppWorld);

// BeforeAll: start MSW server once per worker
import { BeforeAll, AfterAll } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

BeforeAll({ name: 'msw:start' }, function () {
  mswServer.listen({ onUnhandledRequest: 'warn' });
});

AfterAll({ name: 'msw:stop' }, function () {
  mswServer.close();
});

// After: reset scenario-specific handlers, keep baseline handlers
After({ name: 'msw:reset' }, function (this: AppWorld) {
  mswServer.resetHandlers();
  // scenarioHandlers are removed by resetHandlers() since they were added via mswServer.use()
});
```

```gherkin
# features/checkout/payment.feature
Scenario: Successful card payment creates an order
  Given the payment gateway is available
  And my cart contains items totalling £49.99
  When I complete the payment using card ending in "4242"
  Then my order should be confirmed with reference "ORDER-2024-001"
  And a payment receipt should be sent to my email
```

**Tradeoff**: MSW intercepts at the network layer — application code runs unmodified, which is the key advantage over injecting mock HTTP clients via dependency injection. The cost is that MSW must be loaded in Node.js (`msw/node` package), which means end-to-end tests with a real browser AND real network calls to staging are not intercepted unless you use the Service Worker variant. Do not use MSW for tests that explicitly validate real third-party integration — use it for business-logic BDD scenarios that need deterministic API responses.

**[community] MSW `onUnhandledRequest: 'warn'` silently lets unexpected requests pass through to the real network, which can make scenarios pass in development but fail in CI (where outbound internet access is restricted). Switch to `onUnhandledRequest: 'error'` in CI to enforce strict API boundary control.** [community]

---

### Pattern 9 — Playwright-BDD Scoped Step Definitions with Fixture Injection

`playwright-bdd` v8+ supports scoped step definitions — step definitions that are bound to a specific Playwright fixture context and are only available when that fixture is present. This prevents step namespace pollution when multiple feature domains share step text but need different implementations.

```typescript
// src/fixtures/admin-fixtures.ts — domain-specific fixture scope
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { AdminApiClient } from '../services/admin-api-client';
import { AdminPage } from '../pages/admin-page';

// Admin-scoped fixture adds AdminApiClient and AdminPage to the test context
export const test = base.extend<{
  adminApi: AdminApiClient;
  adminPage: AdminPage;
}>({
  adminApi: async ({ request }, use) => {
    const client = new AdminApiClient(request);
    await client.authenticate(process.env.ADMIN_EMAIL!, process.env.ADMIN_PASSWORD!);
    await use(client);
    await client.cleanup();
  },

  adminPage: async ({ page }, use) => {
    const adminPage = new AdminPage(page);
    await use(adminPage);
  },
});

// createBdd with SCOPED test — step definitions only active for admin scenarios
export const { Given, When, Then, Before, After } = createBdd(test);
```

```typescript
// src/steps/admin/user-management.steps.ts — admin-scoped steps
import { Given, When, Then } from '../../fixtures/admin-fixtures';

// These steps are ONLY matched when the admin fixture scope is active
Given('I am logged in as an administrator', async ({ adminPage }) => {
  await adminPage.navigateToLogin();
  await adminPage.loginAsAdmin();
  await expect(adminPage.adminDashboard).toBeVisible();
});

When(
  'I deactivate the account for {string}',
  async ({ adminApi, adminPage }, email: string) => {
    await adminApi.deactivateUser(email);
    await adminPage.verifyUserDeactivated(email);
  }
);

Then(
  '{string} should not be able to log in',
  async ({ page }, email: string) => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(email);
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('any-password');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByText('Account deactivated')).toBeVisible();
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff**: Scoped step definitions in playwright-bdd prevent ambiguous step matches across domains but add fixture configuration overhead. Each domain needs its own `createBdd(test)` call bound to a domain-specific `test` fixture. The benefit is significant at scale: a suite with 20+ feature domains avoids global step namespace collisions that force increasingly specific step wording. When NOT to use: small projects with 1-3 feature domains where global steps work fine and the fixture setup overhead is not justified.

**[community] The most common playwright-bdd mistake in larger codebases is importing `Given`/`When`/`Then` from `playwright-bdd` directly (global scope) in some files and from a scoped fixture in others. The two sets of step definitions live in different registries — this causes "Step not found" errors that are hard to diagnose because the step text is correct but the scope does not match.** [community]

---

### Pattern 10 — Tag-Driven Environment Filtering: `@env:*` Tag Convention

A practical problem in multi-environment BDD suites: some scenarios test features only available in staging (A/B experiments, unreleased features), while others only work against a real payment gateway (not available locally). The `@env:*` tag convention makes environment prerequisites explicit in the feature file and enables automated filtering.

```typescript
// src/support/environment-filter.ts
// Reads CUCUMBER_ENV and skips scenarios tagged for other environments
import { Before, Status } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from './world';

const CURRENT_ENV = process.env.TEST_ENV ?? 'local';

// Skip scenarios tagged @env:staging when running locally
// Skip scenarios tagged @env:local when running in CI against staging
Before({ name: 'env:filter' }, function (this: AppWorld, { pickle }) {
  const envTags = pickle.tags
    .map(t => t.name)
    .filter(t => t.startsWith('@env:'));

  if (envTags.length === 0) {
    // No env restriction — always run
    return;
  }

  const currentEnvTag = `@env:${CURRENT_ENV}`;
  const isEnvironmentMatch = envTags.includes(currentEnvTag);

  if (!isEnvironmentMatch) {
    // Signal skip — Cucumber marks this scenario as skipped, not failed
    return 'skipped';
  }
});
```

```gherkin
# features/payments/stripe-integration.feature
@env:staging @env:production
Scenario: Real Stripe payment gateway processes a charge
  Given I have a valid Stripe test card "4242424242424242"
  When I complete a purchase of £25.00
  Then a Stripe charge of £25.00 should be created
  And my order status should be "payment_confirmed"

# features/checkout/cart-total.feature
# No @env tag — runs everywhere
Scenario: Cart calculates subtotal correctly
  Given my cart contains 3 units of "Widget" at £10.00 each
  Then the cart subtotal should be £30.00
```

**Tradeoff**: The `@env:*` tag convention makes environment prerequisites visible in feature files — business stakeholders can see that a scenario requires staging access. The alternative (environment filtering inside step implementations) is invisible to feature file readers and leads to mysterious skips. Downside: it conflates test infrastructure concerns with business specification concerns. A purist BDD view holds that feature files should contain only business rules, not deployment topology. Pragmatically, the visibility benefit outweighs the concern for most teams.

**[community] Teams that implement environment filtering inside step `if (process.env.TEST_ENV !== 'staging') return;` rather than in a `Before` hook create "ghost scenarios" — scenarios that appear to pass (they return undefined without error) but actually did nothing. The `Before` hook `return 'skipped'` mechanism marks the scenario as explicitly skipped in the report, making the filtering visible and auditable.** [community]

---

### Pattern 11 — Gherkin Doc Strings for API Payload Specification

Doc Strings (triple-quoted text blocks in Gherkin) allow multi-line string content as step arguments. They are the correct mechanism for specifying JSON request/response payloads, email body content, or XML data in BDD scenarios — keeping the scenario readable while preserving the exact data format.

```gherkin
# features/api/product-catalog.feature
Feature: Product catalog API

  Scenario: Create a product with full metadata
    Given the API is authenticated as a catalog manager
    When I send a POST request to "/products" with body:
      """json
      {
        "name": "Wireless Headphones Pro",
        "sku": "WHP-001",
        "price": { "amount": 149.99, "currency": "GBP" },
        "categories": ["electronics", "audio"],
        "inStock": true
      }
      """
    Then the response status should be 201
    And the response body should contain:
      """json
      {
        "id": "@string",
        "name": "Wireless Headphones Pro",
        "slug": "wireless-headphones-pro"
      }
      """
```

```typescript
// src/steps/api/request.steps.ts — DocString step definitions
import { When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { DocString } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { AppWorld } from '../../support/world';

When(
  'I send a POST request to {string} with body:',
  async function (this: AppWorld, path: string, docString: DocString) {
    // docString.content is the raw text; docString.mediaType is the content-type annotation
    const contentType = docString.mediaType ?? 'application/json';
    const body = contentType === 'application/json'
      ? JSON.parse(docString.content)
      : docString.content;

    this.context.lastResponseStatus = 0;
    this.context.lastResponseBody = null;

    const response = await this.app.api.post(path, body, { contentType });
    this.context.lastResponseStatus = response.status;
    this.context.lastResponseBody = await response.json();
  }
);

Then(
  'the response body should contain:',
  async function (this: AppWorld, docString: DocString) {
    const expected = JSON.parse(docString.content);
    const actual = this.context.lastResponseBody as Record<string, unknown>;

    // Pattern-match: "@string" means "any string value present"
    for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(expected)) {
      if (value === '@string') {
        expect(typeof actual[key]).toBe('string');
      } else {
        expect(actual[key]).toEqual(value);
      }
    }
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff**: Doc Strings in API scenarios keep JSON payloads readable inline but can create tight coupling between the Gherkin and the exact API schema. If the API evolves, all scenarios with inline JSON payloads need updating. Alternative: use Scenario Outline with a named fixture key (`When I create a product using the "standard-headphones" fixture`) and load payloads from files. Use Doc Strings when the exact payload structure is the specification being communicated — use fixtures when the payload is incidental detail.

**[community] The backtick (```) Doc String delimiter renders better than triple-quote (`"""`) in most Markdown editors and Confluence — feature files with Doc Strings are often published as living documentation, so the delimiter choice affects readability in rendered contexts. The backtick delimiter is functionally identical to triple-quote in Cucumber.js.** [community]
