### Pattern 2 — playwright-bdd v9 AI Agent Skill for Gherkin Feature File Generation  [official]

playwright-bdd v9.0.0 introduces an AI agent skill that enables AI coding assistants (e.g., Claude, Copilot) to generate Gherkin feature files and corresponding step definition stubs from natural language descriptions or existing test code. The agent skill is exposed as a documentation artifact installed alongside playwright-bdd, providing a structured prompt template that guides the AI to produce well-formed Gherkin with proper Given/When/Then separation, correct use of `Rule:` and `Example:` keywords, and TypeScript step definition stubs that match the playwright-bdd fixture model. This is the first official framework-provided AI generation aid in the BDD ecosystem, complementing community-driven prompt patterns and enabling teams to bootstrap feature coverage from user story descriptions without manually writing boilerplate.

```typescript
// playwright-bdd v9 AI agent workflow — using the agent skill to generate a feature file

// Step 1: Install playwright-bdd and confirm agent skill is available
// npm install playwright-bdd@^9 --save-dev
// The agent skill manifest is at: node_modules/playwright-bdd/.claude/agents/playwright-bdd-skill.md

// Step 2: Prompt the AI agent with a user story:
// "As a customer I want to add items to a wishlist so I can purchase them later"
//
// The agent skill generates a feature file like:
// features/wishlist.feature:
// Feature: Customer Wishlist
//   As a customer
//   I want to add items to a wishlist
//   So I can purchase them later
//
//   Scenario: Add item to empty wishlist
//     Given I am browsing the product catalog as a logged-in customer
//     When I add "Blue Sneakers" to my wishlist
//     Then my wishlist should contain 1 item
//     And "Blue Sneakers" should be visible in my wishlist

// Step 3: Generated step stubs in TypeScript:
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test, expect } from './fixtures';

const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

Given('I am browsing the product catalog as a logged-in customer', async ({ page, auth }) => {
  await auth.loginAsCustomer();
  await page.goto('/catalog');
});

When('I add {string} to my wishlist', async ({ page }, productName: string) => {
  await page.locator(`[data-product-name="${productName}"]`).getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to wishlist' }).click();
});

Then('my wishlist should contain {int} item', async ({ page }, count: number) => {
  await expect(page.getByTestId('wishlist-count')).toHaveText(String(count));
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use the playwright-bdd AI agent skill as a bootstrapping tool during initial feature coverage expansion — it produces well-structured stubs that adhere to playwright-bdd's fixture model, reducing the cognitive overhead of learning the framework while writing new scenarios. Do NOT treat AI-generated Gherkin as final approved specification — all generated feature files must go through a three-amigos review (product owner, developer, tester) to confirm the scenarios accurately represent business requirements before they are committed as executable specs. Alternative: for teams without AI assistant access, the existing `missingSteps: 'skip-scenario'` feature (Pattern 14 from Cycle 35) achieves a similar bootstrapping workflow manually — write Gherkin first, run `playwright-bdd gen` to produce stub specs, then implement step definitions iteratively.

### Pattern 3 — Cucumber.js v12.8.3 Assertion Info in Stack Traces for Precise Failure Diagnosis  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.8.3 (May 2026) fixes the omission of assertion library context from stack traces when a step fails due to an assertion error. Previously, when an `expect()` assertion from Chai, Jest `expect`, or `assert` failed inside a step definition, the Cucumber stack trace terminated at the step execution boundary — developers saw "Expected 5 to equal 3" with a stack trace pointing to Cucumber's internal step runner rather than the line in the step definition where the assertion failed. With v12.8.3, assertion info is included directly in the stack trace, pointing to the exact file and line number of the failing assertion within the step definition. This eliminates a manual investigation step where developers had to cross-reference the failure message with the source code to identify which assertion on a multi-assertion step failed.

```typescript
// Cucumber.js v12.8.3 — assertion info now included in stack traces

// features/step-definitions/checkout.steps.ts
import { When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { strict as assert } from 'node:assert';

When('the checkout summary is displayed', async function () {
  this.summary = await this.page.getByTestId('checkout-summary').allInnerTexts();
});

Then('the order total should be {float} and item count should be {int}', async function (
  expectedTotal: number,
  expectedCount: number,
) {
  // v12.8.3: when this fails, the stack trace now points to THIS line
  assert.strictEqual(this.summary.itemCount, expectedCount,
    `Item count mismatch: got ${this.summary.itemCount}, expected ${expectedCount}`);

  // v12.8.3: if above passes but this fails, stack trace points HERE — not to Cucumber internals
  assert.strictEqual(
    parseFloat(this.summary.total.replace('$', '')),
    expectedTotal,
    `Order total mismatch: got ${this.summary.total}, expected $${expectedTotal}`,
  );
});

// Before v12.8.3, failure output would show:
// AssertionError: Item count mismatch: got 2, expected 3
// at Runtime.runStep (node_modules/@cucumber/cucumber/lib/runtime/index.js:105:18)  <- useless
//
// After v12.8.3, failure output shows:
// AssertionError: Item count mismatch: got 2, expected 3
// at World.<anonymous> (features/step-definitions/checkout.steps.ts:18:3)  <- precise
```

**Tradeoff**: Upgrade to v12.8.3 immediately if your team runs Cucumber.js in a monorepo where multiple feature suites share step definitions — precise assertion stack traces dramatically reduce the time to diagnose failures in shared steps where the same step function is exercised by dozens of scenarios. Do NOT rely solely on improved stack traces as a substitute for splitting overly large step definitions that perform multiple assertions — a step that asserts five independent conditions should be refactored into five separate `Then` steps (or a single step with a structured assertion that clearly names each checked field); stack trace precision helps diagnose failures but does not eliminate the cognitive overhead of debugging multi-assertion steps.

### Pattern 4 — Cucumber.js v12.5 External Plugins for Custom Step Matchers and DSL Extensions  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.5.0 (December 2025) introduces a `plugins` configuration key that allows third-party npm packages to register custom step matchers, parameter type transformers, and World augmentations without requiring consumers to manually import and call registration functions in their support files. A plugin package exports a Cucumber plugin factory function that receives the Cucumber API object; the plugin is loaded before step discovery, ensuring custom parameter types registered by the plugin are available during step definition compilation. This enables tool authors to publish composable BDD extensions (e.g., a `@myorg/cucumber-api-plugin` that adds `{statusCode}`, `{jsonPath}`, and `{isoDate}` custom parameter types) that consumers activate via a single config entry rather than scattered `import` statements.

```typescript
// Cucumber.js v12.5 external plugin — example plugin package

// packages/bdd-http-plugin/src/index.ts — plugin factory
import type { ICucumberPlugin } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

const httpPlugin: ICucumberPlugin = (cucumberApi) => {
  // Register custom parameter types that become available in all step definitions
  cucumberApi.defineParameterType({
    name: 'statusCode',
    regexp: /\d{3}/,
    transformer: (s: string) => parseInt(s, 10),
    useForSnippets: false,
  });

  cucumberApi.defineParameterType({
    name: 'httpMethod',
    regexp: /GET|POST|PUT|PATCH|DELETE/,
    transformer: (s: string) => s.toUpperCase(),
    useForSnippets: false,
  });
};

export default httpPlugin;

// cucumber.config.ts — consuming project activates plugin via config key
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

export default {
  default: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    import: ['src/steps/**/*.ts'],
    plugins: ['@myorg/bdd-http-plugin'],  // loaded before step discovery
    format: ['progress-bar', 'html:reports/cucumber.html'],
  },
} satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>;

// Now step definitions can use {statusCode} and {httpMethod} without any extra imports:
// Given('I send a {httpMethod} request to {string}', async function (method, path) { ... })
// Then('the response should have status {statusCode}', async function (code) { ... })
```

**Tradeoff**: Use the `plugins` config key to publish shared BDD extension packages in monorepos or across teams that share a common test vocabulary — centralizing parameter type and World augmentation logic in a plugin eliminates the manual `import` coordination problem where teams forget to import registration files and only discover the omission when step definitions fail to match at runtime. Do NOT use plugins to inject global state that affects test isolation — plugin-registered code runs once per Cucumber process, so any mutable global state set by a plugin (e.g., a shared HTTP client instance) will persist across all test runs in that process; instead, expose plugin-registered factories that create fresh instances per World.

### Pattern 5 — Gherkin `Rule` Keyword for Business Rule Grouping Within a Feature  [official]

The Gherkin `Rule:` keyword (available since Gherkin 6, but widely underused as of 2024-2026) groups related scenarios under a single business rule within a feature file, providing a natural mid-level organizational unit between the feature and individual scenarios. A `Rule:` block encapsulates the business rule as prose and contains one or more `Example:` scenarios (the preferred alias for `Scenario:` introduced alongside `Rule:`). Using `Rule:` allows feature files to document multiple related but distinct business rules in a single file — without it, teams either create one scenario per file (fragmented) or mix unrelated scenarios under a single feature (confusing). Gherkin v39.0.0 expanded the `Rule:` keyword's internationalization support, adding Korean and extended Turkish translations.

```gherkin
# features/cart-pricing.feature — using Rule: to group scenarios by business rule

Feature: Shopping Cart Pricing
  As a customer
  I want transparent pricing in my cart
  So I can make informed purchasing decisions

  Rule: Quantity discounts apply above threshold
    Customers who add 5 or more identical items receive a 10% discount per item.

    Example: No discount below threshold
      Given my cart contains 4 units of "Blue Sneakers" at $50 each
      When I view the cart total
      Then the subtotal should be $200.00
      And no discount should be applied

    Example: Discount applies at threshold
      Given my cart contains 5 units of "Blue Sneakers" at $50 each
      When I view the cart total
      Then a 10% quantity discount should be applied
      And the subtotal should be $225.00

  Rule: Free shipping applies above minimum order value
    Orders with a merchandise total of $100 or more qualify for free standard shipping.

    Example: Free shipping qualifies
      Given my cart subtotal is $105.00
      When I proceed to shipping selection
      Then "Free Standard Shipping" should be available
```

```typescript
// Step definitions for the Rule-grouped scenarios
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { strict as assert } from 'node:assert';

Given('my cart contains {int} units of {string} at ${float} each',
  async function (qty: number, product: string, unitPrice: number) {
    await this.cartService.addItem({ product, quantity: qty, unitPrice });
  });

When('I view the cart total', async function () {
  this.cartSummary = await this.cartService.getSummary();
});

Then('the subtotal should be ${float}', async function (expectedTotal: number) {
  assert.strictEqual(this.cartSummary.subtotal, expectedTotal);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `Rule:` when a feature file naturally contains 6 or more scenarios that cluster around 2-3 distinct business rules — without `Rule:`, readers must infer the grouping from scenario naming conventions or comments, which degrade over time. Do NOT use `Rule:` as a replacement for splitting a feature file when the rules are truly independent domains — if Rule A and Rule B have completely separate Given preconditions and involve different system actors, they belong in separate feature files; `Rule:` is for related rules that operate on the same domain concept. Alternative: if your BDD tooling predates `Rule:` support (very old Cucumber versions), use `@` tags to simulate rule grouping, filtering by tag in CI to run rule-specific subsets.

### Pattern 6 — Cucumber.js v12.7 CLI Path Merge Warnings for Overlapping Config and CLI Paths  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.7.0 (February 2026) adds explicit warnings when `paths` specified via CLI arguments overlap with `paths` from the configuration file. Previously, teams running `cucumber-js features/checkout/**` in CI while also specifying `paths: ['features/**']` in `cucumber.config.ts` would silently execute a merged (duplicated) path set, causing scenarios to run twice — once from each path source. The duplication produced doubled test counts in reports and intermittent database constraint violations in parallel runs where the same scenario's setup steps ran concurrently. With v12.7, a warning is emitted at startup listing which paths were merged from config vs CLI, giving teams visibility to detect and resolve the overlap by either removing the redundant config paths or using a named profile configuration.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — base config for local development
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

export default {
  default: {
    // Local dev: run all features
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    import: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    parallel: 2,
  },
  // Named CI profile that restricts paths — avoids the overlap warning
  ci: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],  // CI uses this exclusively via --profile ci
    import: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    parallel: 8,
    format: ['progress-bar', 'junit:reports/cucumber-junit.xml'],
  },
  // Named smoke profile for targeted checkout-only runs
  smoke: {
    paths: ['features/checkout/**/*.feature'],  // restricted path
    import: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    parallel: 2,
    tags: '@smoke',
  },
} satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>;

// package.json scripts — profiles prevent CLI/config path overlap:
// "test:bdd": "cucumber-js --profile default"
// "test:bdd:ci": "cucumber-js --profile ci"
// "test:bdd:smoke": "cucumber-js --profile smoke"
// AVOID: "test:bdd:checkout": "cucumber-js features/checkout/**"
//         (merges with default config paths -> v12.7 emits overlap warning)
```

**Tradeoff**: Define named config profiles for every non-default execution context (CI, smoke, regression) instead of passing `paths` as CLI arguments — this eliminates the path merge overlap, makes the full configuration visible in version-controlled `cucumber.config.ts`, and allows developers to reproduce CI runs locally by switching profile names. Do NOT suppress v12.7 path merge warnings as a workaround — the warnings indicate a genuine configuration problem that can cause scenarios to run multiple times; treat each warning as a configuration bug to fix before merging to main. Alternative: if you need to run a feature file subset ad hoc without defining a named profile, use the `--tags` flag to filter by scenario tag rather than specifying path overrides on the CLI.

### Pattern 7 — playwright-bdd v8.5.1 Playwright 1.60+ Compatibility and Trace Fixture Integration  [official]

playwright-bdd v8.5.1 (May 2026) adds compatibility with Playwright 1.60+ which introduced a revised `page.tracing` API with a new `$trace` fixture injection model. In Playwright 1.60, trace collection is integrated into the built-in test fixture system — playwright-bdd v8.5.1 ensures that step-level trace attachment (where each step's trace segment is embedded in the Cucumber report) continues to work correctly with this new fixture signature. Teams upgrading to Playwright 1.60+ without upgrading playwright-bdd to 8.5.1 would encounter TypeScript compilation errors on step definition files that reference `page.tracing` and missing trace attachments in Cucumber reports.

```typescript
// playwright-bdd v8.5.1 — step-level trace collection with Playwright 1.60+

// fixtures.ts — extend base test with trace-aware fixture
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';

export const test = base.extend<{
  stepTracing: void;
}>({
  // Playwright 1.60+ compatible: use fixture-based trace collection
  stepTracing: [async ({ page }, use, testInfo) => {
    // Start trace at scenario start (playwright-bdd v8.5.1 handles per-step segments)
    await page.context().tracing.start({
      screenshots: true,
      snapshots: true,
      sources: true,
    });
    await use();
    // Playwright 1.60 trace API: stop with outputPath
    const tracePath = testInfo.outputPath('trace.zip');
    await page.context().tracing.stop({ path: tracePath });
    await testInfo.attach('trace', { path: tracePath, contentType: 'application/zip' });
  }, { auto: true }],
});

export const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

// step definition — unchanged from v8.4; v8.5.1 handles compatibility transparently
Given('I navigate to the checkout page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Checkout' })).toBeVisible();
});

When('I enter payment details for {string}', async ({ page }, cardType: string) => {
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill(cardType === 'visa' ? '4242424242424242' : '5555555555554444');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/30');
  await page.getByLabel('CVV').fill('123');
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Pin `playwright-bdd` and `@playwright/test` versions together in `package.json` using compatible ranges (e.g., `"playwright-bdd": "^8.5.1"` with `"@playwright/test": "^1.60.0"`) and enforce the pairing in a `check:versions` npm script that runs in CI — the two packages have interdependencies in their fixture APIs that cause silent runtime failures when mismatched. Do NOT upgrade Playwright alone without simultaneously verifying playwright-bdd compatibility via the compatibility matrix in the playwright-bdd README — Playwright minor releases frequently change internal fixture APIs that playwright-bdd depends on.

### Pattern 8 — Cucumber Community Ownership Migration: Removing SmartBear Registry Override  [official]

In December 2024, Cucumber returned to full community ownership following SmartBear's acquisition. The practical impact for teams is that the `@cucumber/cucumber` npm package is now published exclusively to the public npm registry, and any `npmrc` configurations pointing to the SmartBear package registry for `@cucumber/*` scopes must be removed. Teams with enterprise `npmrc` files that proxied `@cucumber` packages through the SmartBear commercial registry began receiving 404 errors for `@cucumber/cucumber` installs after the registry migration. The community-owned package retains the same package name and API — there are no breaking changes from the registry migration itself — but teams must update their `npmrc` to remove the scoped registry override.

```typescript
// Migration checklist for SmartBear registry to community npm registry

// BEFORE (with SmartBear registry override — causes 404 after community migration):
// .npmrc:
// @cucumber:registry=https://registry.smartbear.com/

// AFTER — remove the scoped override; let npm resolve @cucumber from public registry:
// .npmrc — remove the @cucumber:registry line entirely
// Or if your npmrc has a corporate proxy, ensure @cucumber is in the public-passthrough list

// Verify the migration worked:
// npm info @cucumber/cucumber version
// Expected: resolves to the latest community release (12.8.3 as of May 2026)

// package.json — no changes needed to package names or import paths
// {
//   "devDependencies": {
//     "@cucumber/cucumber": "^12.8.3",  // same package name, now community-owned
//     "@cucumber/html-formatter": "^21.7.0",
//     "cucumber-html-reporter": "^7.1.0"
//   }
// }

// cucumber.config.ts — unchanged; no API changes from registry migration
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

export default {
  default: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    import: ['src/steps/**/*.ts'],
    format: ['progress-bar', 'html:reports/cucumber.html'],
    parallel: 4,
  },
} satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>;

// Community governance is now managed via the Open Cucumber GitHub organization
// https://github.com/cucumber
```

**Tradeoff**: Update all `.npmrc` files (project-level, CI pipeline environment, Docker build images) simultaneously when migrating away from the SmartBear registry — a partial migration where the CI pipeline still uses the SmartBear registry while local development resolves from the public registry creates a version drift scenario where CI installs a cached (potentially old) version while developers install the latest community release. Do NOT wait for the SmartBear registry to be formally deprecated before migrating — the registry may serve stale or outdated packages indefinitely, causing teams to miss critical bug fixes published only to the community npm registry.

### Pattern 9 — Gherkin `DocString` Media Type Declaration for Structured Payload Testing  [official]

Gherkin's DocString construct supports an optional media type hint (`"""json`, `"""yaml`, `"""xml`) that was formalized in the Gherkin specification and is now carried through to the `$step` fixture in playwright-bdd v9 via the new `docStringType` property. When a step definition receives a DocString, the media type hint tells the step implementation how to parse the raw string — enabling type-safe JSON parsing, XML validation, or YAML deserialization within the step body without requiring string inspection heuristics. playwright-bdd v9's `$step` fixture exposes `$step.docString` (the raw text) and `$step.docStringType` (the declared media type), allowing step definitions to branch on media type for content-aware processing.

```gherkin
# features/api-validation.feature — using DocString media type hints

Feature: API Response Validation
  Scenario: Create product with JSON payload
    When I POST to "/products" with body:
      """json
      {
        "name": "Blue Sneakers",
        "sku": "SHOE-001",
        "price": 49.99,
        "stock": 100
      }
      """
    Then the response status should be 201
    And the response body should match:
      """json
      {
        "id": "<<any>>",
        "name": "Blue Sneakers",
        "sku": "SHOE-001"
      }
      """
```

```typescript
// Step definition using $step.docStringType from playwright-bdd v9
import { When, Then } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

When('I POST to {string} with body:', async ({ request, $step }, path: string) => {
  const contentType = $step.docStringType === 'json' ? 'application/json' : 'text/plain';
  const body = $step.docStringType === 'json'
    ? JSON.parse($step.docString!)
    : $step.docString;

  (this as any).response = await request.post(path, {
    data: body,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': contentType },
  });
});

Then('the response body should match:', async ({ $step }) => {
  const responseBody = await (this as any).response.json();
  const expectedPattern = JSON.parse($step.docString!);
  // Match all keys from expected pattern, ignoring <<any>> placeholders
  for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(expectedPattern)) {
    if (value !== '<<any>>') {
      expect(responseBody[key]).toEqual(value);
    }
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use DocString media type hints whenever a step receives structured data that requires parsing — it makes the content-type contract explicit in the Gherkin and enables step definitions to enforce correct parsing without guessing. Do NOT use DocString for long test data payloads that vary frequently between scenarios; instead, use `Scenario Outline` with `Examples:` tables for parametric data or an external fixture file for large static payloads — DocStrings embedded in Gherkin are hard to diff in code review and can make feature files unwieldy when the payload exceeds ~15 lines.

### Pattern 10 — Cucumber.js `setParallelCanAssign` for Dependency-Aware Parallel Scenario Scheduling  [official]

Cucumber.js's `setParallelCanAssign` function allows teams to declare which pairs of scenarios are unsafe to run concurrently, giving the parallel scheduler explicit conflict rules rather than relying on arbitrary tag-based group partitioning. When two scenarios share a named resource (a user account, a database row, a named test fixture), `setParallelCanAssign` can inspect both scenarios' tags and return `false` if they conflict — the scheduler will then queue one scenario until the conflicting scenario completes. This is more precise than the `@serial` tag approach (which forces all `@serial`-tagged scenarios to run one at a time globally) because `setParallelCanAssign` can express pairwise constraints: Scenario A and Scenario B conflict, but Scenario A and Scenario C are safe to run together.

```typescript
// support/parallel-assign.ts — pairwise conflict declaration

import { setParallelCanAssign, ITestCaseHookParameter } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

// Scenarios tagged @uses-user-alice and @uses-user-bob conflict if they share a user
// Scenarios tagged @uses-user-alice should not run concurrently with each other
// But @uses-user-alice and @uses-user-carol are independent

setParallelCanAssign(function canAssign(
  inProgress: ITestCaseHookParameter[],
  candidate: ITestCaseHookParameter,
): boolean {
  const candidateTags = candidate.pickle.tags.map((t) => t.name);

  for (const running of inProgress) {
    const runningTags = running.pickle.tags.map((t) => t.name);

    // Find shared @uses-user-* tags between candidate and any running scenario
    const candidateUsers = candidateTags.filter((t) => t.startsWith('@uses-user-'));
    const runningUsers = runningTags.filter((t) => t.startsWith('@uses-user-'));
    const sharedUsers = candidateUsers.filter((u) => runningUsers.includes(u));

    if (sharedUsers.length > 0) {
      // Conflict: both scenarios use the same named user fixture — defer candidate
      return false;
    }

    // Check DB sequence conflicts: @uses-seq-* tags are singleton resources
    const candidateSeqs = candidateTags.filter((t) => t.startsWith('@uses-seq-'));
    const runningSeqs = runningTags.filter((t) => t.startsWith('@uses-seq-'));
    if (candidateSeqs.some((s) => runningSeqs.includes(s))) {
      return false;
    }
  }

  // No conflicts with any currently running scenario — can proceed
  return true;
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `setParallelCanAssign` when your test suite has 10+ scenarios that share named resources but most scenarios are safe to run in parallel — it recovers the parallelism lost by blunt `@serial` tagging while maintaining correct isolation for resource-conflicting scenarios. Do NOT use `setParallelCanAssign` as a substitute for proper test data isolation — the function adds scheduling overhead proportional to the number of running scenarios, and complex conflict rules can serialize most of your suite if tag coverage is poor; audit resource ownership tags quarterly to ensure conflict declarations remain accurate as the test suite grows.

### Pattern 11 — BDD Scenario for Browser Geolocation and Permission APIs with Playwright  [community]

Teams building location-aware features (store finders, delivery address suggestions, weather widgets) frequently struggle to write BDD scenarios that exercise geolocation permission flows without triggering real browser permission dialogs. Playwright's `browserContext.grantPermissions(['geolocation'])` and `browserContext.setGeolocation()` APIs enable deterministic geolocation injection — playwright-bdd step definitions can configure these context-level settings in a `Before` hook tagged to geolocation scenarios, enabling the full permission-granted and permission-denied paths to be tested in CI without user interaction. Community members on GitHub discussions note that forgetting to grant permissions before navigating (vs. after) causes silent failures where the geolocation API returns the default position rather than the injected one.

```typescript
// features/store-finder.feature
// Feature: Store Finder
//   @with-geolocation
//   Scenario: Suggest nearest store when location is permitted
//     Given my location is set to latitude 37.7749 longitude -122.4194
//     When I open the store finder
//     Then the nearest store "Union Square SF" should appear first

// step-definitions/geolocation.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then, Before } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Grant permission BEFORE navigation — must be set at context level
Before({ tags: '@with-geolocation' }, async ({ context }) => {
  await context.grantPermissions(['geolocation']);
});

Given('my location is set to latitude {float} longitude {float}',
  async ({ context }, lat: number, lng: number) => {
    await context.setGeolocation({ latitude: lat, longitude: lng });
  });

When('I open the store finder', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/store-finder');
  // Wait for geolocation to resolve — look for the loading spinner to disappear
  await expect(page.getByTestId('location-loading')).not.toBeVisible({ timeout: 5000 });
});

Then('the nearest store {string} should appear first', async ({ page }, storeName: string) => {
  const firstResult = page.getByTestId('store-result').first();
  await expect(firstResult.getByTestId('store-name')).toHaveText(storeName);
});

// Testing the denied path — use a separate @geolocation-denied tag
Before({ tags: '@geolocation-denied' }, async ({ context }) => {
  // Do NOT grant permission — browser API will return PermissionDeniedError
  // Still set a fallback to prevent test runner from waiting indefinitely
  await context.setGeolocation({ latitude: 0, longitude: 0 });
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `context.grantPermissions` and `context.setGeolocation` in tagged `Before` hooks rather than inline in `Given` steps — the permission grant must happen at context creation time before any navigation for it to apply correctly, and if the permission grant is inside a `Given` step, race conditions can occur when the page starts loading before the permission is granted. Do NOT hardcode geographic coordinates in step definitions — use a named location registry (`LocationFixtures.SAN_FRANCISCO`) to make scenarios readable and refactoring-safe when test locations need updating.

### Pattern 12 — playwright-bdd `defineParameterType` for Domain-Specific Custom Step Parameters  [official]

playwright-bdd v8.5.0 improved documentation and support for `defineParameterType` from `@cucumber/cucumber`, enabling teams to register custom parameter types that transform captured strings into strongly-typed domain objects within step definitions. A `{productSku}` parameter type can validate SKU format and return a typed `ProductSku` object; a `{isoDate}` type parses ISO date strings into `Date` objects. Registering domain-specific parameter types eliminates repetitive parsing boilerplate at the top of every step definition that receives structured data, centralizes validation logic, and improves error messages — a malformed SKU caught by `defineParameterType` produces a `ParameterType transformation failed` error that names the parameter type, rather than a cryptic `TypeError` inside the step function.

```typescript
// support/parameter-types.ts — register domain-specific parameter types

import { defineParameterType } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

// ProductSku parameter type — validates format and creates typed object
defineParameterType({
  name: 'productSku',
  // Matches strings like "SHOE-001", "SHIRT-XL-RED", etc.
  regexp: /[A-Z]{2,8}-[A-Z0-9-]{1,20}/,
  transformer(rawSku: string): { code: string; category: string } {
    const parts = rawSku.split('-');
    return {
      code: rawSku,
      category: parts[0].toLowerCase(),
    };
  },
  useForSnippets: true,
});

// ISO date parameter type — parses date strings to Date objects
defineParameterType({
  name: 'isoDate',
  regexp: /\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}/,
  transformer(dateStr: string): Date {
    const d = new Date(dateStr);
    if (isNaN(d.getTime())) {
      throw new Error(`Invalid ISO date: ${dateStr}`);
    }
    return d;
  },
  useForSnippets: false,
});

// step-definitions/inventory.steps.ts — clean step definitions with typed params
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Given('product {productSku} is in stock with {int} units',
  async function (sku: { code: string; category: string }, units: number) {
    await this.inventoryService.setStock(sku.code, units);
    // category is already parsed — no string manipulation needed in the step
    this.currentCategory = sku.category;
  });

When('I filter the catalog by SKU {productSku}',
  async function (sku: { code: string; category: string }) {
    await this.page.getByPlaceholder('Search SKU').fill(sku.code);
    await this.page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Search' }).click();
  });
```

**Tradeoff**: Register `defineParameterType` in a dedicated `support/parameter-types.ts` file that is imported globally (via Cucumber's `require`/`import` config) rather than inline in step definition files — parameter type registration is order-dependent and must complete before step definition parsing; defining types in ad hoc locations causes intermittent "parameter type not found" errors depending on file load order. Do NOT create parameter types that perform async operations (e.g., database lookups) — `transformer` functions in `defineParameterType` are synchronous; async data loading belongs in `Given` step bodies or World setup hooks.

### Pattern 13 — Cucumber.js Formatter Plugin Architecture for Custom CI Report Pipelines  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.5's plugin system extends to custom formatter plugins, enabling teams to publish npm packages that implement a Cucumber formatter without embedding the formatter source in the test project. A formatter plugin receives Cucumber message stream events and can emit to any output sink — Allure report directories, TestRail API endpoints, or Slack webhooks — without requiring consumers to configure custom format strings or maintain formatter scripts inside their test project. Custom formatter plugins are registered in `cucumber.config.ts` under the `plugins` key; Cucumber loads them before message emission, ensuring all scenario messages are processed by the plugin's formatter handler.

```typescript
// Example: custom formatter plugin for Cucumber.js v12.5+

// packages/cucumber-summary-plugin/src/index.ts
import type { ICucumberPlugin } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import * as fs from 'fs';
import * as path from 'path';

const summaryPlugin: ICucumberPlugin = (cucumberApi) => {
  // Register a custom formatter via the plugin API
  cucumberApi.registerFormatter('json-summary', class JsonSummaryFormatter {
    private results: Array<{ name: string; status: string; duration: number }> = [];
    private outputFile: string;

    constructor(options: { parsedArgvOptions?: { outputFile?: string } }) {
      this.outputFile = options.parsedArgvOptions?.outputFile ?? 'reports/summary.json';

      options.eventBroadcaster.on('envelope', (envelope) => {
        if (envelope.testCaseFinished) {
          const status = envelope.testCaseFinished.willBeRetried ? 'retried' : 'finished';
          this.results.push({
            name: envelope.testCaseFinished.testCaseStartedId,
            status,
            duration: envelope.testCaseFinished.timestamp?.seconds ?? 0,
          });
        }
        if (envelope.testRunFinished) {
          fs.mkdirSync(path.dirname(this.outputFile), { recursive: true });
          fs.writeFileSync(this.outputFile, JSON.stringify(this.results, null, 2));
        }
      });
    }
  });
};

export default summaryPlugin;

// cucumber.config.ts — activate the formatter plugin
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

export default {
  default: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    import: ['src/steps/**/*.ts'],
    plugins: ['@myorg/cucumber-summary-plugin'],
    format: [
      'progress-bar',
      'json-summary',  // name registered by the plugin
      'html:reports/cucumber.html',
    ],
  },
} satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>;
```

**Tradeoff**: Use the v12.5 plugin formatter architecture for reporting integrations that are shared across multiple projects or that require bidirectional communication (e.g., writing results to a test management system's API) — the plugin system provides proper lifecycle management that fragile custom `--format` script paths cannot guarantee. Do NOT implement report integration logic directly inside `AfterAll` Cucumber hooks — hooks run per worker in parallel mode and produce fragmented output that must be manually merged; formatter plugins receive messages from the coordinator process and see the complete run.

### Pattern 14 — BDD Scenario for Service Worker and Offline Mode Testing with Playwright  [community]

Progressive Web App (PWA) features — offline mode, push notifications, background sync — are systematically undertested in BDD suites because service worker registration is asynchronous and state is scoped to the browser context. Playwright provides `context.setOffline(true)` for deterministic offline simulation, enabling BDD scenarios for cached content delivery, offline banners, and background sync queuing. Community members note that the most common failure mode is navigating to the app before the service worker registers and caches the shell, causing offline scenarios to fail with a genuine network error rather than the expected cached response. The fix is a mandatory `waitForFunction` checking `navigator.serviceWorker.controller !== null` in the `Before` hook before any offline network interception.

```typescript
// features/pwa-offline.feature
// Feature: PWA Offline Mode
//   @pwa-offline
//   Scenario: Show cached content when offline
//     Given the app is loaded and the service worker is registered
//     When the network connection is lost
//     Then the product catalog should be visible from cache
//     And an "Offline Mode" banner should be displayed

// step-definitions/pwa.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then, Before } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Before({ tags: '@pwa-offline' }, async ({ page }) => {
  // Load app online first so service worker can register and cache the shell
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle');
  // Wait for service worker to activate — critical before switching to offline
  await page.waitForFunction(() =>
    navigator.serviceWorker.controller !== null,
    { timeout: 10_000 },
  );
});

Given('the app is loaded and the service worker is registered', async ({ page }) => {
  // Pre-condition verified by Before hook — navigate to catalog while online
  await page.goto('/catalog');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-grid')).toBeVisible();
});

When('the network connection is lost', async ({ context }) => {
  // Playwright: set offline mode at context level — affects all new requests
  await context.setOffline(true);
});

Then('the product catalog should be visible from cache', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.reload();
  // Service worker serves from cache — grid should still render
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-grid')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 8_000 });
  // No network-error overlay
  await expect(page.getByTestId('network-error')).not.toBeVisible();
});

Then('an {string} banner should be displayed', async ({ page }, bannerText: string) => {
  await expect(page.getByRole('banner', { name: bannerText })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `context.setOffline(true)` at the Playwright context level rather than using `page.route` to intercept all requests — context-level offline mode correctly simulates the browser's actual offline state (including WebSocket closure and XMLHttpRequest failures), while request interception with `page.route` only blocks matching routes, potentially leaving non-intercepted requests to succeed silently. Do NOT run `@pwa-offline` scenarios in parallel workers that share the same browser context — offline mode is a context-level state change; if two scenarios share a context and one sets offline mode, the other scenario's requests will also fail unexpectedly.

### Pattern 15 — playwright-bdd v9 JUnit Reporter Canonical Name Migration from `junit-modern`  [official]

playwright-bdd v9.0.0 deprecates the `junit-modern` reporter alias in favor of the canonical `junit` reporter name, and makes Cucumber-compatible testcase naming the default for the JUnit reporter output. In playwright-bdd v8.x, teams used `reporter: [['junit-modern', { outputFile: 'results/junit.xml' }]]` in `playwright.config.ts` to get Cucumber-style test names in JUnit XML — the `junit-modern` alias was introduced in v8.3 to distinguish the Cucumber-format JUnit output from Playwright's native JUnit reporter. In v9, the canonical JUnit reporter absorbs this behaviour as the default, the `junit-modern` alias emits a deprecation warning, and teams should migrate to `reporter: [['junit', { outputFile: 'results/junit.xml', nameFormat: 'cucumber' }]]`.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — migration from junit-modern to canonical junit in playwright-bdd v9

import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/**/*.ts',
});

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  // playwright-bdd v9: migrate from 'junit-modern' alias to canonical 'junit'
  reporter: [
    // BEFORE (playwright-bdd v8.3-v8.x):
    // ['junit-modern', {
    //   outputFile: 'reports/junit.xml',
    //   nameFormat: 'cucumber',  // was required explicitly in v8.3
    // }],

    // AFTER (playwright-bdd v9 -- 'junit-modern' emits deprecation warning):
    ['junit', {
      outputFile: 'reports/junit.xml',
      // nameFormat: 'cucumber' is now the DEFAULT in v9 -- can omit or make explicit:
      nameFormat: 'cucumber',  // explicit for clarity; same as default
    }],
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'reports/playwright-html' }],
    // Cucumber HTML report is generated separately by playwright-bdd
    ['./node_modules/playwright-bdd/reporter/cucumber-html', {
      outputFile: 'reports/cucumber-report.html',
    }],
  ],
  use: {
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Migrate from `junit-modern` to `junit` during the v8 to v9 upgrade window before the alias is removed in a future v9 patch — the deprecation warning is currently non-fatal but will become a hard error in a future playwright-bdd release. Do NOT change the `nameFormat` value from `cucumber` to `playwright` when migrating — changing to `playwright` naming breaks CI systems (Azure DevOps, Jenkins, GitHub Actions) that match JUnit testcase names to Gherkin scenario titles for flaky test detection and trend analysis; if you need Playwright-native naming for Playwright-native reporting, configure a separate `junit` reporter entry with `outputFile: 'reports/playwright-junit.xml'` and `nameFormat: 'playwright'`.

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 36

**[community] Gotcha 1 — playwright-bdd `AfterStep` hooks do not execute when the preceding step throws an error because the step invoker calls after-step hooks in the non-error path only without a `try/finally` guarantee, causing diagnostic attachments (screenshots, logs) to be silently omitted for the exact step that failed, which is the step most in need of a diagnostic attachment**: Teams that configure `AfterStep` to capture a per-step screenshot and attach it to the Cucumber report discover in post-mortem analysis that the screenshot for the failing step is always missing — only screenshots up to the step before the failure are present. A GitHub issue (#383 on vitalets/playwright-bdd, April 2026) confirmed the root cause: the step invoker in `src/runtime/bddStepInvoker.ts` calls after-step hooks sequentially without a `try/finally` around the step execution. WHY developers assume it will run: Playwright's own test fixture `afterEach` always runs regardless of test outcome, so developers expect `AfterStep` to follow the same contract — but playwright-bdd's `AfterStep` is not the same as Playwright's `afterEach`. Fix: add a global `After` hook that captures a full-page screenshot on `testInfo.status === 'failed'` — this always runs and captures the end-of-scenario page state; combine with a trace file attachment to see the step-by-step action history leading to the failure.

**[community] Gotcha 2 — Cucumber.js parallel execution with `--shard` produces different effective shard sizes when some feature files have many more scenarios than others, causing the last shard to finish significantly earlier than the first shard and wasting CI wall-clock time that developers attribute to infrastructure variance rather than uneven work distribution**: Teams that shard their Cucumber suite across 8 CI workers report that some workers complete 45 minutes before others, and initially assume the slowdown is infrastructure-related. The real cause is Cucumber's round-robin scenario assignment, which assigns scenarios by index — if feature files are loaded in lexicographic order and all long-running scenarios are in a single feature file, one shard accumulates all the long scenarios while others get only short scenarios. WHY teams miss this: single-machine `--parallel` runs balance load naturally because all scenarios are in the same process; sharding exposes the imbalance. Fix: add `@slow` tags to scenarios that take over 30 seconds, and use `setParallelCanAssign` or tag-based shard assignment to distribute `@slow` scenarios evenly across shards. Alternatively, split large feature files so that no single file accounts for more than 5% of the total scenario count.

**[community] Gotcha 3 — Using Gherkin `Rule:` keyword in feature files breaks older Cucumber.js versions (pre-6.0) installed transitively as test runner dependencies in monorepos, causing cryptic parse errors that appear to be indentation issues rather than version incompatibility errors, because the parser treats `Rule:` as an unknown keyword and reports the next line as the unexpected token**: Teams in large monorepos where different packages use different versions of `@cucumber/cucumber` encounter parse errors when a shared feature file uses `Rule:` — the error message from the older parser reads `expected: #EOF, #Language, #TagLine, #FeatureLine, #Comment, #Empty, got 'Rule: ...'`, which looks like a whitespace problem. The actual cause is that the older Cucumber.js version predates the `Rule:` keyword support. WHY the error is misleading: the older parser treats `Rule:` as an unexpected token in what should be a scenario context, producing a message that looks like an indentation error rather than a missing keyword error. Fix: add a monorepo-wide constraint in the root `package.json` `resolutions` field (`"@cucumber/cucumber": ">=12.0.0"`) to force all transitive cucumber dependencies to v12+, and add a CI check that validates the resolved cucumber version.

**[community] Gotcha 4 — Cucumber.js v12.4 native TypeScript config loading via Node.js strip-types does not support `import type` re-exports from complex declaration file chains, causing `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'default')` when `cucumber.config.ts` imports a type from a `.d.ts` file re-export chain, an error that only reproduces with Node.js strip-types and not with `tsx` or `ts-node`**: After upgrading to v12.4 and removing `tsx`, teams that import interface types from `@cucumber/cucumber` using `import type { IConfiguration }` in `cucumber.config.ts` sometimes encounter `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` at config load time. The error message points to the import statement, but `import type` should be entirely erased at runtime — the contradiction confuses developers who spend time debugging what appears to be a runtime type error. The root cause is a Node.js strip-types limitation when processing complex re-export chains through declaration files. WHY this confuses developers: `import type` is a TypeScript-only construct that should be erased entirely; the error suggests the type import has a runtime effect, which contradicts TypeScript's type erasure semantics. Fix: replace `import type { IConfiguration }` with `import { IConfiguration }` (value import) in config files processed by strip-types; alternatively, inline the type annotation using the `satisfies` operator without the external type import.

**[community] Gotcha 5 — Teams using playwright-bdd with multiple `createBdd(test)` calls in separate fixture files get duplicate step registrations that cause ambiguous step definition errors when two fixture variants register the same Gherkin step text, but the error message names only the duplicate pattern without indicating which fixture file registered it, making it difficult to identify which `createBdd` call is the source of the duplication**: In monorepos where different feature suites extend a base test fixture with different augmentations, developers sometimes create multiple `createBdd(test)` instances in separate files and then accidentally import `Given` from two different fixture files in the same step definition file. Both `Given` functions share the same global Cucumber step registry, so registering the same pattern twice produces an "Ambiguous step definition" error. WHY teams create multiple `createBdd` instances: each feature area has its own fixture file, and the pattern `export const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(myTest)` looks like a local export — developers do not realize that `createBdd` registers into a single global step registry, not a per-fixture registry. Fix: create exactly one `createBdd(test)` call in a single `bdd.ts` file that uses the most fully-composed fixture, and export `Given`, `When`, `Then` from that file only. All step definition files import from `bdd.ts`, never from intermediate fixture files.

**[community] Gotcha 6 — Gherkin `Background:` steps are re-executed once per `Examples:` row in a `Scenario Outline`, causing teams that seed database state in Background to inadvertently attempt to seed the same data multiple times in parameterized scenarios, leading to unique-constraint violations that appear only when the `Examples:` table has more than one row**: A feature file with a `Background:` that creates a user account and a `Scenario Outline` with five rows in the `Examples:` table will attempt to create the same user five times — once per example. Many teams discover this only after adding a second row to an `Examples:` table that previously had one row. WHY one row hides the bug: with a single example, the Background runs once and the scenario runs once — no duplication. Adding a second row triggers the Background a second time, surfacing the constraint violation. Fix: use `BeforeAll` hooks for data that should be created once per feature execution, or use upsert semantics in Background step implementations (INSERT with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE) to make repeated Background execution idempotent. Never use raw INSERT statements in Background steps that create unique-keyed records.
