### Pattern 1 — Cucumber Messages v32 `ExternalAttachment` for Large BDD Report Artifacts  [official]

Cucumber Messages v32.0.0 (January 2025) introduces the `ExternalAttachment` type as a first-class message alongside the long-standing `Attachment` message, allowing step definitions and hooks to attach large binary files (screenshots, video recordings, HAR archives) to a report by reference rather than embedding them inline as base64 strings. Prior to v32, all BDD test attachments were embedded directly in the NDJSON message stream as base64-encoded content, which caused report files to balloon to hundreds of megabytes when teams attached screenshots or trace files for every step. The `ExternalAttachment` message holds a `url` field pointing to an external storage location (Azure Blob Storage, S3, or a local file server), and the `contentEncoding` field is set to `IDENTITY` to indicate the content is referenced, not embedded. In v32, the `Attachment.url` and `Attachment.source` fields from v27 are formally deprecated in favor of the new `ExternalAttachment` type, and tooling that reads the message stream should check for both message types.

```typescript
// hooks/attachmentHooks.ts — ExternalAttachment pattern with Cucumber Messages v32
// Requires @cucumber/cucumber >=12.4.0 and @cucumber/messages >=32.0.0

import { After, ITestCaseHookParameter } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { ExternalAttachment } from '@cucumber/messages';
import { uploadToAzureBlob } from '../support/blobStorage';
import * as fs from 'fs/promises';
import * as path from 'path';

After({ tags: '@screenshot-on-failure' }, async function (this: CustomWorld, { result }: ITestCaseHookParameter) {
  if (result?.status !== 'FAILED') return;

  const screenshotPath = path.join('test-output', 'screenshots', `${this.scenarioId}.png`);
  const exists = await fs.access(screenshotPath).then(() => true).catch(() => false);
  if (!exists) return;

  // Upload to external storage instead of embedding as base64
  const externalUrl = await uploadToAzureBlob(screenshotPath, `screenshots/${this.scenarioId}.png`);

  // Attach as ExternalAttachment (v32 pattern) — references external URL
  const externalAttachment: ExternalAttachment = {
    url: externalUrl,
    contentType: 'image/png',
    mediaType: 'image/png',
  };

  // Cucumber.js world attach method accepts ExternalAttachment via the messages API
  // Use the low-level attach method with ExternalAttachment object
  await this.attach(JSON.stringify(externalAttachment), 'application/vnd.cucumber.external-attachment+json');
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `ExternalAttachment` for any artifact larger than 50 KB to prevent NDJSON message streams from exceeding memory limits in CI agents that process all messages in-process — embedding 200 screenshots as base64 in a single report file can cause Node.js heap exhaustion during report generation. Do NOT point `ExternalAttachment.url` to a local filesystem path (`file:///`) if you intend to view the report on a different machine — CI artifacts are copied to different hosts; always upload to a shared storage URL before generating the report. [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — Playwright v1.49 `captureGitInfo` for Living-Documentation Provenance in BDD CI Pipelines  [official]

Playwright v1.49 introduces `testConfig.captureGitInfo` in `playwright.config.ts`, which instructs the test runner to capture git metadata (commit hash, branch name, and uncommitted diff summary) and embed it in the HTML test report and trace files. In a BDD workflow, this feature closes the provenance gap between a Cucumber HTML report and the source code it validates: stakeholders can view a scenario result in the report and immediately see which commit and branch produced it, removing the need to cross-reference CI build numbers manually. When `captureGitInfo` is enabled, the HTML report header displays the commit SHA and branch alongside the test run date, making living documentation reports genuinely traceable to a specific code version. This is particularly valuable for compliance-driven BDD workflows where auditors need to match a passing feature file to a deployable artifact.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — captureGitInfo for BDD living-documentation provenance
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/**/*.ts',
  // Generate self-contained report with git provenance
  outputDir: '.bdd',
});

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  reporter: [
    // Playwright HTML report with git provenance embedded
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'reports/playwright-html', open: 'never' }],
    // Cucumber HTML report for stakeholder consumption
    ['playwright-bdd/reporter/cucumber-html', {
      outputFile: 'reports/living-docs/index.html',
    }],
  ],
  // v1.49: capture git commit SHA, branch, and diff for living-doc provenance
  captureGitInfo: {
    commit: true,  // embed commit SHA in reports
    diff: true,    // include uncommitted diff summary for in-progress CI runs
  },
  use: {
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Enable `captureGitInfo: { commit: true, diff: false }` in production CI to avoid embedding potentially sensitive diff content in reports distributed to external stakeholders — diff content may include environment-specific secrets in comments or configuration values that were not yet committed. Do NOT rely on `captureGitInfo` as a substitute for tagging your Docker image or build artifact with the commit SHA in your CI pipeline; `captureGitInfo` embeds metadata in the report file only, and if the report is re-generated from a different commit, the provenance will be incorrect. [official]

---

### Pattern 3 — Playwright v1.50 `test.step.skip()` for Conditional BDD Step Execution in Data-Driven Scenarios  [official]

Playwright v1.50 adds `test.step.skip()` as a first-class method on the `test.step` API, allowing individual steps within a test to be conditionally skipped rather than requiring the entire scenario to be skipped or a conditional branch to be embedded in step definition logic. In playwright-bdd, each Gherkin step corresponds to a `test.step` call internally; `test.step.skip()` surfaces as a declarative mechanism to mark a specific step as intentionally not executed without failing the test or hiding the step from the report. This is particularly useful in data-driven `Scenario Outline` step definitions where some `Examples` rows represent data combinations that legally skip a particular verification: rather than using an `if` guard that silently skips logic, `test.step.skip()` explicitly marks the step as skipped in the Playwright HTML report, giving visibility into which data combinations exercised which assertions.

```typescript
// steps/promotionSteps.ts — test.step.skip() for conditional BDD step execution
import { Given, When, Then } from './bdd';
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

interface PromotionWorld {
  productPrice: number;
  promoCode: string | null;
  finalPrice: number;
}

declare module '@cucumber/cucumber' {
  interface World extends PromotionWorld {}
}

Given('a product costs {float} dollars', async function (this: PromotionWorld, price: number) {
  this.productPrice = price;
});

Given('I have a promo code {string}', async function (this: PromotionWorld, code: string) {
  this.promoCode = code === 'NONE' ? null : code;
});

When('I apply the promo code at checkout', async function (
  this: PromotionWorld,
  { page }: { page: import('@playwright/test').Page },
) {
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Promo code' }).fill(this.promoCode ?? '');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Apply' }).click();
  const priceText = await page.getByTestId('final-price').textContent();
  this.finalPrice = parseFloat(priceText?.replace('$', '') ?? '0');
});

Then('the discount should be applied to the price', async function (this: PromotionWorld) {
  await test.step('Verify discount applied', async (stepInfo) => {
    if (!this.promoCode) {
      // Explicitly skip — no promo code for this Examples row, step is intentionally inapplicable
      await stepInfo.skip();
      return;
    }
    expect(this.finalPrice).toBeLessThan(this.productPrice);
  });
});

Then('the final price should be {float} dollars', async function (
  this: PromotionWorld,
  expectedPrice: number,
) {
  expect(this.finalPrice).toBeCloseTo(expectedPrice, 2);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `test.step.skip()` sparingly and only when a step is semantically inapplicable for a given data combination, not when a step is failing — using `skip()` to suppress failures produces a green report that hides real regressions. Do NOT use `test.step.skip()` as a substitute for splitting your `Scenario Outline` into separate scenarios when two `Examples` rows represent fundamentally different business rules; if more than 30% of your `Examples` rows skip the same step, that is a design signal to decompose the outline into separate scenarios with distinct When-Then blocks. [official]

---

### Pattern 4 — Playwright v1.51 `locator.filter({ visible: true })` for Dynamic-UI BDD Step Assertions  [official]

Playwright v1.51 adds the `visible: true` option to `locator.filter()`, allowing step definitions to scope assertions to only the DOM elements that are currently visible on the page rather than relying on `toBeVisible()` assertions on each element individually. In BDD step definitions that assert the state of a list (e.g., "Then I should see 3 active promotions"), teams previously had to use `locator.all()` and filter the resulting array manually with `toBeVisible()` checks or use CSS `:visible` selectors that are not universally reliable. With `locator.filter({ visible: true })`, a single chain call narrows the match set to visible elements before the count assertion, producing a more predictable and readable step definition.

```typescript
// steps/promotionListSteps.ts — locator.filter({ visible: true }) for list-count BDD assertions
import { Then } from './bdd';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Then(
  'I should see {int} active promotions',
  async ({ page }, count: number) => {
    // v1.51: filter({ visible: true }) scopes to on-screen items only
    // works correctly even when hidden promotions exist in the DOM (e.g. display:none)
    const visiblePromotions = page
      .getByRole('listitem', { name: /promotion/i })
      .filter({ visible: true });

    await expect(visiblePromotions).toHaveCount(count);
  }
);

Then(
  'the {string} promotion should be highlighted',
  async ({ page }, promoName: string) => {
    const visiblePromos = page
      .getByTestId('promotion-card')
      .filter({ visible: true })
      .filter({ hasText: promoName });

    await expect(visiblePromos).toHaveCount(1);
    await expect(visiblePromos.first()).toHaveClass(/highlighted/);
  }
);

Then(
  'no expired promotions should be visible',
  async ({ page }) => {
    const expiredVisible = page
      .getByTestId('promotion-card')
      .filter({ visible: true })
      .filter({ has: page.getByTestId('expired-badge') });

    await expect(expiredVisible).toHaveCount(0);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `locator.filter({ visible: true })` for BDD step assertions on lists where the DOM may contain hidden elements from server-side rendering or lazy-load patterns — it is more reliable than CSS `:visible` selectors (which do not account for `opacity: 0` or `visibility: hidden` elements) and more readable than post-hoc filtering with `.all()`. Do NOT combine `filter({ visible: true })` with a zero-count expectation as the sole assertion in a step — if an element is entirely absent from the DOM (never rendered), `filter({ visible: true })` correctly returns 0, but if the element exists but is hidden, it also returns 0; when "no elements should be shown" is a business rule, add a secondary assertion that checks the element's absence from the DOM to distinguish "absent" from "hidden". [official]

---

### Pattern 5 — Cucumber.js v12.3.0 Named `BeforeAll`/`AfterAll` Hooks with `order` Option for Deterministic Suite Lifecycle  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.3.0 (December 2024) extends the `BeforeAll` and `AfterAll` hook APIs to accept a `name` string and an `order` number as options, enabling teams to give lifecycle hooks human-readable identifiers that appear in error messages and reports, and to control the sequence in which multiple hooks of the same type execute when they are defined across different support files. Prior to v12.3, when two `BeforeAll` hooks in different support files both attempted to seed the same shared database, the execution order was load-order dependent — whichever file happened to be loaded first would execute its `BeforeAll` first, creating a brittle dependency on file system enumeration order. With `order`, lower numbers execute first (default is 10000, same as existing behavior), and `name` surfaces in Cucumber's HTML report and error output so that a failing `BeforeAll` identifies itself as "seed:admin-users" rather than "anonymous hook".

```typescript
// support/hooks/dbHooks.ts — named BeforeAll/AfterAll with order for deterministic suite lifecycle
import { BeforeAll, AfterAll } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { DatabaseClient } from '../db/DatabaseClient';
import { SeedService } from '../db/SeedService';

let db: DatabaseClient;
let seedService: SeedService;

// order: 100 — runs first: establish connection before any seeding
BeforeAll({ name: 'db:connect', order: 100 }, async function () {
  db = await DatabaseClient.connect(process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL!);
  (globalThis as any).__testDb = db;
});

// order: 200 — runs after db:connect: seed reference data required by all scenarios
BeforeAll({ name: 'seed:reference-data', order: 200 }, async function () {
  seedService = new SeedService((globalThis as any).__testDb);
  await seedService.seedCountries();
  await seedService.seedCurrencies();
});

// order: 300 — runs last in BeforeAll sequence: seed admin users that depend on reference data
BeforeAll({ name: 'seed:admin-users', order: 300 }, async function () {
  await seedService.seedAdminUsers();
});

// AfterAll order mirrors BeforeAll in reverse: clean up in dependency order
AfterAll({ name: 'cleanup:scenario-data', order: 100 }, async function () {
  await seedService.cleanupScenarioData();
});

AfterAll({ name: 'cleanup:reference-data', order: 200 }, async function () {
  await seedService.cleanupReferenceData();
});

AfterAll({ name: 'db:disconnect', order: 300 }, async function () {
  await db.disconnect();
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `order` values in multiples of 100 so that future hooks can be inserted between existing ones without renumbering — if you use `order: 1` and `order: 2` and need to insert a hook between them, you have no room; multiples of 100 leave 99 slots between each pair. Do NOT rely on `name` alone to enforce ordering across support files loaded by different Cucumber profiles — `name` is informational and does not affect execution order; only `order` does. [official]

---

### Pattern 6 — Cucumber.js v12.4.0 TypeScript Config Loading via Node.js Strip-Types with `satisfies`  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.4.0 (December 2024) introduces native TypeScript configuration file loading without requiring `tsx`, `ts-node`, or any TypeScript compilation step at runtime, by leveraging Node.js 22+'s built-in `--experimental-strip-types` flag to strip type annotations at load time. Teams can now name their config file `cucumber.config.ts` and export a typed `IConfiguration` object using the `satisfies` operator instead of maintaining a separate `cucumber.config.js` or a dual `.ts`/`.js` pair. The `satisfies` keyword (TypeScript 4.9+) is the preferred pattern because it validates the configuration shape at compile time without widening the inferred type, catching errors like typos in profile names at `tsc` time rather than at runtime. This feature is gated on Node.js 22 or later; projects on Node.js 20 must continue using `tsx` or `ts-node`.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — native TypeScript config with satisfies (v12.4.0 + Node.js 22+)
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

// 'satisfies' validates against IConfiguration without widening the type —
// typos in property names (e.g. 'profles' instead of 'profiles') are caught at tsc time
export default {
  default: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    require: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    format: ['progress-bar', 'html:reports/cucumber.html'],
    formatOptions: { snippetInterface: 'async-await' },
    worldParameters: {
      baseUrl: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    },
    parallel: 4,
  },
  ci: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    require: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    format: [
      'progress-bar',
      `html:reports/cucumber-${process.env.CI_BUILD_ID ?? 'local'}.html`,
      'json:reports/cucumber.json',
    ],
    parallel: parseInt(process.env.CI_WORKERS ?? '8', 10),
    failFast: true,
  },
} satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>;
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>` rather than `as IConfiguration` — `as` is a type assertion that suppresses type errors, while `satisfies` validates the type and still preserves narrowed literal types needed for IDE autocomplete on profile names. Do NOT use `import type` for `IConfiguration` in `cucumber.config.ts` when loaded via Node.js strip-types — strip-types has limitations with complex re-export chains from declaration files; use `import { IConfiguration }` (value import) which also works correctly because TypeScript erases interface imports from compiled output anyway. [official]

---

### Pattern 7 — Playwright v1.52 `toContainClass()` for CSS-State-Driven BDD Assertions  [official]

Playwright v1.52 (2025) adds `expect(locator).toContainClass()` as a new assertion method that tests for the presence of an individual CSS class name within a `class` attribute, avoiding the brittle string-matching behavior of `toHaveClass()` which requires the full class string or a regex. In BDD step definitions that validate UI state changes (e.g., "Then the submit button should be disabled"), CSS utility frameworks like Tailwind and Bootstrap encode state in class names (`disabled`, `is-loading`, `has-error`, `active`). Before `toContainClass()`, teams used either `toHaveClass(/disabled/)` (fragile regex) or `getAttribute('class')` followed by string parsing — both approaches break when the SUT changes its class ordering or adds new utility classes. `toContainClass()` checks for exact class-token membership, not substring matching.

```typescript
// steps/formSteps.ts — toContainClass() for CSS-state BDD assertions (Playwright v1.52+)
import { Then } from './bdd';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Then('the submit button should be in a loading state', async ({ page }) => {
  const submitBtn = page.getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i });
  // v1.52: toContainClass() checks for 'is-loading' as a CSS class token,
  // not a substring — 'is-loading-animation' would NOT match
  await expect(submitBtn).toContainClass('is-loading');
  await expect(submitBtn).toContainClass('cursor-not-allowed');
});

Then('the password field should show a validation error', async ({ page }) => {
  const passwordField = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: /password/i });
  await expect(passwordField).toContainClass('border-red-500');
  await expect(passwordField).toHaveAttribute('aria-invalid', 'true');
});

Then('the active navigation item should be {string}', async ({ page }, itemLabel: string) => {
  const navItem = page.getByRole('link', { name: itemLabel });
  await expect(navItem).toContainClass('active');
  await expect(navItem).toHaveAttribute('aria-current', 'page');
});

Then('the form should not have any field-level errors', async ({ page }) => {
  const errorFields = page.locator('[class*="error"]').filter({ visible: true });
  await expect(errorFields).toHaveCount(0);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `toContainClass()` over `toHaveClass(/regex/)` for all CSS-state assertions in BDD step definitions — regex-based class assertions break silently when component libraries add new utility classes to elements (e.g., a style system upgrade that adds `transition-colors` to all buttons will cause `toHaveClass(/^btn disabled$/)` to fail even though the button is correctly disabled). Do NOT use `toContainClass()` to assert that a class is absent — the method only asserts presence; for absence assertions, use `expect(locator).not.toContainClass('error-state')`. [official]

---

### Pattern 8 — Cucumber Messages v32 `ExternalAttachment` Migration: Deprecating `Attachment.url`  [official]

Cucumber Messages v32.0.0 formally deprecates the `Attachment.url` and `Attachment.source` fields that were used in v27 as an ad-hoc mechanism for externalizing attachment content, replacing them with the dedicated `ExternalAttachment` message type which has clearer semantics and a consistent `contentType`/`mediaType` pair. Teams building custom formatters or reading the Cucumber NDJSON message stream directly must update their message consumers to handle both `Attachment` and `ExternalAttachment` message types during the migration window, because `@cucumber/messages` v32 will produce `ExternalAttachment` messages from tooling that has been upgraded while the runner still emits `Attachment` messages with deprecated fields for tooling that has not yet upgraded. The `ExternalAttachment` message also introduces a `size` field (optional) for pre-flight size checks in report aggregators.

```typescript
// support/reporting/messageConsumer.ts — handling Attachment + ExternalAttachment (v32 migration)
import { Envelope, Attachment, ExternalAttachment } from '@cucumber/messages';

export class BddMessageConsumer {
  private attachments: Array<{ scenarioId: string; content: string; url?: string }> = [];

  processEnvelope(envelope: Envelope): void {
    if (envelope.attachment) {
      this.handleAttachment(envelope.attachment);
    }
    // v32: handle ExternalAttachment as a separate top-level envelope type
    if (envelope.externalAttachment) {
      this.handleExternalAttachment(envelope.externalAttachment);
    }
  }

  private handleAttachment(attachment: Attachment): void {
    const { testCaseStartedId, body, url, mediaType } = attachment;
    if (url) {
      // v27 deprecated path: attachment references external URL via Attachment.url
      console.warn(`[BDD Reporter] Attachment.url is deprecated in @cucumber/messages v32. `
        + `Migrate to ExternalAttachment. testCaseStartedId=${testCaseStartedId}`);
      this.attachments.push({ scenarioId: testCaseStartedId!, url, content: '' });
    } else {
      this.attachments.push({ scenarioId: testCaseStartedId!, content: body ?? '' });
    }
  }

  private handleExternalAttachment(external: ExternalAttachment): void {
    // v32 canonical path: ExternalAttachment with explicit url + contentType
    const { testCaseStartedId, url, contentType, size } = external;
    if (size !== undefined && size > 50 * 1024 * 1024) {
      console.warn(`[BDD Reporter] Large attachment detected (${size} bytes): ${url}`);
    }
    this.attachments.push({ scenarioId: testCaseStartedId!, url, content: '' });
  }
}
```

**Tradeoff**: Update custom message consumers to handle `ExternalAttachment` envelopes before upgrading `@cucumber/messages` to v32 — tooling that only handles `Attachment` envelopes will silently miss externalized attachments in v32 reports without any runtime error, producing incomplete reports that appear correct. Do NOT access `envelope.attachment.url` in new code even though it compiles without error — the TypeScript type definition still includes it in v32 for backward compatibility but the field is deprecated and will be removed in v33; use `envelope.externalAttachment.url` from the dedicated `ExternalAttachment` type instead. [official]

---

### Pattern 9 — playwright-bdd v9 URI-Indexed Pickle Lookup for Large Feature-File Suites  [official]

playwright-bdd v9.0.0-beta.0 (May 2025) optimizes the internal pickle lookup mechanism by replacing a linear scan over all pickles with a URI-indexed map, reducing test generation time from O(n×m) (pickles × features) to O(1) per feature file lookup. This change is transparent for suites with fewer than 100 feature files but produces significant improvements for enterprise suites with 500+ feature files: `bddgen` (the playwright-bdd test generation CLI) dropped from 45 seconds to under 3 seconds in a case study with 800 feature files. The change is implemented in the `bddgen` codepath and requires no configuration changes — existing `playwright.config.ts` files work unchanged. For teams that call `bddgen` as a CI pre-step before `playwright test`, the wall-clock savings directly reduce CI queue time.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — no config changes needed for v9 URI-indexed pickle lookup
// but enabling verbose mode shows pickle lookup timing for diagnosis
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/**/*.feature',
  steps: [
    'src/steps/common/**/*.ts',
    'src/steps/domain/**/*.ts',
  ],
  outputDir: '.bdd',
  // v9: enrichReporterData option was removed — use Playwright trace instead
  verbose: true,  // shows URI-indexed pickle lookup timing in --verbose mode
});

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  fullyParallel: true,
  workers: process.env.CI ? 8 : 4,
  reporter: [
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'reports/html', open: 'never' }],
    ['junit', { outputFile: 'reports/junit.xml', nameFormat: 'cucumber' }],
  ],
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
  ],
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The URI-indexed lookup improvement in v9 benefits `bddgen` test generation time, not Playwright test execution time — if your CI bottleneck is test execution (scenarios running slowly), the v9 optimization will not help; profile `bddgen` separately from `playwright test` to determine whether generation or execution dominates your CI wall-clock time. Do NOT use the `--cpus` flag to override the v9 worker concurrency cap when running `bddgen` — v9 caps concurrency at `Math.floor(os.cpus().length / 2)` specifically to prevent OOM on machines with 4+ cores; the cap is intentional and lowering it further (not raising it) is the correct tuning direction for memory-constrained CI agents. [official]

---

### Pattern 10 — Playwright v1.53 `testInfo.snapshotPath({ kind })` for Multi-Variant BDD Snapshot Management  [official]

Playwright v1.53 (2025) extends `testInfo.snapshotPath()` with a `kind` option that controls which snapshot naming template is applied, enabling teams to maintain separate snapshot sets for different test variants (e.g., mobile vs. desktop, authenticated vs. anonymous) within the same BDD scenario without creating separate scenario files for each variant. Before v1.53, teams that ran the same scenario against multiple viewport configurations stored all snapshots in the same directory and used long naming conventions to avoid collisions (`checkout-step-1-mobile-1280x720.png`). The `kind` option maps to a named template in `testProject.snapshotPathTemplate`, allowing short, semantic snapshot names in step definitions while the template handles path disambiguation.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — snapshotPath kind option for multi-variant BDD snapshots (v1.53+)
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/visual/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/visual/**/*.ts',
  outputDir: '.bdd',
});

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  snapshotPathTemplate: '{testDir}/__snapshots__/{testFilePath}/{arg}-{kind}{ext}',
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'desktop-chrome',
      snapshotPathTemplate: '{testDir}/__snapshots__/desktop/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] },
    },
    {
      name: 'mobile-safari',
      snapshotPathTemplate: '{testDir}/__snapshots__/mobile/{testFilePath}/{arg}{ext}',
      use: { ...devices['iPhone 14'] },
    },
  ],
});

// steps/visual/checkoutVisualSteps.ts
import { Then } from '../bdd';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Then('the checkout page should match the approved design', async ({ page }, testInfo) => {
  // v1.53: kind option selects the naming template variant
  const snapshotPath = testInfo.snapshotPath('checkout-page', { kind: 'semantic' });

  await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(snapshotPath, {
    maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01,
    animations: 'disabled',
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use separate `snapshotPathTemplate` per project (as shown above) rather than the `kind` option when you want project-level snapshot isolation — project-level templates are simpler to reason about and produce cleaner directory structures. Use `kind` when you need dynamic variant selection within a single step definition (e.g., a step that takes both a `full-page` and an `above-fold` screenshot and stores them under different names). Do NOT mix `kind`-based naming and project-level `snapshotPathTemplate` in the same suite without documenting the convention — the interaction between the two produces path templates that are difficult to predict without running a generation dry-run. [official]

---

### Pattern 11 — Cucumber.js Formatter Redesign: `includeAttachments` Replacing `printAttachments`  [official]

The Cucumber.js formatter architecture redesign (unreleased / next major branch) renames the `printAttachments` option to `includeAttachments` in the HTML formatter configuration, deprecates the `SummaryFormatter` and `ProgressFormatter` classes in favor of new functional formatter identifiers (`summary`, `progress`, `progress-bar`, `pretty`), and aligns attachment rendering behavior with the `ExternalAttachment` message type introduced in `@cucumber/messages` v32. The `includeAttachments: true` option controls whether the HTML report renders attachment content inline (images, logs, traces) or omits attachment content from the rendered report while retaining attachment metadata in the underlying NDJSON for programmatic consumption. When `includeAttachments` is `true` and an attachment is an `ExternalAttachment`, the HTML formatter renders an anchor tag pointing to the external URL rather than trying to embed the content inline.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — includeAttachments option (replaces printAttachments in formatter redesign)
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber/api';

export default {
  default: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    require: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    format: [
      // New formatter name (formatter redesign — replaces class-based formatters)
      'progress',
      'html:reports/cucumber.html',
    ],
    formatOptions: {
      // BEFORE (deprecated): printAttachments: true
      // AFTER (formatter redesign): includeAttachments
      includeAttachments: true,
    },
  },
  ci: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    require: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    format: [
      'progress',
      `html:reports/cucumber-ci.html`,
      'json:reports/cucumber.json',
    ],
    formatOptions: {
      // In CI, disable inline embedding for large binary attachments to prevent OOM
      includeAttachments: false,
    },
    parallel: 8,
  },
} satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>;
```

**Tradeoff**: Set `includeAttachments: false` in CI profile configurations where scenarios attach large binary files (screenshots, video recordings, HAR archives) — the Cucumber HTML formatter holds all attachment content in memory before writing the report file, and embedding 200 screenshots inline can exhaust Node.js heap during report generation. Do NOT set `includeAttachments: false` in the development profile when developers rely on the HTML report to debug test failures locally — without inline attachment rendering, developers must navigate to external URLs or trace files separately, significantly increasing debug cycle time. [official]

---

### Pattern 12 — Playwright v1.46 `--only-changed` for Fast BDD Iteration Feedback Loops  [official]

Playwright v1.46 introduces the `--only-changed` CLI flag (and the equivalent `onlyChanged` test config option) that instructs the test runner to execute only tests in files that have been modified since the last git commit, enabling BDD practitioners to get sub-10-second feedback during step definition authoring without waiting for the full suite. In BDD workflows, the typical inner loop is: edit feature file → update step definition → run affected tests → verify behavior. Before `--only-changed`, teams either ran a specific feature file by path (manual and error-prone) or ran the full suite (slow). With `--only-changed`, `playwright test --only-changed` automatically identifies modified `.ts` step definition files via `git status` and runs only the generated test files that import changed step definitions.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — onlyChanged option gated on development environment
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/**/*.ts',
  outputDir: '.bdd',
});

const isDev = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development';
const isCI = !!process.env.CI;

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  // v1.46: only run tests for modified files in dev mode
  ...(isDev && !isCI ? { onlyChanged: true } : {}),
  reporter: isDev
    ? [['list']]
    : [['html', { outputFolder: 'reports/html', open: 'never' }],
       ['junit', { outputFile: 'reports/junit.xml' }]],
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: isDev ? 'on' : 'retain-on-failure',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `--only-changed` during step definition authoring but disable it before committing — `--only-changed` does not detect changes in support files (World class, fixture definitions, shared utilities) that are imported by step definitions but not themselves test files; a change to the World class that breaks all steps will show zero failing tests with `--only-changed` because the World file itself was not changed. Do NOT use `--only-changed` in CI pipelines — CI must run the full suite to provide regression confidence; `--only-changed` is a developer-experience optimization for the local inner loop only. [official]

---

### Pattern 13 — Playwright v1.54 `noSnippets` HTML Reporter for Clean BDD Artifact Distribution  [official]

Playwright v1.54 adds the `noSnippets` configuration option to the HTML reporter, suppressing the code snippet display that normally appears alongside failing test output in the Playwright HTML report. In BDD workflows where the HTML report is distributed to non-developer stakeholders (product owners, QA managers, compliance auditors), the code snippet display exposes implementation details that are irrelevant or confusing to non-technical audiences and may include framework-internal stack frames that make the report appear more complex than the corresponding Gherkin scenario description. Setting `noSnippets: true` produces a cleaner stakeholder-facing report that matches the Cucumber HTML report's stakeholder-oriented presentation without requiring teams to maintain two separate report formats.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — noSnippets for stakeholder-facing BDD reports (v1.54+)
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/**/*.ts',
  outputDir: '.bdd',
});

const isStakeholderReport = process.env.REPORT_MODE === 'stakeholder';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  reporter: [
    [
      'html',
      {
        outputFolder: 'reports/html',
        open: 'never',
        // v1.54: suppress code snippets for clean stakeholder distribution
        noSnippets: isStakeholderReport,
      },
    ],
    // Cucumber HTML report is always clean (no code snippets by design)
    ['playwright-bdd/reporter/cucumber-html', {
      outputFile: 'reports/living-docs/index.html',
    }],
    ['junit', { outputFile: 'reports/junit.xml', nameFormat: 'cucumber' }],
  ],
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `noSnippets: true` for the report generated at the end of a CI pipeline that uploads artifacts to a stakeholder portal, and keep a separate developer report with `noSnippets: false` so developers can debug failures from the detailed report. Do NOT use `noSnippets: true` as the only report format in development workflows — without snippets, developers must navigate to the full trace file to see the step code context for a failing assertion, which adds friction to the debug loop that `noSnippets` is specifically designed to remove for non-developer audiences. [official]

---

### Pattern 14 — Playwright v1.48 `page.routeWebSocket()` for Real-Time BDD Scenario Mocking  [official]

Playwright v1.48 introduces `page.routeWebSocket()` and `browserContext.routeWebSocket()` for intercepting, mocking, and asserting on WebSocket connections, enabling BDD scenarios to test real-time collaboration features, live dashboards, and notification systems without requiring a live WebSocket server. Before v1.48, teams testing WebSocket-dependent features in BDD had two brittle options: run a real WebSocket server in the CI environment (complex infrastructure dependency) or use `page.route()` to intercept HTTP upgrade requests (which only worked for some WebSocket libraries and required low-level HTTP knowledge). `page.routeWebSocket()` provides a high-level API that mirrors the `page.route()` experience, with `ws.send()`, `ws.receive()`, and `ws.close()` methods for controlling the mock server's behavior from step definitions.

```typescript
// steps/notificationSteps.ts — WebSocket mocking with page.routeWebSocket() (v1.48+)
import { Given, When, Then } from './bdd';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import type { WebSocketRoute } from '@playwright/test';

// Store per-scenario in World in production — module-level shown for brevity
let wsRoute: WebSocketRoute | null = null;

Given('I am viewing my order dashboard', async ({ page }) => {
  // Intercept WebSocket connection before navigating — route must be set up first
  await page.routeWebSocket('wss://api.example.com/notifications', (route) => {
    wsRoute = route;
    route.connect();
  });
  await page.goto('/dashboard/orders');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'My Orders' })).toBeVisible();
});

When(
  'the order processing system sends an {string} event',
  async ({ page }, eventType: string) => {
    if (!wsRoute) throw new Error('WebSocket route not initialized');
    // Send a mock WebSocket message from the server to the browser
    await wsRoute.send(JSON.stringify({
      type: eventType,
      orderId: 'ORD-2026-001',
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      message: 'Your order has shipped!',
    }));
  }
);

Then('I should see a {string} notification badge', async ({ page }, message: string) => {
  const badge = page.getByRole('status', { name: message });
  await expect(badge).toBeVisible({ timeout: 5_000 });
});

Then('the notification count should be {int}', async ({ page }, count: number) => {
  const counter = page.getByTestId('notification-count');
  await expect(counter).toHaveText(count.toString());
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `browserContext.routeWebSocket()` instead of `page.routeWebSocket()` when a BDD scenario involves multiple pages that share the same WebSocket connection (e.g., a multi-tab test) — page-level routes intercept connections initiated by that specific page only; context-level routes intercept all WebSocket connections from any page in the context. Do NOT store `wsRoute` as a module-level variable in production step definitions — use the playwright-bdd World to store `wsRoute` per-scenario to ensure test isolation; module-level state leaks between parallel scenarios and causes flaky tests in `--workers > 1` mode. [official]

---

### Pattern 15 — Playwright v1.52 `testProject.workers` for Per-Project Worker Allocation in Mixed BDD Suites  [official]

Playwright v1.52 adds `testProject.workers` as a per-project configuration option, complementing the existing global `workers` option, allowing BDD suites with multiple test projects (e.g., separate API and UI test projects) to allocate different worker counts per project based on the resource requirements of each project's scenarios. API-level BDD scenarios (no browser, fast) can run with 16 workers while UI-level BDD scenarios (full browser, slow) run with 4 workers — both can share the same `playwright.config.ts` and run in the same `playwright test` invocation, with the runner managing worker pools independently per project. This eliminates the need for separate CI steps with different `--workers` flags for different scenario tiers.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — per-project workers for mixed API+UI BDD suites (Playwright v1.52+)
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig } from 'playwright-bdd';

const apiBddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/api/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/api/**/*.ts',
  outputDir: '.bdd/api',
});

const uiBddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/ui/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/ui/**/*.ts',
  outputDir: '.bdd/ui',
});

export default defineConfig({
  workers: process.env.CI ? 4 : 2,
  reporter: [
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'reports/html', open: 'never' }],
    ['junit', { outputFile: 'reports/junit.xml', nameFormat: 'cucumber' }],
  ],
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'api-bdd',
      testDir: apiBddConfig.testDir,
      // v1.52: API scenarios are CPU-light — run with 16 workers in CI
      workers: process.env.CI ? 16 : 4,
      use: {
        baseURL: process.env.API_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
      },
    },
    {
      name: 'ui-bdd-chrome',
      testDir: uiBddConfig.testDir,
      // UI scenarios are browser-heavy — limit to 4 workers to prevent OOM
      workers: process.env.CI ? 4 : 2,
      use: {
        baseURL: process.env.UI_BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
        browserName: 'chromium',
        headless: true,
        trace: 'retain-on-failure',
        screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
      },
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Use `testProject.workers` to encode the resource profile of each scenario tier in configuration rather than in CI pipeline scripts — configuration-as-code for worker counts means that project members and CI pipeline maintainers can see the rationale for different concurrency levels in the same file as the test configuration, reducing the risk of well-intentioned CI "optimizations" that over-allocate workers to browser tests and cause OOM crashes. Do NOT set `testProject.workers` higher than `Math.floor(os.cpus().length / browserCount)` for browser-based test projects — each Playwright worker spawns a separate browser process, and overallocating browser workers on a 4-core CI agent causes context switches that slow test execution rather than accelerating it. [official]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 37

**[community] Gotcha 1 — Cucumber.js ESM mode breaks TypeScript path alias resolution configured via `tsconfig.json` `paths`, causing step definition files that use `@/` or `~/` import aliases to fail with `Cannot find module '@/support/world'` at runtime even though `tsc --noEmit` compiles the same code without errors, because Node.js ESM loader does not read `tsconfig.json` and does not perform path alias substitution**: Teams that migrate from CommonJS to ESM Cucumber.js while using path aliases for shared step definition utilities encounter runtime module resolution failures that do not appear during type checking. WHY this is confusing: `tsc --noEmit` succeeds because TypeScript resolves aliases during type checking but does not write output files — the alias resolution happens transparently during compilation but is never applied to the ESM runtime import, and the error message names the alias literally (`@/support/world`) rather than the resolved path, which looks like a typo or missing file to developers unfamiliar with how TypeScript path aliases work. Fix: add `tsconfig-paths/register` via an ESM loader hook in `cucumber.config.ts` using `loader: ['tsx']`, or replace TypeScript path aliases with `package.json` `imports` field (`"#support/*": "./src/support/*.js"`) which Node.js ESM resolves natively without any loader hook.

**[community] Gotcha 2 — Cucumber.js v12.4.0 `import` statement in `cucumber.config.ts` when loaded via Node.js strip-types produces `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'default')` rather than a clear missing-module error, because Node.js strip-types processes type annotations but does not run the TypeScript module resolver, causing any `import` that resolves to a `.ts` file (rather than a pre-compiled `.js` file) to fail at runtime with an opaque undefined-property access**: Teams that place a `cucumber.config.ts` in the project root and import from relative paths (e.g., `import { TEST_USERS } from './src/support/testData'`) encounter the `TypeError` when the imported module is a `.ts` file that has not been pre-compiled. WHY teams miss this: the same import works perfectly when using `tsx` as the Cucumber loader because `tsx` compiles `.ts` files on the fly; after removing `tsx` for v12.4 native TypeScript support, the same `import` fails because Node.js strip-types does not compile, it only strips type annotations. Fix: only import from pre-compiled JavaScript files in `cucumber.config.ts` when using Node.js strip-types, or keep `tsx` as the loader for config loading even after upgrading to v12.4.

**[community] Gotcha 3 — playwright-bdd `defineBddProject()` generates an unexpected double-nested folder structure when the `outputDir` path already contains the project name as a path segment, producing a `.bdd/ui/ui/` directory instead of `.bdd/ui/`, because `defineBddProject` appends the project name to `outputDir` automatically, and the `testDir not found` error from `playwright test` does not mention `defineBddProject` by name, appearing to be a filesystem configuration problem rather than a naming collision**: Teams that set `outputDir: '.bdd/ui'` in a `defineBddProject` call for a project named `ui` discover that the generated test directory is `.bdd/ui/ui`. WHY this is surprising: the project name duplication behavior is not documented in the `defineBddProject` API reference, and the convention of setting `outputDir` to match the project name is a natural naming choice that works for `defineBddConfig` but not for `defineBddProject`. Fix: set `outputDir: '.bdd'` (no project name suffix) when using `defineBddProject` — the function appends the project name automatically; use `.bdd/<project-name>` only in `defineBddConfig` (the non-project variant) where no automatic appending occurs.

**[community] Gotcha 4 — Cucumber.js HTML formatter with external attachments renders as blank anchor tags when the report HTML is opened from the local filesystem (`file:///`) rather than from an HTTP server, because the formatter uses JavaScript `fetch()` to load the attachment preview content from the external URL, and `fetch()` is blocked by CORS policy when the page origin is `null` (the origin assigned to `file:///` pages in all modern browsers)**: Teams that generate Cucumber HTML reports in CI and download them as build artifacts for local review find that external attachment links render as blank anchors with no hover text or accessible name, and the browser console shows `CORS error: null origin not allowed` for the fetch requests. WHY teams don't notice this in CI: in CI, reports are served from an artifact server (HTTP origin), so fetch succeeds; the issue surfaces only when developers download the report ZIP and open `index.html` directly from disk. Fix: serve the report using `npx serve reports/` (a local HTTP server) rather than opening the HTML file directly from the filesystem; alternatively, use `includeAttachments: true` in development report profiles to embed attachments inline and avoid external attachment fetch entirely.

**[community] Gotcha 5 — Teams using playwright-bdd `BeforeScenario`/`AfterScenario` hook aliases in test suites that also use plain Cucumber.js `Before`/`After` hooks imported from `@cucumber/cucumber` discover that both hook sets execute, producing duplicate setup/teardown logic, because `BeforeScenario`/`AfterScenario` from playwright-bdd are fixtures-based hooks that execute via Playwright's fixture lifecycle while `Before`/`After` from Cucumber.js execute via Cucumber's runtime hook queue, and the two hook systems are independent and both active when playwright-bdd generates test files that include both imports**: Teams migrating from plain Cucumber.js to playwright-bdd incrementally keep their existing `@cucumber/cucumber` `Before`/`After` hooks and add playwright-bdd `BeforeScenario`/`AfterScenario` hooks for Playwright-specific setup. WHY teams don't notice immediately: the duplicate hooks are often idempotent (seeding the same data twice succeeds silently if upsert semantics are used), and the issue only surfaces when a non-idempotent hook causes a unique-constraint violation or an authentication rate-limit error after multiple runs. Fix: choose one hook system and migrate all hooks to it — use playwright-bdd `BeforeScenario`/`AfterScenario` exclusively when using playwright-bdd; remove all `@cucumber/cucumber` `Before`/`After` imports from files that run under playwright-bdd's test runner.

**[community] Gotcha 6 — Cucumber.js `FORCE_COLOR=1` environment variable (the v12.6 replacement for `colorsEnabled: true`) has no effect when Cucumber.js is spawned as a child process by a CI orchestrator that strips environment variables before forwarding them to test worker processes, because `v12.7` env var propagation to parallel workers only applies to variables passed via the `env` config option in `cucumber.config.ts`, not to variables inherited from the parent process environment**: After upgrading to v12.6+ and removing `colorsEnabled: true` from their format options in favor of `FORCE_COLOR=1` in the CI environment, teams find that parallel worker processes do not inherit `FORCE_COLOR`. WHY teams miss the `env` option: the v12.7 release notes mention env var propagation as a parallel-execution improvement, not as a color output fix, so teams reading the changelog for the color fix do not see the `env` option. Fix: add `env: ['FORCE_COLOR']` to the `default` (and any other parallel) profile in `cucumber.config.ts` to ensure worker processes inherit the `FORCE_COLOR` variable from the parent environment.

### Pattern 1 — Cucumber.js v12.8.3 Assertion Info in Stack Traces for BDD Failure Diagnosis  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.8.3 (released May 9, 2026) adds assertion information to stack traces produced when a step definition throws an assertion error, embedding the expected vs. actual values directly in the trace rather than requiring a developer to re-run with `--format message` to extract the failure details. This changes the standard failure output from a bare `AssertionError` line with a file/line reference to an enriched trace that includes the assertion subject, operator, and both operands inline, matching the detail level that Jest and Vitest reporters already provided for unit tests. The improvement is especially valuable for BDD suites running in headless CI where stdout is the only window into a failure: stakeholders reading a CI log can now see that `Expect "Pending" to equal "Confirmed"` without pulling the artifact archive. Previously, teams worked around this by catching assertion errors in After hooks and re-throwing with a custom message — that workaround is now unnecessary and can be removed.

```typescript
// features/step-definitions/order-status.steps.ts
// Cucumber.js v12.8.3 — enriched assertion stack traces
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { strict as assert } from 'node:assert';
import { OrderService } from '../../src/services/order-service.js';

let orderService: OrderService;
let orderId: string;

Given('an order {string} has been placed', async (id: string) => {
  orderService = new OrderService();
  orderId = id;
  await orderService.create({ id, status: 'Pending' });
});

When('the payment is confirmed', async () => {
  await orderService.confirmPayment(orderId);
});

Then('the order status should be {string}', async (expectedStatus: string) => {
  const order = await orderService.findById(orderId);
  // v12.8.3: if this fails, the stack trace now includes:
  //   AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Expected values to be strictly equal:
  //   + actual - expected
  //   + 'Pending'
  //   - 'Confirmed'
  //
  // Previously only showed: AssertionError at order-status.steps.ts:22
  assert.strictEqual(order.status, expectedStatus);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The enriched stack trace output only applies to errors thrown by Node.js `assert` (and assertion libraries that produce `AssertionError` instances with `.actual` and `.expected` properties, such as Chai's `assert` mode). Libraries that throw plain `Error` instances with descriptive messages (Jest `expect`, Playwright `expect`) are unaffected — their messages already contain the assertion detail. Do NOT remove custom error-enrichment After hooks that handle non-`AssertionError` throws (e.g., HTTP 500 responses stored on World) — those cover failures that `v12.8.3` does not. [official]

---

### Pattern 2 — playwright-bdd v8.5.1: Playwright 1.60 Compatibility Patch and Upgrade Path  [official]

playwright-bdd v8.5.1 (released May 12, 2026) is a targeted compatibility patch that resolves a runtime failure where Playwright 1.60's internal refactoring of the `configLoader` module caused `bddgen` to crash with `Cannot find module '@playwright/test/lib/common/configLoader'` before generating any test files. The patch updates playwright-bdd's internal import resolution to use the public Playwright API surface rather than private internal modules, making it robust against future Playwright internal restructuring. Teams on playwright-bdd v8.5.0 and Playwright 1.60 must upgrade to v8.5.1 before any BDD scenarios can run — the failure happens at code generation time, not test execution, so `playwright test` exits immediately with no test results. The v8.5.1 patch carries no breaking changes and can be applied as a drop-in replacement.

```typescript
// package.json minimum version requirements after playwright-bdd v8.5.1 release
// {
//   "devDependencies": {
//     "playwright-bdd": "^8.5.1",      // v8.5.0 crashes with Playwright 1.60+
//     "@playwright/test": "^1.60.0"    // any 1.60.x is safe after v8.5.1 patch
//   }
// }

// playwright.config.ts — setup unchanged by the patch
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig, BddFixtures } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/**/*.ts',
  outputDir: '.bdd',
});

export default defineConfig<BddFixtures>({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  reporter: [
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'reports/html', open: 'never' }],
    ['junit', { outputFile: 'reports/junit.xml' }],
  ],
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
  },
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { browserName: 'chromium' },
    },
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Always pin playwright-bdd to a minor version range (`^8.5.1`) rather than an exact version (`8.5.1`) to receive future patch releases automatically — playwright-bdd follows semver and patch releases fix compatibility breaks without API changes. Do NOT pin to `^8.5.0` after Playwright 1.60 is installed — the configLoader crash is reproducible 100% of the time on any project using `bddgen` and no workaround exists short of downgrading Playwright. If your project uses `pnpm` with a lockfile and `playwright-bdd` is a transitive dependency of another tool, verify the lockfile resolves to `>=8.5.1` explicitly; `pnpm why playwright-bdd` shows the resolved version. [official]

### Pattern 3 — playwright-bdd v9.0.0-beta.0: Strict Cucumber-Compatible Step Arity Validation  [official]

playwright-bdd v9.0.0-beta.0 introduces strict Cucumber-compatible arity validation for step definitions at `bddgen` time, rejecting step functions whose TypeScript parameter count does not match the number of capture groups produced by the step's Cucumber Expression or Regular Expression. This is a breaking change from v8.x, where a mismatch between expression captures and function parameters was silently allowed, sometimes causing `undefined` to be passed for missing parameters at runtime. The validation fires during code generation (before any test runs), so the failure is visible immediately in the `bddgen` output rather than as a cryptic `undefined is not a function` error during scenario execution. The error message names both the step expression and the function signature, making the mismatch obvious without reading the source.

```typescript
// features/step-definitions/payment.steps.ts
// playwright-bdd v9.0.0-beta.0 strict arity validation

// BEFORE (v8.x silently accepted this — 2 captures, 1 param):
// Given('the user {string} pays {float}', async (amount: number) => {
//   // 'username' capture is silently discarded; amount receives username string
//   // This caused confusing "NaN" errors at runtime
// });

// AFTER (v9.0 bddgen error: "Step has 2 captures but function has 1 parameter"):
// Fix: always declare all capture parameters in the correct order
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test } from './fixtures.js';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

// v9.0: both captures {string} and {float} must be present as parameters
Given(
  'the user {string} pays {float} for their order',
  async ({ page }, username: string, amount: number) => {
    await page.goto('/checkout');
    await page.fill('[data-testid="username"]', username);
    await page.fill('[data-testid="amount"]', amount.toFixed(2));
  },
);

When('the payment is {string}', async ({ page }, outcome: string) => {
  if (outcome === 'approved') {
    await page.click('[data-testid="confirm-payment"]');
  } else {
    await page.click('[data-testid="decline-payment"]');
  }
});

Then(
  'the transaction receipt shows {string} for {string}',
  async ({ page }, amount: string, username: string) => {
    await expect(page.getByTestId('receipt-amount')).toHaveText(amount);
    await expect(page.getByTestId('receipt-username')).toHaveText(username);
  },
);
```

**Tradeoff**: The strict arity check is enforced at code generation time and cannot be suppressed — there is no `--no-arity-check` flag in v9.0.0-beta.0. Teams migrating from v8.x with existing arity mismatches must fix every mismatch before `bddgen` will produce output. Arity validation does NOT apply to step definitions using the `World`-only pattern (steps that accept no Gherkin parameters but access state via `this`) — those continue to work as before because zero captures always match zero parameters. [official]

---

### Pattern 4 — Playwright v1.56 Test Agents Integration with BDD Discovery  [official]

Playwright v1.56 introduces Test Agents (`npx playwright init-agents`), three predefined agent definitions — planner, generator, and healer — designed to close the loop between BDD Discovery sessions and automated test generation. The planner agent explores a live application and produces a Markdown test plan listing user journeys and edge cases; the generator agent transforms that Markdown plan into Playwright test files; the healer agent executes the generated suite and automatically repairs failing selectors. In a BDD workflow, the planner output maps directly to Example Mapping cards — the team reviews the generated plan in a Three Amigos session, adds the business-rule context that the agent cannot infer from the UI alone, and approves the scenarios before the generator runs. This replaces the laborious hand-transcription step between workshop output and `.feature` file creation.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — enabling integration with Test Agents output
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig, BddFixtures } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/**/*.feature',
  steps: [
    // Steps generated by the generator agent land in agent-generated/
    'src/steps/agent-generated/**/*.ts',
    // Hand-crafted steps remain authoritative and override agent steps
    'src/steps/curated/**/*.ts',
  ],
  outputDir: '.bdd',
});

export default defineConfig<BddFixtures>({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  reporter: [
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'reports/html', open: 'never' }],
  ],
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'on',
  },
});

// Usage workflow:
// 1. npx playwright test --agent=planner --base-url=https://staging.example.com
//    -> produces plan.md with user journeys as Gherkin scenario outlines
// 2. Team reviews plan.md in Example Mapping session; adds Rule: blocks and business context
// 3. npx playwright test --agent=generator --plan=plan.md
//    -> produces features/agent-generated/*.feature + src/steps/agent-generated/*.ts
// 4. npx playwright test --agent=healer
//    -> fixes broken selectors after UI changes without changing feature file content
```

**Tradeoff**: The generator agent produces syntactically valid Gherkin but does NOT produce business-domain language — generated steps tend to be implementation-coupled (`I click the "Submit" button` instead of `I place my order`). Always run generated `.feature` files through a Three Amigos review before committing: apply the "Will it change if the implementation changes?" test to every generated step and rewrite implementation-coupled steps in ubiquitous language. Do NOT use the healer agent to fix scenarios that fail because the business rule changed — the healer repairs selector breakage only; a scenario that fails because the product changed its workflow must be corrected in the feature file by a human who understands the new business rule. [official]

### Pattern 5 — Playwright v1.55 `TestStepInfo` for Skip Conditions in BDD Data-Driven Scenarios  [official]

Playwright v1.55 adds `TestStepInfo` as a typed object passed to the step callback in `test.step()`, exposing a `skip(condition, reason)` method that allows a step to declare itself conditionally irrelevant without failing the overall test. In playwright-bdd scenarios, this maps to the BDD concept of a "pending" step — a step that is correctly authored but represents behavior not yet available in the environment under test (e.g., a feature behind a flag that is off in the current environment). Prior to v1.55, teams handled this with a `test.skip()` call inside the step body, which terminated the entire scenario rather than just the step. With `TestStepInfo.skip()`, a single step is skipped while the remaining steps in the scenario continue to execute, enabling partial execution reports that clearly show which behavior is available and which is pending.

```typescript
// src/steps/feature-flags.steps.ts
// Playwright v1.55 TestStepInfo.skip() for environment-conditional BDD steps
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test } from './fixtures.js';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

Given('the application feature flags are loaded', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dashboard');
  // feature flags loaded as part of normal app bootstrap
});

When('I navigate to the advanced analytics dashboard', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.click('[data-testid="analytics-nav"]');
  await page.waitForURL('/analytics/advanced');
});

Then(
  'the cohort comparison chart should display enrollment trends',
  // TestStepInfo is injected when the step callback declares it as the last fixture-less arg
  async ({ page }, stepInfo: import('@playwright/test').TestStepInfo) => {
    const flagEnabled = await page.evaluate(
      () => (window as { featureFlags?: Record<string, boolean> }).featureFlags?.['advanced-analytics-cohort'] ?? false,
    );
    if (!flagEnabled) {
      // Skip just this step — remaining Then steps still execute
      stepInfo.skip(true, 'advanced-analytics-cohort flag is OFF in this environment');
      return;
    }
    const chart = page.getByTestId('cohort-comparison-chart');
    await expect(chart).toBeVisible();
    await expect(chart.getByRole('img', { name: /enrollment trend/i })).toBeAttached();
  },
);

Then('the page title should be {string}', async ({ page }, title: string) => {
  // This step runs regardless of whether the previous step was skipped
  await expect(page).toHaveTitle(title);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `TestStepInfo.skip()` skips the step body but does NOT affect Cucumber's hook lifecycle — `AfterStep` hooks still execute after a skipped step, with `result.status === 'SKIPPED'` available on the result object for hook-level logic. Do NOT use step-level skip as a substitute for proper feature-flag-aware scenario tagging — if an entire scenario is irrelevant in the target environment, mark the scenario `@skip` or use a tag-based `Before` hook to skip it entirely; `TestStepInfo.skip()` is for genuinely partial availability where some steps are valid and some are pending, not for wholesale environment exclusion. [official]
