### Pattern 19 — Playwright v1.60 `browser.on('context')` for Global BDD Route Interception  [official]

Playwright v1.60 adds a `browser.on('context', handler)` event that fires whenever a new `BrowserContext` is created under a `Browser` instance, enabling playwright-bdd suites to register route interceptors and authentication state on every context from a single global fixture rather than duplicating `context.route()` calls across multiple `BeforeScenario` fixtures. Before v1.60, global route interception in BDD suites required either wrapping `browser.newContext()` in a custom fixture that inserted interceptors before yielding the context, or using `APIRequestContext` for API-only scenarios while keeping a separate context fixture for UI scenarios — both approaches produced fixture composition complexity when multiple interceptor sets needed to compose. The `browser.on('context')` handler receives the new context synchronously before any pages are opened, making it the earliest possible injection point.

```typescript
// src/support/global-intercept-fixture.ts
// Playwright v1.60 browser.on('context') for global BDD route interception
import { test as base } from 'playwright-bdd';

// Track registered contexts to avoid re-registering routes (contexts can be created
// multiple times in long-running browser sessions)
const interceptedContexts = new WeakSet<import('@playwright/test').BrowserContext>();

export const test = base.extend({
  browser: async ({ browser }, use) => {
    // Register the handler once per browser instance
    browser.on('context', (ctx) => {
      if (interceptedContexts.has(ctx)) return;
      interceptedContexts.add(ctx);

      // Block analytics and telemetry in all BDD scenarios globally
      ctx.route(/\/(analytics|telemetry|metrics)\//, (route) => route.abort());

      // Stub feature flag API so scenarios don't depend on remote flag state
      ctx.route('**/api/feature-flags', async (route) => {
        await route.fulfill({
          contentType: 'application/json',
          body: JSON.stringify({ flags: { newCheckout: true, legacyCart: false } }),
        });
      });
    });

    await use(browser);
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The `browser.on('context')` handler fires for all contexts created by the browser instance, including contexts created by `browser.newContext()` calls inside individual scenarios — if a scenario creates a second context for a specific purpose (e.g., an admin context alongside a user context), both contexts receive the global route interceptors, which may interfere with scenarios that intentionally send real requests from the second context. Guard against this by using a context property or parameter (set via `browser.newContext({ extraHTTPHeaders: { 'x-skip-global-intercept': '1' } })`) that your `browser.on('context')` handler reads to opt specific contexts out of the global routes. [official]

---

### Pattern 20 — Cucumber.js v12.3 Named `BeforeAll`/`AfterAll` Hooks for Shared Infrastructure Lifecycle  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.3.0 extends the `BeforeAll` and `AfterAll` hook registration API to accept a `name` string as the first argument — `BeforeAll('Start database', async function() { ... })` — which is then included in the `TestRunHookStarted` and `TestRunHookFinished` messages emitted to the message stream, making it possible for custom formatters, plugins, and CI dashboards to attribute infrastructure setup time to specific named lifecycle hooks rather than to an anonymous "before all tests" bucket. Named hooks also improve error attribution: when a `BeforeAll` hook throws, the error message now includes the hook name in the stack trace output, making it immediately clear that a "database seeding" step failed rather than showing a generic "BeforeAll hook failed" message. The `TestRunHookStarted`/`TestRunHookFinished` message pair is consumed by the Cucumber HTML formatter to render a separate "Hooks" section above the scenario list.

```typescript
// src/support/database-lifecycle.ts
// Cucumber.js v12.3 named BeforeAll/AfterAll hooks for infrastructure lifecycle
import { BeforeAll, AfterAll, setWorldConstructor } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

let dbPool: Pool;

// v12.3: First argument is the hook name — appears in messages and stack traces
BeforeAll('Connect database pool', async function () {
  dbPool = new Pool({
    connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL ?? 'postgresql://localhost:5432/test_db',
    max: 10,
    idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
  });
  // Verify connectivity before scenarios begin
  const client = await dbPool.connect();
  await client.query('SELECT 1');
  client.release();
  // Expose pool via World parameters for step definitions
  this.parameters.dbPool = dbPool;
});

BeforeAll('Seed reference data', async function () {
  // Named hooks run in registration order — seeding runs after pool is connected
  const client = await dbPool.connect();
  try {
    await client.query(`
      INSERT INTO product_categories (name, slug) VALUES
        ('Electronics', 'electronics'),
        ('Clothing', 'clothing')
      ON CONFLICT (slug) DO NOTHING
    `);
  } finally {
    client.release();
  }
});

AfterAll('Close database pool', async function () {
  await dbPool.end();
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Named `BeforeAll`/`AfterAll` hooks still do not receive a World instance — `this` inside the hook body provides only `this.parameters` (the world parameters object from config), not the full World with `this.page`, `this.context`, or any custom properties set in `setWorldConstructor`. Do NOT attempt to access World properties in `BeforeAll`/`AfterAll` hooks — the World is scoped to individual scenarios and does not exist at the suite lifecycle level; use module-level variables (as in the `dbPool` example above) or a singleton service locator to share state between named suite hooks and individual scenario hooks. [official]

---

### Pattern 21 — Cucumber.js v12.7 ESM Source References and Parallel `process.env` Propagation  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.7.0 fixes two distinct issues that affected TypeScript ESM projects in parallel execution: (1) source reference URIs in error messages and formatter output now use correct `file://` URLs for ESM step definition files rather than relative paths that broke source-map resolution in IDEs, and (2) environment variables set after `process.env` manipulation in the main process are now correctly propagated to the child processes spawned by `parallel: N` mode, resolving a class of CI failures where `dotenv.config()` called at the top of `cucumber.config.ts` populated `process.env` in the coordinator but not in workers. The propagation fix is particularly relevant for playwright-bdd ESM setups that use `import.meta.url` in step definition paths and rely on `process.env.BASE_URL` being available in parallel workers.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — v12.7 ESM source refs + env propagation
// dotenv.config() now propagates to parallel workers in v12.7
import { config as dotenvConfig } from 'dotenv';
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

// v12.7: environment variables set here propagate to parallel worker processes
dotenvConfig({ path: process.env.ENV_FILE ?? '.env.test' });

// ESM source references now use correct file:// URIs for IDE click-through navigation
export default {
  default: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    // ESM import using file:// URL — v12.7 source references resolve correctly
    import: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    format: [
      'progress',
      ['html', { outputFile: 'reports/cucumber.html' }],
    ],
    parallel: parseInt(process.env.WORKERS ?? '0', 10),
    worldParameters: {
      // v12.7: process.env values populated by dotenvConfig() are now available here
      // AND in the parallel worker processes that execute scenarios
      baseUrl: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
      apiKey: process.env.API_KEY ?? '',
    },
  },
} satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>;

// src/steps/auth.steps.ts — ESM step file
// v12.7 source reference: stack traces now show the correct file:// URL
// enabling VS Code / WebStorm to navigate directly to the failing step line
import { Given, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

Given('I am authenticated as {string}', async function (role: string) {
  // process.env.API_KEY now available — propagated from parent by v12.7
  const apiKey = process.env.API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error('API_KEY not propagated to worker — check .env.test');
  this.authToken = await this.apiClient.login({ role, apiKey });
});

Then('my session should have {string} permissions', function (permission: string) {
  if (!this.authToken.permissions.includes(permission)) {
    throw new Error(`Expected permission '${permission}' not found in session`);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The `process.env` propagation fix in v12.7 applies to variables set in the coordinator process before workers are spawned — dynamic `process.env` mutations that happen inside `BeforeAll` hooks (which also run in the coordinator) are NOT propagated to workers because workers are already running by the time `BeforeAll` executes. Do NOT rely on `BeforeAll` hooks to set `process.env` values for worker processes; set all required environment variables in the configuration file or via the shell before invoking Cucumber. [official]

---

### Pattern 22 — playwright-bdd v9 `$step.docStringType` Fixture for Typed Doc String Step Definitions  [official]

playwright-bdd v9.0.0-beta.0 adds `docStringType` as a property on the `$step` fixture, exposing the media type declared in the Gherkin doc string delimiter (e.g., `"""json` or `"""yaml`) to the step definition body, enabling type-aware parsing of multi-line string arguments without requiring step definitions to infer the format from the string content. Before v9, playwright-bdd step definitions that accepted doc strings received only the raw string; teams either wrote a single step that attempted JSON parse and fell back to YAML, or duplicated the step definition for each media type with different expressions. The `docStringType` property is `string | undefined` — undefined when the feature file uses plain `"""` without a media type tag.

```typescript
// src/steps/api-payload.steps.ts
// playwright-bdd v9 $step.docStringType for typed doc string parsing
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test } from './fixtures.js';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { parse as parseYaml } from 'yaml';

const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

When(
  'I send a POST request to {string} with body:',
  async ({ page, request, $step }, endpoint: string, body: string) => {
    // v9: $step.docStringType is 'json' | 'yaml' | undefined based on the """ delimiter
    let parsedBody: unknown;
    if ($step.docStringType === 'yaml') {
      parsedBody = parseYaml(body);
    } else if ($step.docStringType === 'json' || $step.docStringType === undefined) {
      // Treat untagged doc strings as JSON for backward compatibility
      parsedBody = JSON.parse(body);
    } else {
      throw new Error(`Unsupported doc string type: ${$step.docStringType}`);
    }

    const response = await request.post(endpoint, { data: parsedBody });
    // Store for assertion steps
    (page as { _lastResponse?: unknown })._lastResponse = {
      status: response.status(),
      body: await response.json().catch(() => response.text()),
    };
  },
);

Then('the response status should be {int}', async ({ page }, expectedStatus: number) => {
  const lastResponse = (page as { _lastResponse?: { status: number } })._lastResponse;
  expect(lastResponse?.status).toBe(expectedStatus);
});
```

**Tradeoff**: `$step.docStringType` is available only when the step is invoked with a Gherkin doc string argument — accessing it in a step definition that does not have a doc string parameter (e.g., a `Given` step with only a table argument) returns `undefined` regardless of whether the feature file included a media type. Do NOT use `$step.docStringType` as the sole dispatch mechanism for parsing without a fallback — feature files written before the media type was standardized on your team will have `docStringType === undefined`, and your step definition must handle the untagged case explicitly to avoid silent data corruption from passing a YAML string to `JSON.parse()`. [official]

---

### Pattern 23 — playwright-bdd v9 `junit` Canonical Reporter with `nameFormat` for Structured CI Reporting  [official]

playwright-bdd v9.0.0-beta.0 promotes the `junit` reporter to canonical status (deprecating the `junit-modern` alias), adds a `nameFormat` option that controls the `classname` and `name` attributes of JUnit XML test case elements, and aligns the default output with the Cucumber JUnit schema consumed by major CI platforms (Jenkins, GitHub Actions test-results, Allure). Before v9, the `junit-modern` alias produced a format subtly incompatible with Jenkins's JUnit plugin — the `classname` attribute used the Playwright test title rather than the Gherkin feature name, causing Jenkins to group results by internal test ID rather than by feature, breaking the feature-level pass/fail dashboard. The `nameFormat` option accepts a template string with `{feature}`, `{scenario}`, and `{tags}` interpolation tokens.

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts — playwright-bdd v9 junit canonical reporter
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { defineBddConfig } from 'playwright-bdd';

const bddConfig = defineBddConfig({
  features: 'features/**/*.feature',
  steps: 'src/steps/**/*.ts',
});

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: bddConfig.testDir,
  reporter: [
    // v9: 'junit' is the canonical name — 'junit-modern' is deprecated
    [
      'playwright-bdd/reporters/junit',
      {
        outputFile: 'reports/junit.xml',
        // nameFormat: controls classname and name in JUnit XML
        // {feature} = Gherkin Feature title, {scenario} = Scenario title, {tags} = joined tag list
        nameFormat: {
          classname: '{feature}',                         // Groups by feature in Jenkins
          name: '{scenario} [{tags}]',                    // Includes tags for traceability
        },
        // stripAnsi: removes ANSI color codes from error messages in JUnit output
        stripAnsi: true,
      },
    ],
    // Keep HTML for human review alongside JUnit for CI parsing
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'reports/html', open: 'never' }],
  ],
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000',
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The `nameFormat` template tokens `{feature}` and `{scenario}` are derived from the Gherkin feature title and scenario title respectively — Scenario Outline instances include the example table values interpolated into the scenario title (e.g., `Login with valid credentials [user: admin, role: superuser]`), which may exceed the character limits that some CI platforms impose on test case names (Jenkins truncates at 255 characters by default). For Scenario Outline-heavy suites, use `nameFormat: { name: '{scenario}' }` without `{tags}` to stay within limits, and rely on the JUnit `classname` grouping by feature for tag-level filtering in the CI dashboard. Do NOT use the `junit-modern` alias in new playwright-bdd v9 projects — it will be removed in a future stable release and using it generates a deprecation warning in `bddgen` output. [official]

---

### Pattern 24 — Gherkin `Rule` Keyword for Business Rule Grouping and Scenario Organization  [official]

The Gherkin `Rule` keyword (available since Gherkin v6, fully supported in Cucumber.js v7+ and playwright-bdd) provides a semantic container for grouping related scenarios under a named business rule within a single feature file, reducing the need to split tightly related behavior across multiple feature files purely for organizational purposes. A `Rule` block can contain its own `Background` section that applies only to scenarios within that rule, allowing two logically distinct setup contexts to coexist in the same feature file without polluting the global `Background`. In playwright-bdd, the rule title appears in the HTML report's scenario tree, in JUnit `classname` output when `nameFormat.classname` includes `{feature}`, and in `TestCaseStarted` messages consumed by custom formatters.

```gherkin
# features/payment-processing.feature
# Gherkin Rule keyword — groups scenarios by business rule within one feature

Feature: Payment Processing

  Rule: Customers with valid payment methods can complete checkout

    Background:
      Given a customer account exists with email "buyer@example.com"
      And the customer has a valid Visa card on file

    Scenario: Successful purchase completes and sends confirmation email
      When the customer places an order for "Wireless Headphones" at $149.99
      Then the order status should be "confirmed"
      And a confirmation email should be sent to "buyer@example.com"

    Scenario: Duplicate order within 60 seconds is rejected
      When the customer places an order for "Wireless Headphones" at $149.99
      And the customer immediately places the same order again
      Then the second order should be rejected with error "Duplicate order detected"

  Rule: Customers with expired payment methods cannot complete checkout

    Background:
      Given a customer account exists with email "expired@example.com"
      And the customer has an expired Mastercard on file

    Scenario: Checkout fails with expired card and prompts for update
      When the customer attempts to place an order for "USB Hub" at $29.99
      Then the checkout should fail with error "Payment method expired"
      And the customer should be prompted to update their payment information
```

```typescript
// src/steps/payment.steps.ts — Rule-aware step definitions
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test } from './fixtures.js';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

Given(
  'a customer account exists with email {string}',
  async ({ page }, email: string) => {
    await page.goto(`/admin/test-setup/create-account?email=${encodeURIComponent(email)}`);
    await expect(page.getByTestId('setup-complete')).toBeVisible();
  },
);

When(
  'the customer places an order for {string} at ${float}',
  async ({ page }, productName: string, price: number) => {
    await page.goto('/shop');
    await page.getByText(productName).click();
    await page.getByTestId('add-to-cart').click();
    await page.getByTestId('checkout').click();
  },
);

Then(
  'the order status should be {string}',
  async ({ page }, expectedStatus: string) => {
    await expect(page.getByTestId('order-status')).toHaveText(expectedStatus);
  },
);
```

**Tradeoff**: `Rule`-level `Background` steps run after the Feature-level `Background` (if any) and before each scenario within the rule — teams that add a Feature-level `Background` later may inadvertently produce a two-phase setup sequence (Feature Background then Rule Background) that is harder to reason about than a single flat `Background`. Do NOT use `Rule` blocks as a substitute for proper feature file decomposition when rules have entirely independent domain contexts — the `Rule` keyword is designed for business rules within the same feature domain; if the rules could be documented independently to a product owner, they likely belong in separate feature files. [official]

---

### Pattern 25 — Cucumber.js v12.8 `customExternalisingOptions` for Large Scenario Suite Chunking  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.8.0 adds `customExternalisingOptions` (accessible via the configuration's `externalizing` key or the plugin `pluginOptions` object) that controls how large scenario suites are split into external "work items" for distribution across parallel workers — previously the externalizing strategy was internal-only and not configurable, causing uneven load distribution when feature files varied widely in scenario count. The custom options allow specifying `chunkSize` (scenarios per work item), `groupBy` (`'file'` to keep all scenarios from one feature file in the same worker, or `'scenario'` for maximum parallelism at the individual scenario level), and `orderBy` (`'duration'` to use historical timing data from a previous run's JSON report for optimal bin-packing). This is primarily relevant for suites with 200+ scenarios where CI wall-clock time optimization matters.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts — v12.8 customExternalisingOptions for load-balanced parallel execution
import type { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { readFileSync, existsSync } from 'node:fs';

// Load previous run timing data for duration-based ordering (bin-packing optimization)
function loadPreviousTimings(): Record<string, number> | undefined {
  const timingFile = 'reports/scenario-timings.json';
  if (!existsSync(timingFile)) return undefined;
  try {
    return JSON.parse(readFileSync(timingFile, 'utf-8')) as Record<string, number>;
  } catch {
    return undefined;
  }
}

export default {
  default: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    import: ['src/steps/**/*.ts', 'src/support/**/*.ts'],
    parallel: parseInt(process.env.WORKERS ?? '4', 10),
    externalizing: {
      // v12.8 customExternalisingOptions: control work item chunk size and grouping
      chunkSize: 5,         // up to 5 scenarios per work item
      groupBy: 'scenario',  // maximum parallelism — each scenario runs independently
      orderBy: 'duration',  // use historical timings for bin-packing if available
      previousTimings: loadPreviousTimings(),
    },
    format: [
      'progress',
      ['json', { outputFile: 'reports/cucumber.json' }],
    ],
  },
} satisfies Record<string, IConfiguration>;
```

**Tradeoff**: `groupBy: 'scenario'` maximizes parallelism but breaks `BeforeAll`/`AfterAll` hook sequencing assumptions — if your `BeforeAll` hook creates infrastructure that is shared via module-level state (e.g., a database pool), `groupBy: 'scenario'` distributes scenarios across workers that each spawn their own `BeforeAll`, potentially creating multiple concurrent pools that exhaust database connection limits. Use `groupBy: 'file'` for suites where feature files share infrastructure through `BeforeAll` hooks, or refactor shared infrastructure into a pre-run setup script invoked before Cucumber rather than in `BeforeAll` hooks. Do NOT use `orderBy: 'duration'` without a valid `previousTimings` file — Cucumber falls back to unordered execution when timings are unavailable, but an empty or malformed timings file may cause an error in some v12.8 patch releases. [official]

---

### Pattern 26 — Playwright `getByRole()` `description` Option for ARIA-Described BDD Assertions  [official]

Playwright v1.60 adds a `description` option to `getByRole()` that filters by the element's `aria-describedby` text content or `aria-description` attribute value, complementing the existing `name` option that filters by `aria-label` or visible text. In BDD scenarios testing accessible UI components, this enables step definitions to target elements with both a role name and a description without falling back to CSS selectors — for example, `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit', description: 'Submit the order for processing' })` uniquely identifies a submit button with a tooltip description, where `getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })` alone would match multiple submit buttons across the page. The description filter uses the same accessibility name computation algorithm as `name`, supporting both direct attribute values and text content of linked elements.

```typescript
// src/steps/accessible-ui.steps.ts
// Playwright v1.60 getByRole() description option for ARIA-described BDD assertions
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test } from './fixtures.js';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

Given('the order summary page is loaded', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout/summary');
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Summary' })).toBeVisible();
});

When(
  'I click the {string} button described as {string}',
  async ({ page }, buttonName: string, description: string) => {
    // v1.60 getByRole description: targets button by both name AND aria-describedby text
    // Without description, 'Submit' could match multiple buttons on multi-form pages
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: buttonName, description }).click();
  },
);

Then(
  'the {string} field should be described as {string}',
  async ({ page }, fieldLabel: string, expectedDescription: string) => {
    const field = page.getByRole('textbox', { name: fieldLabel });
    // Verify the description is rendered correctly for screen reader users
    await expect(field).toHaveAccessibleDescription(expectedDescription);
  },
);

Then('the form submission should succeed', async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: 'Order confirmed' })).toBeVisible({
    timeout: 10_000,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff**: The `description` option matches against the computed accessible description using the full accessibility name computation algorithm — this means it resolves `aria-describedby` IDs to their referenced element's text content at the time of the `getByRole()` call. Dynamic tooltips that populate `aria-describedby` text asynchronously (e.g., validation messages injected on form blur) may not be present when `getByRole()` executes, causing the locator to find zero matching elements rather than retrying. Use `locator.waitFor()` before `getByRole({ description })` when the description is dynamically populated, or assert on `toHaveAccessibleDescription()` separately after the element is already located by name. [official]

---

### Pattern 27 — Conjunction Step Anti-Pattern: Splitting Compound Steps for Reusability  [community]

One of the most common BDD anti-patterns teams encounter is writing "conjunction steps" — step definitions that bundle multiple domain concepts into a single step text joined by `and` (e.g., `Given I have logged in and my cart has 3 items and I am on the checkout page`). These compound steps are written for convenience but violate the principle that each step should express a single domain concept, because reusing half the compound step in another scenario requires either duplicating the compound step with a different second clause or extracting a helper function that is invisible in the feature file. WHY teams fall into this pattern: when migrating existing test setup methods into Gherkin, each `beforeEach` call that performed multiple setup actions is transcribed as a single long `Given` step rather than decomposed into atomic steps, because decomposition requires the step author to also rewrite existing feature files that reference the long step. The fix is to decompose compound steps into atomic steps using Gherkin's `And` keyword, and to extract the shared setup logic into a helper function called by each atomic step definition.

```gherkin
# BEFORE — conjunction step (anti-pattern)
Feature: Checkout

  Scenario: Complete purchase
    Given I have logged in and my cart has 3 items and I am on the checkout page
    When I submit my payment
    Then the order should be confirmed

# AFTER — atomic steps using And keyword (correct pattern)
Feature: Checkout

  Background:
    Given I am logged in as "customer@example.com"

  Scenario: Complete purchase with items in cart
    Given my cart contains 3 items
    And I am on the checkout page
    When I submit my payment
    Then the order should be confirmed
```

```typescript
// src/steps/checkout.steps.ts — atomic step definitions replacing conjunction steps
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test } from './fixtures.js';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

// Atomic step — reusable across any scenario needing an authenticated user
Given('I am logged in as {string}', async ({ page }, email: string) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.fill('[data-testid="email"]', email);
  await page.fill('[data-testid="password"]', 'test-password');
  await page.click('[data-testid="login-submit"]');
  await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
});

// Atomic step — reusable for any scenario needing cart state
Given('my cart contains {int} item(s)', async ({ page }, count: number) => {
  // Use API to seed cart state — faster than UI interaction
  await page.request.post('/api/test/seed-cart', { data: { itemCount: count } });
});

// Atomic step — navigation concern separated from state concerns
Given('I am on the checkout page', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await expect(page.getByTestId('checkout-form')).toBeVisible();
});

When('I submit my payment', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.click('[data-testid="submit-payment"]');
});

Then('the order should be confirmed', async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByTestId('order-confirmed')).toBeVisible({ timeout: 10_000 });
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Decomposing conjunction steps into atomic steps increases the number of lines in each feature file scenario, which some stakeholders find verbose and harder to scan quickly. WHY the verbosity is worth it: atomic steps remain individually reusable across dozens of scenarios while conjunction steps require near-duplication for every variation, and Cucumber's `Background` keyword was specifically designed to move repeated atomic steps out of scenario bodies to restore readability. Do NOT decompose steps so atomically that individual steps have no business meaning on their own — a step like `Given the database connection pool size is 10` belongs in test infrastructure, not in a Gherkin feature file read by product owners. [community]

---

### Pattern 28 — Scenario Independence Violation: Shared Mutable State via World Properties  [community]

A pervasive BDD gotcha is silently breaking scenario independence by writing step definitions that mutate World properties in one scenario and rely on those mutations persisting into the next scenario — a pattern that works in serial execution where scenarios run in file order but fails non-deterministically in parallel execution where Cucumber creates a new World instance per scenario worker. WHY this is not caught in local development: Cucumber creates a new World object before each scenario regardless of serial or parallel mode, so the mutation should not persist — the actual failure mode is typically test data pollution in the external system (database rows created by one scenario not cleaned up and matched by a `Given` step in a different scenario), not World object mutation. Teams conflate "the World is fresh" with "the test environment is clean" and neglect teardown steps. The fix is to write `After` hooks that clean up all test data created in `Given`/`When` steps, keyed by a scenario-scoped identifier generated in `Before`.

```typescript
// src/support/world.ts — scenario-scoped cleanup with correlation ID
import { setWorldConstructor, Before, After, World } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { v4 as uuidv4 } from 'uuid';
import type { ApiClient } from '../api/client.js';

class CustomWorld extends World {
  scenarioId: string = '';
  createdUserIds: string[] = [];
  createdOrderIds: string[] = [];
  apiClient!: ApiClient;

  // Helper: register a created resource for teardown
  trackUser(userId: string) { this.createdUserIds.push(userId); }
  trackOrder(orderId: string) { this.createdOrderIds.push(orderId); }
}

setWorldConstructor(CustomWorld);

Before(async function (this: CustomWorld) {
  // Each scenario gets a unique correlation ID — use it as a prefix for all test data
  // This prevents cross-scenario data pollution even when cleanup fails
  this.scenarioId = `test-${uuidv4().slice(0, 8)}`;
  this.apiClient = new ApiClient({ baseUrl: this.parameters.baseUrl });
  this.createdUserIds = [];
  this.createdOrderIds = [];
});

After(async function (this: CustomWorld) {
  // WHY explicit teardown is required: external systems retain state across scenarios
  // even though the World object is recreated; a new World does not clean the database
  for (const orderId of this.createdOrderIds) {
    await this.apiClient.deleteOrder(orderId).catch(() => { /* best-effort */ });
  }
  for (const userId of this.createdUserIds) {
    await this.apiClient.deleteUser(userId).catch(() => { /* best-effort */ });
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Tracking created resources in World properties and cleaning them in `After` hooks adds boilerplate to every step that creates test data — teams with large numbers of entity types may find the tracking list grows unwieldy. WHY the boilerplate is necessary: relying on database truncation in `AfterAll` instead of per-scenario cleanup causes scenarios to become order-dependent (earlier scenarios' data is visible to later ones in the same run), which surfaces as intermittent failures when a data-creating scenario fails mid-run and leaves orphaned rows that a subsequent scenario matches unexpectedly. For suites where per-scenario cleanup is expensive, use a database transaction wrapper that rolls back after each scenario instead of explicit delete calls, but be aware that transaction-wrapped scenarios cannot test behavior across transaction boundaries (e.g., testing that a commit triggers a database trigger). [community]

---

### Pattern 29 — Over-Specified Gherkin: UI Implementation Language Bleeding Into Business Steps  [community]

A common Gherkin anti-pattern is writing step text that describes UI implementation details rather than business behavior — steps like `When I click the blue "Submit Order" button in the top-right corner of the order form` instead of `When I submit the order`. WHY teams write implementation-specific steps: when developers write BDD tests rather than product owners or BAs, they naturally describe what they see on screen rather than what business goal is being achieved, because the developer's mental model is the UI implementation rather than the domain behavior. The consequence is that every UI redesign (button moved, label changed, color updated) breaks dozens of scenarios even when the business behavior is unchanged — the tests become a regression test for the visual layout rather than a specification of the business rules. The fix is to review step text with the question "would this step still be true if the UI were completely redesigned?" and rewrite any step that fails that test.

```gherkin
# BEFORE — implementation-specific steps (anti-pattern)
Feature: Order Submission

  Scenario: Customer submits valid order
    Given I am on the "/checkout/step-3" page
    When I fill in the text field with id "card-number-input" with "4111111111111111"
    And I click the green button labeled "Place Order Now ($49.99)"
    And I wait for the spinner to disappear
    Then I should see the text "Thank you for your order!" in the green banner

# AFTER — business behavior steps (correct pattern)
Feature: Order Submission

  Scenario: Customer successfully places an order with a valid credit card
    Given I am ready to complete my $49.99 order
    When I provide a valid credit card number
    And I submit the order
    Then my order should be confirmed
```

```typescript
// src/steps/order-submission.steps.ts — business-language step definitions
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test } from './fixtures.js';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);

// Business language: "ready to complete an order" — hides URL and page structure
Given('I am ready to complete my ${float} order', async ({ page }, amount: number) => {
  // Seed the cart via API — decouples from UI navigation details
  await page.request.post('/api/test/seed-cart', { data: { totalAmount: amount } });
  await page.goto('/checkout');
  await page.waitForURL(/\/checkout/);
});

// Business language: "provide a valid credit card number" — hides field selectors
When('I provide a valid credit card number', async ({ page }) => {
  // Use test card number — which card and which field are implementation details
  await page.getByLabel('Card number').fill('4111111111111111');
  await page.getByLabel('Expiry').fill('12/28');
  await page.getByLabel('CVC').fill('123');
});

// Business language: "submit the order" — hides button label and location
When('I submit the order', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /place order/i }).click();
});

// Business language: "order should be confirmed" — hides exact success message text
Then('my order should be confirmed', async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByRole('alert', { name: /order confirmed/i })).toBeVisible({
    timeout: 15_000,
  });
});
```

**Tradeoff**: Writing business-language steps requires more upfront discussion with product owners to establish the correct domain vocabulary — teams under time pressure skip this and write implementation steps as a faster path to green tests. WHY the investment pays off: a suite of 200 business-language scenarios survives a full UI framework migration (e.g., from React to Vue) with only the step definition implementations changing, while an equivalent suite of implementation-language scenarios requires each scenario to be rewritten; the maintenance ratio favors business language proportionally to the frequency of UI changes. Do NOT take business language so far that step text omits necessary domain precision — `When I submit the order` is good, but `When I do the thing` is too vague to be executable as a specification. [community]

---

### Pattern 30 — `BeforeScenario` vs Playwright Fixture Timing: Route Registration Before Background Steps  [community]

A frequently misunderstood playwright-bdd execution model issue is that `BeforeScenario` hooks execute after `Background` steps, not before them — the hook fires after Playwright's fixture setup (which creates the `page` and `context`) but after Background steps have already run against those fixtures. WHY this surprises teams: Cucumber's `Before` hook documentation shows hooks running before the first `Given` step in a scenario, which is true for a scenario's own steps, but Background steps are considered part of the scenario and execute before the scenario-body steps while still executing before `BeforeScenario` in playwright-bdd's composited lifecycle. Teams that put `page.route()` interceptors in `BeforeScenario` discover that Background steps make unintercepted real network requests, causing test environment dependency failures. WHY this is particularly dangerous: the issue is environment-dependent — in CI environments where background services are not running, Background steps that make unintercepted API calls fail with connection errors; in environments where services are running, Background steps succeed but with real data, and the `BeforeScenario` interceptors then silently override subsequent requests.

```typescript
// src/support/fixtures.ts
// FIX: register page.route() interceptors in a fixture, not in BeforeScenario
// Fixtures are set up BEFORE Background steps — BeforeScenario hooks are NOT
import { test as base } from 'playwright-bdd';

interface ApiMockFixtures {
  mockedApi: void;
}

export const test = base.extend<ApiMockFixtures>({
  mockedApi: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // This runs BEFORE Background steps — correct place for route interceptors
    await page.route('**/api/**', async (route, request) => {
      // Allow requests to test-specific endpoints through
      if (request.url().includes('/api/test/')) {
        await route.continue();
        return;
      }
      // Mock all other API calls by default — prevents real backend dependency
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 200,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify({ mocked: true, url: request.url() }),
      });
    });

    await use();
    // Route handlers are automatically unregistered when page is closed
  },
});

// In feature files, include 'mockedApi' fixture in the test object
// so it's automatically activated before Background steps:
// @fixture:mockedApi   <- playwright-bdd fixture tag activates the fixture for tagged scenarios
```

```gherkin
# features/product-search.feature
@fixture:mockedApi
Feature: Product Search

  Background:
    Given the product catalog API is available
    # ^ This step would make a REAL API call if page.route() was in BeforeScenario
    # With mockedApi fixture, it's intercepted before Background runs

  Scenario: Search returns matching products
    When I search for "wireless headphones"
    Then I should see at least 1 result
```

**Tradeoff**: Moving route interceptors from `BeforeScenario` into fixtures couples the fixture to a specific API mocking strategy — all scenarios that use the fixture receive the same set of route interceptors, which may be too broad for scenarios that need to test real error responses from specific endpoints. WHY the trade-off is acceptable: use feature-level or scenario-level `@fixture:` tags to activate different fixture combinations for different scenario groups; a `mockedApi` fixture and a `realApi` fixture can coexist and be applied selectively via tags, while `BeforeScenario` cannot be conditionally applied with the same granularity. Do NOT create a single monolithic route-interceptor fixture — build composable fixtures that intercept specific API domains (`@fixture:mockedAuthApi`, `@fixture:mockedProductApi`) so scenarios activate only the interceptions they need. [community]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 40

**[community] Gotcha 1 — playwright-bdd v9 `tinyglobby` migration breaks Windows-style backslash paths silently passed to `defineBddConfig({ steps: [...] })`, because `tinyglobby` (which replaced `fast-glob`) does not normalize backslashes to forward slashes on Windows, causing `bddgen` to find zero step files with no error message — just an empty step file list — when the `steps` array contains paths like `'src\\steps\\*.ts'` that `fast-glob` previously normalized automatically**: Teams that upgrade from playwright-bdd v8 to v9 on Windows developer machines discover that their playwright.config.ts works locally with v8 but produces "Missing step definitions" for every scenario after upgrading to v9. WHY this is silent: `tinyglobby` returns an empty array for unmatched patterns rather than throwing, and playwright-bdd interprets an empty match as "no steps found in this pattern" rather than "this pattern is invalid", so `bddgen` silently generates test files with all steps marked as undefined rather than reporting a configuration error. Fix: replace all backslashes with forward slashes in `steps` array values (`'src/steps/**/*.ts'`), or use `path.posix.join()` instead of `path.join()` when constructing step paths programmatically.

**[community] Gotcha 2 — Cucumber.js v12.5 plugins that register `pickles:order` transforms and are loaded via the `plugin` configuration key are NOT applied when Cucumber is invoked via the `@cucumber/cucumber` programmatic API (`runCucumber()`), because the programmatic API bypasses the plugin loader used by the CLI, causing test orchestration tools that embed Cucumber programmatically to silently receive unordered pickles even when a plugin is configured**: Teams that integrate Cucumber into a custom CI orchestrator using `runCucumber()` add a `pickles:order` plugin to `cucumber.config.ts` and verify it works with `npx cucumber-js`, then discover it has no effect when the orchestrator calls `runCucumber()` directly with the same configuration object. WHY this happens: the `runCucumber()` API accepts the resolved configuration object but invokes the plugin loader only when the `plugin` key contains file paths; when the orchestrator resolves `cucumber.config.ts` at the JS level and passes the exported object directly, the file paths in `plugin` are never loaded. Fix: explicitly call the plugin's `coordinator` function within the programmatic API setup code, or use the CLI invocation path (`exec('npx cucumber-js')`) rather than the programmatic API when plugins are required.

**[community] Gotcha 3 — playwright-bdd `@fixture:` tags applied to a `Background` block (via a `@fixture:myFixture` tag on the line immediately above `Background:`) are silently ignored — the fixture is NOT activated for Background steps — because playwright-bdd's tag-to-fixture resolution scans scenario-level tags only, not block-level tags on `Background`, causing teams to believe their Background steps run with the fixture active when they actually run without it**: Teams that read the playwright-bdd documentation for `@fixture:` tags and experiment with placing the tag above the `Background:` keyword observe that the Background steps execute but the fixture's setup code never runs, and no error is raised. WHY this is confusing: Gherkin permits tags on most block types including `Background`, and other tag-based features (like `@skip` in some BDD tools) do apply to `Background` blocks, so the expectation that `@fixture:` works on `Background` is reasonable but incorrect. Fix: place `@fixture:` tags on the `Feature` block (to apply to all scenarios in the file) or on individual `Scenario` blocks; if all scenarios in a feature require a fixture, tag the `Feature` line rather than the `Background` line.

**[community] Gotcha 4 — Cucumber.js named `BeforeAll` hooks (v12.3+) that throw errors produce a failure message attributed to the hook name in the HTML report but do NOT stop subsequent named `BeforeAll` hooks from executing — all registered `BeforeAll` hooks run even after one fails, and each failing hook adds its error to the report independently, causing teams to see a cascade of infrastructure failures when the first named hook (e.g., "Connect database pool") fails and all subsequent hooks ("Seed reference data", "Start mock server") also fail because they depend on resources the first hook was supposed to create**: Teams that add named `BeforeAll` hooks for a multi-step infrastructure setup (connect DB, run migrations, seed data, start mock servers) discover that when the DB connection hook fails in CI (e.g., database not ready), all subsequent hooks also fail and produce separate error entries in the report, creating a noisy failure dump. WHY this matters: in prior Cucumber versions, anonymous `BeforeAll` hooks also all ran on failure, but the unnamed errors appeared as a single undifferentiated block; named hooks expose each failure individually, making the cascade more visible but also more alarming. Fix: add an explicit readiness check in the first `BeforeAll` hook that throws a `SkipError` or sets a module-level `infrastructureReady = false` flag that subsequent hooks check before executing, so a single root-cause failure produces a single diagnostic error.

**[community] Gotcha 5 — Scenario Outline examples that contain pipe characters (`|`) in cell values (e.g., a permissions string like `read|write|admin`) break the Gherkin table parser because the unescaped `|` is interpreted as a column delimiter, producing a parse error that Gherkin reports as "Table cell count mismatch" rather than "Illegal character in cell value", causing teams to spend time counting columns in the examples table before realizing the content contains a pipe character that needs escaping**: Teams writing BDD scenarios for permission-based features commonly use pipe-delimited permission strings as example values. WHY the error message is misleading: Gherkin's parser sees an extra column delimiter and counts one more cell than the header row has headers, reporting a structural error rather than a value-content error; the fix (escaping the pipe as `\|`) is not mentioned in the "Table cell count mismatch" error message. Fix: escape pipe characters in Gherkin table cells as `\|` (e.g., `| read\|write\|admin |`), or restructure permission values to use a different delimiter (comma, colon) that does not conflict with Gherkin table syntax, and document this constraint in the team's Gherkin style guide to prevent recurrence. [community]
