## Cycle 45 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 31 — Playwright v1.60 `test.abort()` for Unrecoverable BDD Step Guard Rails  [official]

Playwright v1.60 introduced `test.abort(message?)` as a first-class method for immediately terminating the currently running test from within any route handler, fixture, or step body. In BDD scenarios, this is the correct mechanism for guarding against misuse that would corrupt shared infrastructure — for example, preventing a `Then` step from accidentally issuing a write to a production endpoint by placing a `test.abort()` call inside a `page.route()` handler that matches the forbidden URL pattern. The test is immediately marked as failed, execution stops, and the abort message appears in the HTML report alongside the scenario name and step that triggered the guard. Unlike throwing a raw `Error`, `test.abort()` signals intentional early termination, which Playwright distinguishes from an unexpected assertion failure when generating test result summaries.

```typescript
// features/steps/guard-steps.ts
import { When, Then } from './bdd';

// Guard fixture that prevents accidental production writes in BDD test runs
export const guardFixture = base.extend<{ productionGuard: void }>({
  productionGuard: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await page.route('**/api/v*/production/**', async (route) => {
      // Abort the test immediately rather than fulfilling or continuing the request
      test.abort(
        `BDD scenario attempted a write to production endpoint: ${route.request().url()}. ` +
        `Use a staging or mock API base URL in the scenario context.`
      );
      await route.abort();
    });
    await use();
  },
});

// Step definitions that rely on the guard fixture being active
When('I submit the order form', async ({ page, productionGuard: _guard }) => {
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit Order' }).click();
});

Then('the order confirmation is displayed', async ({ page }) => {
  await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Order Confirmed/ })).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `test.abort()` stops all remaining steps immediately, so subsequent `Then` steps that would have provided diagnostic context (e.g., a screenshot of the page state at the moment of the violation) are skipped. WHY this is acceptable: the abort message includes the exact URL that triggered the guard, which is more actionable than a screenshot; combine `test.abort()` with a route handler that logs the full request body to `test.info().attach()` before aborting if richer diagnostics are needed. Do NOT use `test.abort()` for expected failure cases — those belong in `test.fail()` annotations or `expect().toFail()` patterns.

---

### Pattern 32 — Playwright `expect.soft()` for Multi-Assertion BDD `Then` Steps  [official]

Playwright's `expect.soft()` allows a `Then` step to collect multiple assertion failures without terminating after the first failed assertion, which is the correct approach for BDD scenarios that need to verify several independent observable outcomes of a single action. A `Then` step that asserts on page title, visible headings, and URL simultaneously using `expect.soft()` will capture all mismatches in a single test run rather than surfacing them one at a time across successive re-runs. After all soft assertions complete, the step implementation calls `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` to convert accumulated failures into a single step-level error that Cucumber's reporting layer attributes to the correct `Then` step. This pattern is especially valuable for BDD suites running against frequently changing UI where multiple layout properties change in a single deployment, enabling QA to see the full extent of regression in one run.

```typescript
// features/steps/checkout-steps.ts
import { Then } from './bdd';

Then(
  'the order confirmation page displays all required elements',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Soft assertions — all run even when one fails
    await expect.soft(page).toHaveTitle(/Order Confirmed — Acme Store/);
    await expect.soft(page.getByRole('heading', { level: 1 }))
      .toHaveText('Your order has been placed!');
    await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('order-number')).toBeVisible();
    await expect.soft(page.getByTestId('estimated-delivery')).toBeVisible();
    await expect.soft(page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Continue Shopping' }))
      .toBeVisible();
    await expect.soft(page).toHaveURL(/\/orders\/[A-Z0-9]{8}/);

    // Fail the step if any soft assertion above collected an error
    // — this attribute is ONLY checked here, not automatically
    expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Soft assertions require the step implementor to remember to add the `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` guard at the end; if the guard is omitted, the test is reported as passed even when soft assertions failed, silently swallowing real regressions. WHY this is a common omission: the `expect.soft()` API does not enforce the final check — it is purely opt-in, and teams that adopt `expect.soft()` from documentation examples may not notice the guard requirement. Add a custom ESLint rule (or a project `afterEach` fixture that re-checks `test.info().errors`) to catch steps that use `expect.soft()` without the closing guard.

---

### Pattern 33 — Playwright `page.routeFromHAR()` for Deterministic BDD API Replay  [official]

`page.routeFromHAR(harFile, { url, update })` lets BDD `Given` steps activate network replay from a recorded HAR file rather than standing up a live mock server or a full backend. The pattern separates two concerns cleanly: a `Given` step sets up the HAR replay, and subsequent `When`/`Then` steps interact with the UI as if a real API were responding. Setting `update: false` ensures tests are fully deterministic — the same response body, headers, and status codes are returned on every run without network variance. The HAR file is committed to source control alongside the feature file it serves, making the BDD scenario self-contained and auditable: reviewers can inspect the HAR to understand exactly which API responses drive the acceptance criteria.

```typescript
// features/steps/product-catalog-steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then } from './bdd';
import path from 'path';

const HAR_DIR = path.resolve(__dirname, '../../fixtures/hars');

Given(
  'the product catalog API returns the standard electronics inventory',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Activate HAR replay for all API calls matching the catalog endpoint
    await page.routeFromHAR(
      path.join(HAR_DIR, 'product-catalog-electronics.har'),
      {
        url: '**/api/v2/catalog/**',
        update: false,           // Never re-record — use committed HAR data
        notFound: 'fallback',    // Pass through requests not in the HAR
      }
    );
    // Navigate to the page that will trigger catalog API calls
    await page.goto('/products');
  }
);

When('I filter by category {string}', async ({ page }, category: string) => {
  await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Category' }).selectOption(category);
});

Then('I should see {int} product listings', async ({ page }, count: number) => {
  await expect(page.getByTestId('product-card')).toHaveCount(count);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** HAR files grow stale when the API contract changes — a `Then` step asserting on a field that was renamed in the API will pass against the old HAR while failing against the live service. WHY this creates false confidence: the BDD scenario appears green in CI (which uses the HAR) while failing in production (which hits the real service); the contract drift is invisible until a release. Fix: add a weekly scheduled CI job that runs the same BDD scenarios with `update: true` against a staging environment to refresh HAR files, and treat a HAR diff as a required review artifact in pull requests that change API contracts.

---

### Pattern 34 — Playwright `page.ariaSnapshot()` for Structural BDD Accessibility Assertions  [official]

`page.ariaSnapshot()` (Playwright v1.59+) captures the live accessibility tree of the page as a YAML string, which can be compared against a committed baseline using `expect(page).toMatchAriaSnapshot()`. In BDD `Then` steps, aria snapshot assertions replace brittle CSS-selector-based structural checks with semantics-first assertions: instead of asserting that a `div.card-list` contains three `article` elements, the step asserts that the accessibility tree contains a `list` with three `listitem` entries each containing a `heading`. Partial matching (the default) means snapshot comparisons only enforce the elements explicitly named in the template, so dynamic timestamps or IDs that change between runs do not break the baseline. The snapshots are updated via `npx playwright test --update-snapshots`, and the `.aria.yml` baseline files are committed to source control alongside the feature files.

```typescript
// features/steps/dashboard-steps.ts
import { Then } from './bdd';

Then('the dashboard navigation structure is accessible', async ({ page }) => {
  // toMatchAriaSnapshot uses a committed .aria.yml baseline by default
  // Partial matching: only the elements listed in the template are enforced
  await expect(page.getByRole('navigation', { name: 'Main' }))
    .toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
      - navigation "Main":
        - list:
          - listitem:
            - link "Dashboard" [current=page]
          - listitem:
            - link "Products"
          - listitem:
            - link "Orders"
          - listitem:
            - link "Settings"
    `);
});

Then(
  'the product search results are keyboard navigable',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Use page.ariaSnapshot() programmatically to capture and compare inline
    const snapshot = await page.locator('[data-testid="search-results"]')
      .ariaSnapshot();
    // Inline assertion using a YAML template with regex for dynamic content
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="search-results"]'))
      .toMatchAriaSnapshot(`
        - list:
          - listitem:
            - heading /Wireless Headphones/ [level=3]
          - listitem:
            - heading /Bluetooth Speaker/ [level=3]
      `);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Aria snapshots are meaningless for applications that have poor accessibility markup — an application that renders all content inside `div` elements with no ARIA roles will produce a flat, uninformative snapshot that does not catch structural regressions. WHY teams discover this late: the snapshot is generated programmatically from the live DOM, so if the DOM has no role attributes, the snapshot will be almost empty, and assertions against an empty snapshot will always pass even when the structure breaks. Use aria snapshot assertions as a forcing function to improve accessibility markup, not as a substitute for it.

---

### Pattern 35 — Playwright `test.step()` with `{ box: true }` for BDD Step Wrapper Tracing  [official]

`test.step(name, body, { box: true })` (Playwright v1.59+) allows BDD step definition wrappers — utility functions shared across multiple step files — to report errors at their call site rather than deep in the wrapper internals. In playwright-bdd suites where shared helper functions wrap common multi-step UI interactions (login sequences, form submission routines, navigation helpers), wrapping each helper in a `test.step(..., { box: true })` call causes failures to point to the line in the step definition file that called the helper rather than to line 47 of `loginHelper.ts`. This makes Playwright's HTML report directly actionable: the failure annotation names the BDD step that invoked the helper and the step name from `test.step()`, without requiring the developer to trace through intermediate stack frames to understand which Gherkin step triggered the failure.

```typescript
// features/support/login-helper.ts
import { Page, test } from '@playwright/test';

export async function performLogin(
  page: Page,
  username: string,
  password: string
): Promise<void> {
  // box: true ensures failures point to the caller (the step definition),
  // not to the internals of this helper function
  await test.step(`Login as ${username}`, async () => {
    await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Username' }).fill(username);
    await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Password' }).fill(password);
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign In' }).click();
    await page.waitForURL('**/dashboard');
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: /Welcome/ })).toBeVisible();
  }, { box: true });
}

// features/steps/auth-steps.ts
import { Given } from './bdd';
import { performLogin } from '../support/login-helper';

Given(
  'I am logged in as {string} with password {string}',
  async ({ page }, username: string, password: string) => {
    await performLogin(page, username, password);
    // If performLogin fails, the error points HERE (step definition line),
    // not to the interior of performLogin — { box: true } ensures this
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `{ box: true }` hides the internal stack trace of the helper function, which is exactly the right behavior for production step definitions but counterproductive during initial development of the helper itself when you need to see the exact line inside the helper that fails. WHY teams over-apply boxing: the clean error attribution at the step level looks appealing during a demo, so teams add `box: true` to every helper immediately. Fix: develop helpers without `box: true`, add it once the helper is stable and the internal implementation is trusted; keep `box: false` (the default) for helpers that are still actively being debugged.

---

### Pattern 36 — Cucumber.js v12.8 `customExternalisingOptions` for Scenario Suite Sharding  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.8.0 introduced `customExternalisingOptions` in the configuration API, enabling custom control over how large scenario suites are split into work packages for parallel execution — the "externalising" step where the coordinator converts the full pickle list into per-worker assignments. Before v12.8, teams working with suites containing thousands of scenarios could only control parallel granularity through `setParallelCanAssign` tag rules, which influenced assignment but could not control work package boundaries. With `customExternalisingOptions`, a configuration plugin can specify chunk sizes, priority weights, or tag-based grouping strategies that the coordinator applies when distributing pickles, allowing a 2000-scenario suite to be split into optimally sized work packages that keep all workers saturated without one worker finishing 1500 scenarios while another finishes 3.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts
import { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

const config: IConfiguration = {
  default: {
    parallel: 8,
    // customExternalisingOptions controls how pickles are chunked per worker
    // Values are passed to the externalising coordinator plugin
    customExternalisingOptions: {
      // Target ~250 scenarios per worker chunk to balance startup overhead
      // against scenario processing time — tune per suite's avg scenario duration
      targetChunkSize: 250,
      // Group scenarios tagged with @slow into their own chunks
      // so slow scenarios don't block workers assigned mixed-speed chunks
      chunkingStrategy: 'tag-aware',
      slowTags: ['@slow', '@integration', '@database'],
    },
    // Plugin that implements the customExternalisingOptions contract
    plugin: ['./scripts/cucumber-chunk-plugin.js'],
    format: [
      'html:reports/cucumber-report.html',
      'json:reports/cucumber-report.json',
    ],
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    require: ['src/steps/**/*.ts'],
    loader: ['tsx'],
  },
} satisfies { default: IConfiguration };

export default config;
```

**Tradeoff.** `customExternalisingOptions` requires a companion plugin (the `plugin` key) that implements the actual chunking logic — the option keys shown above are plugin-defined, not built-in Cucumber constants, so the same configuration has no effect if the plugin is absent or mis-registered. WHY teams encounter this silently: Cucumber does not validate `customExternalisingOptions` keys against any schema, so passing an unrecognized option object to a plugin that doesn't read it produces no error but also no chunking effect; the suite runs with default round-robin assignment as if `customExternalisingOptions` were not set. Always add a CI step that asserts `CUCUMBER_TOTAL_WORKERS` matches the expected parallel count and that each worker's scenario count is within a tolerance band of `total / workers`.

---

### Pattern 37 — Cucumber.js v12.7 `env` Config Option for Parallel Worker Environment Propagation  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.7 added the `env` key to the configuration API, allowing named environment variables from the parent process to be explicitly propagated to parallel worker processes. Before this feature, teams used `CUCUMBER_PARALLEL` and `CUCUMBER_WORKER_ID` to detect parallelism in worker code, but arbitrary variables from the coordinator environment (feature flags, API keys, target environment URLs) were not automatically forwarded — each worker spawned with a bare environment containing only the variables explicitly set in the worker spawn call. The `env` key accepts an array of variable names, and the coordinator forwards their current values from `process.env` to each worker's subprocess environment before the worker begins processing its assigned pickle batch, making it possible to run the same suite against different environments by setting `TARGET_ENV=staging` once at the coordinator level rather than duplicating it in every worker config.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts
import { IConfiguration } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

export default {
  default: {
    parallel: 4,
    // Propagate these variables from the CI environment to all parallel workers.
    // Workers receive the values as they were set in the coordinator's process.env
    // at the time the coordinator started — not at the time the worker spawns.
    env: [
      'TARGET_ENV',         // 'staging' | 'preview' | 'local'
      'FEATURE_FLAGS',      // comma-separated feature flag overrides
      'AUTH_TOKEN',         // shared test auth token for API calls
      'FORCE_COLOR',        // terminal color output propagation (v12.6 replacement)
      'DATABASE_URL',       // test database connection for database step definitions
    ],
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    require: ['src/steps/**/*.ts'],
    loader: ['tsx'],
  },
} satisfies { default: IConfiguration };

// In step definitions, workers can safely read propagated variables:
// const targetEnv = process.env.TARGET_ENV ?? 'local';
// const apiBase = API_BASES[targetEnv];
```

**Tradeoff.** Variables listed in `env` are read from the coordinator's `process.env` at coordinator startup and frozen before any workers spawn — if the coordinator modifies `process.env` during its own initialization (e.g., loading `.env` files via `dotenv` in a `BeforeAll` hook), those modifications occur after the `env` snapshot is taken and are NOT forwarded to workers. WHY this ordering surprises teams: `BeforeAll` hooks appear to run before anything else from the developer's perspective, but in the parallel coordinator model, the `env` snapshot is taken during worker spawn setup, which precedes `BeforeAll` hook execution. Fix: load all required environment variables before invoking Cucumber (in a wrapper script or via `dotenv` loaded in `cucumber.config.ts` at module evaluation time), not in `BeforeAll` hooks.

---

### Pattern 38 — Cucumber Expressions v19 Custom Parameter Types with `transformer` for Domain-Typed BDD Steps  [official]

Cucumber Expressions v19 (January 2026) maintains full support for custom parameter types registered via `defineParameterType()`, enabling BDD steps to accept domain-specific literals (ISO date strings, UUID-format identifiers, currency amounts) and automatically transform them into typed values before the step function receives them. A custom parameter type defined with a `regexp` and `transformer` function means the step definition receives a fully-typed domain object — a `Money` instance, a `UserId`, a `DateRange` — rather than a raw string that every step function must parse independently. This centralizes the parsing logic in one place, makes step function signatures self-documenting (a step that receives `UserId` is clearly not accepting arbitrary strings), and produces cleaner Cucumber expression step text (`the user {userId} places an order`) that is more readable in feature files than `the user with id {string} places an order` combined with `UserId.parse(idString)` in every step body.

```typescript
// features/support/parameter-types.ts
import { defineParameterType } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

// Domain type for money amounts used in e-commerce BDD scenarios
class Money {
  constructor(
    public readonly amount: number,
    public readonly currency: string
  ) {}
  toString(): string { return `${this.currency} ${this.amount.toFixed(2)}`; }
}

defineParameterType({
  name: 'money',
  // Matches patterns like: USD 29.99, EUR 1,234.50, GBP 0.99
  regexp: /([A-Z]{3})\s+([\d,]+\.\d{2})/,
  transformer(currency: string, amountStr: string): Money {
    const amount = parseFloat(amountStr.replace(',', ''));
    return new Money(amount, currency);
  },
});

// Custom UserId type — only accepts valid UUID v4 format
defineParameterType({
  name: 'userId',
  regexp: /[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-4[0-9a-f]{3}-[89ab][0-9a-f]{3}-[0-9a-f]{12}/,
  transformer(uuidStr: string): string {
    return uuidStr; // Keep as string but validate format at parse time
  },
});

// Step definition using custom parameter types:
// Given('the user {userId} has a balance of {money}',
//   async (userId: string, balance: Money) => { ... })
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom parameter types are globally registered — once `defineParameterType({ name: 'money' })` is called, the `{money}` parameter type is available in all step files loaded in the same Cucumber run, which is the intended behavior but becomes a problem when two feature areas need `{money}` to transform to different types (e.g., one area uses a `Money` class, another uses a plain `number`). WHY teams encounter this: large monorepos with multiple BDD suites sharing a step library register conflicting `{money}` types in the shared library and in feature-area-specific step files, and Cucumber raises an "Ambiguous parameter type" error rather than using the most recently registered type. Fix: use namespaced parameter type names in shared libraries (`{shared:money}`, `{ecommerce:money}`) and reserve unqualified names (`{money}`) for the primary feature area; document the naming convention in the project BDD style guide.

---

### Pattern 39 — Playwright `expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` for Visual Regression BDD `Then` Steps  [official]

`expect(page).toHaveScreenshot(name, options)` integrates Playwright's visual comparison engine into BDD `Then` steps, providing a screenshot baseline that is committed to source control and compared pixel-by-pixel on every subsequent test run. In BDD scenarios that test rendering of complex UI components (data tables, charts, rich-text editor output), a visual `Then` step supplements functional assertions by capturing the entire rendered state rather than asserting on individual DOM properties. The baseline screenshot is auto-generated on first run (`--update-snapshots`) and stored in `__screenshots__/` alongside the step definition file. Playwright's comparison engine applies a configurable pixel-difference threshold (`maxDiffPixelRatio`) to tolerate minor anti-aliasing differences between operating systems, and the HTML report embeds the expected, actual, and diff images inline for failed assertions, making visual regressions immediately visible in CI.

```typescript
// features/steps/report-visual-steps.ts
import { Then } from './bdd';

Then(
  'the monthly revenue chart renders correctly',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Functional assertions first — identify what broke before the screenshot
    await expect(
      page.getByRole('img', { name: 'Monthly Revenue Chart' })
    ).toBeVisible();
    await expect(page.getByTestId('chart-legend')).toBeVisible();

    // Visual regression assertion — compares against committed baseline
    // Baseline stored at: __screenshots__/report-visual-steps/
    //   monthly-revenue-chart-renders-correctly-1.png
    await expect(page.getByTestId('revenue-chart-container'))
      .toHaveScreenshot('monthly-revenue-chart.png', {
        maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.02,  // Allow 2% pixel difference for font rendering
        animations: 'disabled',   // Freeze CSS animations before capture
        mask: [page.getByTestId('chart-last-updated')], // Mask dynamic timestamp
      });
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Visual snapshot baselines must be regenerated whenever intentional UI changes are made, and the regeneration command (`npx playwright test --update-snapshots`) updates all baselines for all features simultaneously if no path filter is specified, making it easy to silently accept an unintended visual regression alongside the intended change. WHY teams lose baseline integrity: developers run `--update-snapshots` to accept their feature's new visual design, inadvertently accepting a co-worker's unreviewed visual change in a different feature that happened to have a screenshot captured in the same run. Fix: run `--update-snapshots` with a path filter (`npx playwright test features/reports/ --update-snapshots`) to update only the affected feature's baselines; require screenshot baseline changes to be reviewed in pull requests as a separate PR step.

---

### Pattern 40 — Cucumber.js `setParallelCanAssign` with `atMostOnePicklePerTag` for Database-Isolation BDD Scenarios  [official]

`setParallelCanAssign` combined with the built-in `atMostOnePicklePerTag` helper prevents Cucumber's parallel coordinator from assigning two scenarios that share a database entity tag to the same concurrent execution window. BDD scenarios that create, modify, or delete database records tagged with `@entity:account-42` must not run simultaneously with another scenario that also uses `@entity:account-42`, because concurrent writes to the same record produce non-deterministic test failures that are indistinguishable from real application bugs in CI reports. Registering a `setParallelCanAssign` rule that calls `atMostOnePicklePerTag(/@entity:/)` enforces single-concurrent-execution for all entity-tagged scenarios without requiring a dedicated serial queue or test-order dependency, allowing untagged scenarios to continue running in full parallel while entity-specific scenarios serialize automatically.

```typescript
// features/support/parallel-hooks.ts
import {
  BeforeAll,
  setParallelCanAssign,
  parallelCanAssignHelpers,
} from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import type { Pickle } from '@cucumber/messages';

const { atMostOnePicklePerTag } = parallelCanAssignHelpers;

// Compose multiple parallel constraints:
// 1. Only one scenario per entity tag at a time (database isolation)
// 2. Only one @admin-auth scenario at a time (session token uniqueness)
setParallelCanAssign(
  (pickleInQuestion: Pickle, picklesInProgress: Pickle[]): boolean => {
    // Rule 1: Entity-tagged scenarios must not run concurrently
    const entityIsolated = atMostOnePicklePerTag(
      /@entity:/
    )(pickleInQuestion, picklesInProgress);

    // Rule 2: Admin auth scenarios share a single admin session — serialize them
    const adminSessionIsolated = atMostOnePicklePerTag(
      /@admin-auth/
    )(pickleInQuestion, picklesInProgress);

    return entityIsolated && adminSessionIsolated;
  }
);

BeforeAll(async function () {
  // Global setup runs once per worker — entity cleanup is scenario-level
  await ensureDatabaseIsReady();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `atMostOnePicklePerTag` serializes all scenarios that share a tag value, which can dramatically reduce parallelism when a tag is applied broadly — if 300 of 500 scenarios are tagged `@entity:user`, those 300 scenarios will execute serially even though they use different user records. WHY teams over-apply entity tags: the pattern is introduced to solve a real isolation bug, and teams apply the same tag to all scenarios in a feature file using a file-level tag rather than scenario-level tags, accidentally serializing an entire feature. Fix: apply `@entity:` tags at the scenario level using specific entity identifiers (`@entity:user-42`, `@entity:product-99`) rather than generic category tags; use a linter rule to flag `@entity:` tags applied at the `Feature` level.

---

### Pattern 41 — playwright-bdd Composable Fixture Tag Strategy for Per-Scenario Route Interception  [community]

Rather than building a single monolithic `mockedApi` fixture that intercepts all external requests, teams maintaining large playwright-bdd suites compose narrow, domain-specific route fixtures (`mockedAuthApi`, `mockedProductApi`, `mockedOrderApi`) and activate them selectively per scenario using `@fixture:` tags. Each domain fixture registers `page.route()` interceptors only for its own URL pattern, so a scenario tagged `@fixture:mockedProductApi` receives only product endpoint mocking while its auth and order requests are passed through to a live staging service. This composable approach means integration scenarios can mix live and mocked APIs in fine-grained combinations — a single scenario can test the real auth flow against the live identity provider while keeping the product catalog deterministic with a fixture, without needing separate test environments for every combination.

```typescript
// features/support/fixtures/mocked-product-api.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ mockedProductApi: void }>({
  mockedProductApi: async ({ page }, use) => {
    // Only intercept the product catalog domain — auth and orders pass through
    await page.route('**/api/v*/products/**', async (route) => {
      const url = route.request().url();
      if (url.includes('/products/featured')) {
        await route.fulfill({
          status: 200,
          contentType: 'application/json',
          body: JSON.stringify(FEATURED_PRODUCTS_FIXTURE),
        });
        return;
      }
      // All other product requests: return empty catalog
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 200,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify({ items: [], total: 0 }),
      });
    });
    await use();
    // Route handlers auto-removed when fixture scope ends
  },
});

// playwright.config.ts: compose all domain fixtures into the bdd test object
// import { test } from './fixtures/composed-fixtures';
// export const { Given, When, Then } = createBdd(test);
```

```gherkin
# features/product-search.feature
@fixture:mockedProductApi
Scenario: Featured products display on homepage
  Given I am on the homepage
  Then I should see the featured products section
  # Auth requests go to live staging — only product API is mocked
```

**Tradeoff.** Composing many narrow fixtures creates a fixture dependency graph that can be difficult to visualize — if `mockedOrderApi` internally extends `mockedProductApi` (because order scenarios always need the product data too), and `mockedProductApi` is also applied via a separate `@fixture:` tag, the fixture is instantiated twice with two independent route handlers that both intercept the same URL pattern, causing request doubling. WHY this is hard to diagnose: Playwright does not warn when two route handlers match the same pattern; the first handler that calls `route.fulfill()` wins and the second handler's call to `route.continue()` or `route.fulfill()` throws an unhandled error. Fix: build fixture composition using Playwright's `extend()` call rather than independent fixture tags — `test = mockedOrderTest.extend<{ mockedOrderApi: void }>({ ... })` inherits `mockedProductApi` automatically without double-registration. [community]

---

### Pattern 42 — Gherkin `Rule` Keyword for Structuring Feature Files Around Business Rules  [community]

The `Rule` keyword (Gherkin v6+, fully supported in Cucumber.js v12 and playwright-bdd) groups related scenarios under an explicit business rule heading within a single feature file, providing a structural layer between the `Feature` and individual `Scenario` blocks. Teams maintaining feature files for complex business domains (pricing engines, eligibility checkers, multi-step approval workflows) use `Rule` to communicate which specific business rule each group of scenarios exercises, making the feature file serve as a living requirements document rather than a flat list of examples. Each `Rule` block can have its own `Background` that applies only to scenarios within that rule — a pricing feature might have one `Rule: Standard pricing applies during business hours` with a `Background` that sets the time context, and a separate `Rule: Surge pricing applies after 8pm` with a different `Background`, without mixing the two setups.

```gherkin
# features/pricing/dynamic-pricing.feature
Feature: Dynamic Pricing Engine

  Rule: Standard pricing applies during business hours

    Background:
      Given the current time is 2:00 PM on a weekday
      And the base price for a standard seat is USD 49.99

    Scenario: Single seat purchase uses standard rate
      When a customer purchases 1 seat
      Then the total price is USD 49.99

    Scenario: Bulk purchase applies standard volume discount
      When a customer purchases 10 seats
      Then the total price is USD 424.91

  Rule: Surge pricing multiplier applies outside business hours

    Background:
      Given the current time is 10:00 PM on a weekday
      And the base price for a standard seat is USD 49.99
      And the surge pricing multiplier is 1.5x

    Scenario: Single seat purchase uses surge rate
      When a customer purchases 1 seat
      Then the total price is USD 74.99

    Scenario: Surge pricing is capped at 2x the standard rate
      Given the surge pricing multiplier is 3.0x
      When a customer purchases 1 seat
      Then the total price is USD 99.98
```

**Tradeoff.** `Rule` blocks with their own `Background` are not universally supported by all Cucumber reporting tools — some older HTML reporters render `Rule: Background:` steps as if they belong to the root `Feature` Background, incorrectly attributing step failures to the feature-level setup rather than the rule-level setup, which causes developers to look for the wrong root cause when a rule-scoped Background step fails. WHY teams don't check reporter compatibility early: `Rule` is a relatively recent Gherkin addition and teams adopt it for its organizational clarity without verifying reporter support in CI. Check your HTML reporter's `Rule` rendering with a test feature file before adopting `Rule`-scoped Backgrounds in production scenarios; fall back to `describe`-like naming conventions in scenario names (`[Standard Pricing] Single seat purchase uses standard rate`) if your reporter mishandles `Rule`. [community]

---

### Pattern 43 — Playwright `browser.on('context')` for Global BDD Route Interception Across All Pages  [official]

`browser.on('context', async (context) => { ... })` (Playwright v1.60) fires whenever a new `BrowserContext` is created within the browser instance, enabling BDD test suites to register route interceptors at the browser level rather than at the page or context level. In playwright-bdd suites that open multiple pages in a single scenario (multi-tab shopping cart flows, OAuth popup windows, file download dialogs that open a new context), `page.route()` intercepts only the originating page, and `browserContext.route()` requires a context reference that may not be available when a new page opens. The `browser.on('context')` hook receives the new context object before any navigation occurs, making it the correct place to register route interceptors that should apply to every page opened from any context within the test.

```typescript
// features/support/browser-hooks.fixture.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ globalApiGuard: void }, { browser: never }>({
  // Worker-scoped fixture: runs once per Playwright worker, not per scenario
  globalApiGuard: [
    async ({ browser }, use) => {
      const contextInterceptors: Array<() => void> = [];

      browser.on('context', async (context) => {
        // Register a global interceptor on every new context — including popups
        await context.route('**/api/external-payments/**', async (route) => {
          // Block all real payment API calls — route to a test mock server
          await route.fulfill({
            status: 200,
            contentType: 'application/json',
            body: JSON.stringify({ transactionId: 'test-txn-001', status: 'approved' }),
          });
        });
      });

      await use();
      // Contexts are cleaned up by Playwright's fixture lifecycle
    },
    { scope: 'worker' }, // Apply once per worker, not per scenario
  ],
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped `browser.on('context')` interceptors apply to all scenarios in the worker's execution batch, so a route interceptor added in one scenario's worker-scoped fixture persists into subsequent scenarios assigned to the same worker. WHY this causes unexpected interference: if the payment mock fixture is worker-scoped but the expected behavior test (which needs real payment responses to test error handling) runs later in the same worker, it receives mock payment responses from the still-active interceptor. Fix: use context-scoped fixtures (`scope: 'test'`, the default) rather than worker-scoped fixtures for interceptors that should not persist across scenarios; reserve worker-scoped interceptors only for truly global, non-interfering concerns (blocking telemetry, blocking analytics) that every scenario benefits from unconditionally.

---

### Pattern 44 — Cucumber.js v12.8.3 Thrown-String Error Handling Fix for BDD Hook Diagnostics  [official]

Cucumber.js v12.8.3 (May 2025) fixed a long-standing issue where `BeforeAll`, `AfterAll`, `Before`, and `After` hooks that `throw 'a string'` (throwing a primitive string rather than an `Error` instance) produced an unformatted error message in the HTML report and a missing stack trace, making hook failures from legacy JavaScript step libraries difficult to diagnose. The fix normalizes thrown strings into `Error` objects before recording them in the test result envelope, ensuring the HTML report shows the thrown string as the error message (not `[object Object]` or an empty error card) and the hook's registered name (for named hooks) appears correctly in the failure attribution. Teams migrating Cucumber.js step libraries from JavaScript to TypeScript frequently encounter this when legacy hooks used `throw 'setup failed: database connection refused'` rather than `throw new Error('setup failed: ...')`.

```typescript
// Before v12.8.3 — threw a string, causing unformatted report errors
// AfterAll(async function () {
//   if (!cleanupSucceeded) throw 'Cleanup failed: temp tables still exist';
// });

// After v12.8.3 — still works if you throw a string (normalized to Error),
// but the recommended fix is to always throw Error instances:
import { AfterAll, BeforeAll } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

let dbPool: DatabasePool | null = null;

BeforeAll({ name: 'Connect database pool', timeout: 30_000 }, async () => {
  dbPool = await DatabasePool.connect(process.env.DATABASE_URL!);
  if (!dbPool.isReady()) {
    // Always throw an Error, not a string — gives stack trace in all versions
    throw new Error(
      `BeforeAll hook "Connect database pool" failed: pool not ready after connect. ` +
      `DATABASE_URL=${process.env.DATABASE_URL}`
    );
  }
});

AfterAll({ name: 'Close database pool' }, async () => {
  if (dbPool) {
    await dbPool.end();
    dbPool = null;
  }
  // If cleanup fails, throw an Error with context — never throw a plain string
  // throw new Error('AfterAll: pool.end() rejected: ' + err.message);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The v12.8.3 normalization fix ensures that thrown strings appear as readable errors in reports, but it also silently masks hook author intent: if a thrown string was used as a deliberate "soft" signal (not a real Error, just a status message) the author may have expected different handling. WHY this is rare but possible: some older Cucumber helper libraries throw strings as a convention to indicate "skippable" failures, relying on the caller to distinguish string throws from Error throws via `instanceof`. Fix: audit all `BeforeAll`/`AfterAll` hooks in legacy JavaScript libraries for `throw 'string'` patterns and migrate them to `throw new Error('string')` before upgrading to v12.8.3; update any catch blocks that used `typeof caught === 'string'` to detect hook signals to use error `instanceof` checks instead.

---

### Pattern 45 — Gherkin Docstring Type Declaration for Multi-Format BDD Step Inputs  [community]

Gherkin docstrings (triple-quoted blocks attached to a step) support an optional content type declaration on the opening delimiter line — `"""json`, `"""yaml`, `"""xml` — that Cucumber passes to the step definition as the `docString.mediaType` property. Step definitions that accept a docstring can branch on `mediaType` to apply the correct parser, or use playwright-bdd's `$step.docStringType` fixture (v9+) to require a specific type and reject mismatched inputs with a clear error. This pattern is most valuable for BDD scenarios that test API request/response behavior where the request body is embedded directly in the feature file: the docstring type declaration communicates the payload format to both the step definition and to any human reading the feature file, removing ambiguity about whether `{ "key": "value" }` in the docstring is JSON, a configuration DSL, or plain text.

```gherkin
# features/api/order-api.feature
Feature: Order API BDD Scenarios

  Scenario: Create order with valid JSON payload
    When I POST to /api/v2/orders with body:
      """json
      {
        "customerId": "cust-001",
        "items": [
          { "productId": "prod-100", "quantity": 2 }
        ],
        "shippingAddress": {
          "street": "123 Test Lane",
          "city": "Testville",
          "zip": "90210"
        }
      }
      """
    Then the response status is 201
    And the response body matches:
      """json
      {
        "orderId": "{{ any string }}",
        "status": "pending",
        "itemCount": 2
      }
      """
```

```typescript
// features/steps/api-steps.ts
import { When, Then } from './bdd';

When(
  'I POST to {string} with body:',
  async ({ page, request }, endpoint: string, docString: { content: string; mediaType?: string }) => {
    const mediaType = docString.mediaType ?? 'application/json';
    const body = mediaType === 'application/json'
      ? JSON.parse(docString.content)
      : docString.content; // YAML or XML parsers would branch here

    // Use Playwright's APIRequestContext for direct HTTP assertions in BDD
    const response = await request.post(endpoint, {
      data: body,
      headers: { 'Content-Type': mediaType },
    });
    // Store response on Playwright test info for Then step access
    await page.evaluate(
      ([status, body]) => { (window as any).__lastApiResponse = { status, body }; },
      [response.status(), await response.text()]
    );
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Docstring media type declarations are purely advisory — Cucumber does not validate that the docstring content actually conforms to the declared type, so a step receiving `"""json` can contain malformed JSON that only fails at `JSON.parse()` time inside the step implementation with a cryptic `SyntaxError` rather than a Gherkin parse error. WHY teams expect type validation: the `"""json` syntax looks like a type annotation that should be validated at parse time (similar to how Gherkin validates table column counts), but it is purely a content hint. Fix: add an explicit validation step at the top of every docstring-accepting step definition that checks `JSON.parse(docString.content)` and rethrows with a descriptive message (`Invalid JSON in docstring for step "I POST to ${endpoint}": ${parseError.message}`) so the Cucumber report names the failing step rather than showing an internal `SyntaxError`. [community]

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 45

**[community] Gotcha 1 — Playwright `expect.soft()` assertions that are placed inside a `test.step()` wrapper do NOT accumulate failures on `test.info().errors` until the step callback completes — errors are buffered at the step boundary, causing the final `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` guard placed immediately after a `test.step()` call to see an empty error array even when soft assertions inside the step failed, because Playwright flushes step-scoped soft assertion errors onto `test.info().errors` only after the `test.step()` promise resolves**: Teams that refactor `Then` step implementations by wrapping groups of `expect.soft()` calls in named `test.step()` blocks for better HTML report organization discover that the guard check `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` placed after the `test.step()` block always passes, and the test is marked green even though the soft assertions inside the step collected failures — the failures appear only in the step detail panel of the HTML report, not as test-level failures. WHY this is counterintuitive: `test.info()` is a shared object, and developers assume mutations to `test.info().errors` from inside a `test.step()` are immediately visible outside the step; Playwright's implementation stages soft assertion errors at the step scope and merges them into `test.info().errors` when the step resolves, so the array is empty during the synchronous check after `await test.step(...)`. Fix: place the `expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0)` guard inside the `test.step()` callback as the last line, not after the awaited step call; or restructure so that soft assertions and their guard all live at the same scope level without intermediate `test.step()` wrappers.

**[community] Gotcha 2 — Cucumber.js v12.7 `env` config key only forwards variables that exist in the coordinator's `process.env` at worker spawn time — variables dynamically set on `process.env` by `BeforeAll` hooks (which run after worker spawn) are never forwarded, causing step definitions in parallel workers that depend on coordinator-side `BeforeAll`-computed values (dynamic port assignments, ephemeral tokens from a `beforeAll`-started mock server) to receive `undefined` for those variables even when `env: ['DYNAMIC_PORT']` is listed in the config**: Teams that start an in-process mock server in a `BeforeAll` hook, set `process.env.MOCK_SERVER_PORT = server.port.toString()`, and list `MOCK_SERVER_PORT` in the `env` config key discover that parallel workers always receive `MOCK_SERVER_PORT=undefined` regardless of the hook's execution. WHY the ordering is unexpected: `BeforeAll` documentation describes hooks as running before any scenario, which implies before workers receive their assignments — but in parallel mode the worker spawn (and `env` snapshot) occurs before `BeforeAll` hooks execute in the coordinator. Fix: start infrastructure servers and compute dynamic values in `cucumber.config.ts` at module evaluation time (outside any hook), assign the computed values to `process.env` during config loading, and then reference those keys in the `env` array — config module evaluation happens before worker spawn.

**[community] Gotcha 3 — Playwright `toHaveScreenshot()` baselines captured on macOS with a Retina display (`devicePixelRatio: 2`) do not match when the same test runs on a Linux CI agent with `devicePixelRatio: 1`, causing every visual BDD `Then` step to fail in CI even when the UI has not changed, because Playwright captures screenshots at the device's native pixel ratio and the stored baseline reflects the capture device's pixel density rather than a normalized resolution**: Teams that develop BDD scenarios on MacBook Pros and commit the auto-generated screenshot baselines discover that CI immediately fails all visual assertions with "Screenshot comparison failed" even before any code change occurs. WHY teams don't detect this before commit: `npx playwright test` on the developer machine generates and immediately passes against the just-captured baseline (same machine, same DPR), so the test is green locally and only fails when CI uses a different DPR. Fix: set `viewport: { width: 1280, height: 720 }` and explicitly set `deviceScaleFactor: 1` in `playwright.config.ts` for all screenshot-taking projects; capture and commit baselines only from a CI-equivalent headless Linux environment by running `--update-snapshots` in a Docker container that matches CI before committing baseline images.

**[community] Gotcha 4 — Gherkin `Rule: Background:` steps in Cucumber.js v12 run ONCE per `Rule`-scoped scenario, but teams using database-seeding steps in a `Rule: Background:` that create unique-keyed records encounter unique-constraint violations starting from the second scenario in the `Rule` block — the same failure as feature-level `Background:` with `Scenario Outline` (Gotcha 6 from Cycle 37) but scoped to the `Rule` level, which is less well-documented and surprises teams that already fixed the feature-level version**: Teams that correctly use `BeforeAll` hooks for feature-level data setup but add a `Rule: Background:` for rule-specific records discover the same re-execution issue at the `Rule` scope: each scenario in the `Rule` triggers the `Rule: Background:` steps, and the second scenario's Background fails with a unique-constraint violation on data the first scenario already created. WHY this is under-documented: most community guidance on Gherkin `Background:` re-execution covers the feature-level `Background:` with `Scenario Outline` (the most common case), but the behavior is identical for `Rule: Background:` and the Cucumber.js documentation does not call out the re-execution behavior specifically for `Rule`-scoped Backgrounds. Fix: use the same upsert-or-check-first pattern in `Rule: Background:` step implementations as in feature-level `Background:` steps; alternatively, move `Rule`-specific one-time setup to a named `BeforeAll` hook that checks an `infrastructureReady` flag before re-executing.

**[community] Gotcha 5 — playwright-bdd `@fixture:` tags on a `Scenario` that is part of a `Rule` block are resolved against the fixture registry at the `Scenario` level as expected, but the scenario also inherits the `Feature`-level `@fixture:` tag if one is present — and if both the `Feature` tag and the `Scenario` tag activate the same fixture, the fixture is instantiated twice (once via the Feature-level tag and once via the Scenario-level tag), causing double initialization that produces two sets of `page.route()` interceptors for the same URL pattern, and the first interceptor's `route.fulfill()` call causes the second interceptor's handler to throw "Request is already handled"**: Teams that tag their `Feature` with `@fixture:mockedAuthApi` (to mock auth for all scenarios in the file) and then also add `@fixture:mockedAuthApi` to a specific `Scenario` inside a `Rule` block (e.g., to make an intent explicit) observe that scenarios with the duplicate tag produce `Error: Request is already handled` in `AfterEach`, with no indication in the test failure message that a fixture was double-instantiated. WHY the double tag is hard to spot: the `Feature`-level `@fixture:` tag is written at the top of the file and may be far from the `Rule`/`Scenario` block where the duplicate is added, especially in long feature files with multiple `Rule` blocks; tools that highlight orphan tags do not flag duplicate `@fixture:` tags inherited from a parent scope. Fix: audit feature files that use `Rule` blocks for `@fixture:` tag inheritance — do not repeat a `Feature`-level fixture tag on any `Scenario` within that feature; add a Gherkin linter rule that flags `@fixture:` tags on `Scenario` blocks that are already inherited from the enclosing `Feature` tag.

## Cycle 46 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 045 — Worker-Scoped BDD Fixtures for Shared Infrastructure [official]

Playwright's `test.extend()` supports two fixture scopes: `'test'` (default, one instance per test) and `'worker'` (one instance per worker process). In BDD suites that spin up expensive infrastructure — database connections, mock servers, compiled asset servers — creating a new instance for every scenario inflates suite runtime proportionally with scenario count. Worker-scoped fixtures are initialized once when a worker starts and torn down when the worker exits, so all scenarios dispatched to the same worker share the resource. playwright-bdd forwards the Playwright fixture scope model unchanged: annotate the fixture property with `{ scope: 'worker' }` in the second argument of the `test.extend()` call and the BDD runtime honours the scoping semantics automatically without any Cucumber.js hook involvement.

```typescript
// fixtures/worker-db.ts
import { test as base } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { createPool, Pool } from './db';

type WorkerFixtures = { dbPool: Pool };

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  dbPool: [
    async ({}, use) => {
      // Runs ONCE per worker process, not once per scenario
      const pool = await createPool({ max: 5 });
      await use(pool);
      await pool.end(); // teardown when worker exits
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],
});

// features/steps/db-steps.ts — consuming the worker fixture
import { Given, Then } from './bdd'; // re-exports from fixtures/worker-db

Given('the database has {int} active users', async ({ dbPool }, count: number) => {
  await dbPool.query('DELETE FROM users WHERE active = true');
  const values = Array.from({ length: count }, (_, i) =>
    `('user_${i}', true)`
  ).join(',');
  await dbPool.query(`INSERT INTO users (name, active) VALUES ${values}`);
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped fixtures are shared across all scenarios in a worker, so any mutation that one scenario performs (truncating a table, changing a config value) persists for subsequent scenarios in the same worker unless each scenario explicitly resets state. WHY teams encounter silent cross-scenario pollution: the fixture teardown callback only runs at worker exit, not between scenarios, so a `DELETE FROM users` in one scenario's cleanup step must be the scenario's own responsibility rather than the fixture's; teams that assume the fixture re-initializes between scenarios discover state leakage only when scenarios run in the same worker in a specific order that exposes the accumulated mutations.

---

### Pattern 046 — `expect.toPass()` for Polling Complex Multi-Step BDD Then Assertions [official]

Playwright's `expect(async () => { ... }).toPass({ timeout: 10_000 })` retries an entire async callback block until it completes without throwing, applying a configurable polling interval between attempts. Unlike `expect.poll()`, which polls a single value, `toPass()` can contain multiple `expect` calls that must all pass in a single callback invocation — making it the correct tool for BDD `Then` steps that assert a combination of observable outcomes that converge asynchronously (e.g., a UI counter increments, a status badge changes colour, and a network request completes). The callback retries on any thrown `Error`, including assertion errors, allowing the entire multi-assertion block to stabilize before the timeout expires.

```typescript
// features/steps/order-steps.ts
import { Then } from './bdd';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Then(
  'the order dashboard should show the order as {string} with {int} item(s)',
  async ({ page }, status: string, itemCount: number) => {
    // All three assertions must pass simultaneously in a single callback run
    await expect(async () => {
      await expect(page.getByTestId('order-status')).toHaveText(status);
      await expect(page.getByTestId('item-count')).toHaveText(String(itemCount));
      await expect(page.getByTestId('last-updated')).not.toBeEmpty();
    }).toPass({ timeout: 15_000, intervals: [500, 1000, 2000] });
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `toPass()` intervals default to `[100, 250, 500, 1000]` milliseconds with exponential backoff, meaning a slow backend that updates after 8 seconds will trigger 10–15 retry attempts before succeeding, each of which issues DOM queries; in suites with many such `Then` steps the aggregate DOM query volume can slow headless browser performance. WHY teams reach for `toPass()` instead of individual `await expect(...).toBeVisible({ timeout })` calls: `toPass()` allows expressing a compound post-condition as a unit ("all of these must be true at the same moment"), whereas individual awaited assertions with per-assertion timeouts allow the conditions to satisfy at different points in time, potentially masking timing windows where the UI is in a partially-updated state.

### Pattern 047 — Cucumber.js `retry` Configuration with `@flaky` Tag Guard for Targeted Flake Mitigation [official]

Cucumber.js supports a `retry` configuration option (integer) that re-runs failing scenarios up to N additional times before recording a final failure. When applied globally via `cucumber.config.ts` this can mask genuine failures by silently retrying them. The recommended pattern is to set `retry: 0` in the default profile and define a separate `flaky` profile with `retry: 2` and a `tags: '@flaky'` filter — only explicitly tagged scenarios are eligible for retry. The `@flaky` tag doubles as documentation that the scenario has a known timing or environment dependency requiring remediation.

```typescript
// cucumber.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

export default defineConfig({
  default: {
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    import: ['features/steps/**/*.ts'],
    retry: 0, // No retries by default — failures are genuine
    format: ['progress-bar', 'html:reports/cucumber.html'],
  },
  flaky: {
    // Run with: npx cucumber-js --profile flaky
    paths: ['features/**/*.feature'],
    import: ['features/steps/**/*.ts'],
    retry: 2,
    tags: '@flaky', // Only retry explicitly tagged scenarios
    format: ['progress-bar', 'html:reports/cucumber-flaky.html'],
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `retry` count applies per-scenario, not per-step: a scenario that fails on step 3 of 8 steps retries the entire scenario from the first `Background` step, not from step 3 — so retry amplifies the cost of slow `Background` setup steps (database seeding, auth flows) proportionally with the retry count. WHY teams use `@flaky` tags instead of global retry: global retry masks regressions where a genuine bug causes a non-flaky scenario to start failing intermittently — the bug appears as "retried and passed" in the HTML report, hiding the regression from the team until the scenario fails all retry attempts in a single run, which may take days to manifest reliably.
