### Pattern 106 — Cucumber.js `setWorldConstructor` with TypeScript Generic World for Type-Safe Step Sharing [official]

When multiple step definition files share state through the Cucumber.js `World` object, the default `this` type inside steps is `IWorld` which provides only `attach`, `log`, `parameters`, and lifecycle members. Any custom properties — `page`, `context`, `user`, `apiClient` — are untyped. Declaring a typed `World` class and passing it to `setWorldConstructor` gives TypeScript full type inference inside every step function that references `this`, eliminating `any`-casts and surfacing property mismatches at compile time rather than at runtime.

```typescript
// support/world.ts
import { IWorldOptions, setWorldConstructor, World } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { Browser, BrowserContext, Page, chromium } from '@playwright/test';

export interface AppWorldParameters {
  baseUrl: string;
  headless: boolean;
}

export class AppWorld extends World<AppWorldParameters> {
  browser!: Browser;
  context!: BrowserContext;
  page!: Page;
  currentUser: { email: string; role: string } | null = null;
  lastApiResponse: { status: number; body: unknown } | null = null;

  constructor(options: IWorldOptions<AppWorldParameters>) {
    super(options);
  }

  async openBrowser(): Promise<void> {
    this.browser = await chromium.launch({
      headless: this.parameters.headless ?? true,
    });
    this.context = await this.browser.newContext({
      baseURL: this.parameters.baseUrl,
    });
    this.page = await this.context.newPage();
  }

  async closeBrowser(): Promise<void> {
    await this.context?.close();
    await this.browser?.close();
  }
}

setWorldConstructor(AppWorld);

// support/hooks.ts
import { Before, After } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from './world';

Before(async function (this: AppWorld) {
  await this.openBrowser();
});

After(async function (this: AppWorld) {
  await this.closeBrowser();
});

// step-definitions/auth.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../support/world';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Given(
  'I am logged in as a {string} user',
  async function (this: AppWorld, role: string) {
    // TypeScript knows this.page, this.currentUser — no 'any' needed
    await this.page.goto('/login');
    this.currentUser = { email: `${role}@example.com`, role };
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `setWorldConstructor` with a typed class requires every step definition file to annotate `this` with the concrete World type (e.g., `async function (this: AppWorld)`). If a step is moved to a new file and the annotation is accidentally omitted, `this` silently falls back to `IWorld` and TypeScript emits no error on property access — the type narrowing is opt-in at the call site. WHY teams should enforce typed-World usage via a custom ESLint rule or a `grep`-based CI check that flags step functions whose first parameter is not `this: AppWorld`: omitting the annotation does not cause a runtime failure (Cucumber.js binds the World correctly regardless of the TypeScript annotation), so the regression is silent and only surfaces when a developer tries to access a custom property and gets an `undefined` at runtime.

---

### Pattern 107 — Playwright `locator.fill()` vs `locator.pressSequentially()` Selection Heuristic in BDD Step Definitions [official]

BDD step definitions that simulate user input into text fields have two primary Playwright APIs: `locator.fill()` clears the field and sets its value atomically (one DOM `input` event), while `locator.pressSequentially()` dispatches individual `keydown`/`keypress`/`keyup` events per character. Choosing the wrong one causes silent test failures: `fill()` bypasses keystroke-triggered autocomplete, real-time validation, and character-limit enforcement — all of which depend on individual `keydown` events.

```typescript
// step-definitions/form-input.steps.ts
import { When } from '../fixtures';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// CORRECT for a plain input — value is set atomically, triggers "input" event
When(
  'I enter {string} into the email field',
  async ({ page }, email: string) => {
    await page.locator('[data-testid="email-input"]').fill(email);
  }
);

// CORRECT for an autocomplete dropdown that listens to keydown to load suggestions
When(
  'I type {string} into the address search field',
  async ({ page }, query: string) => {
    // pressSequentially dispatches individual key events, triggering the
    // autocomplete's keydown->debounced-fetch->suggestions-render pipeline
    await page.locator('[data-testid="address-search"]').pressSequentially(
      query,
      { delay: 80 }  // 80ms between keystrokes mimics typing cadence
    );
    // Wait for suggestions to render before the next step asserts on them
    await page.locator('[data-testid="suggestion-list"]').waitFor();
  }
);

// CORRECT for an OTP / PIN input with per-character validation
When(
  'I enter the OTP code {string}',
  async ({ page }, otp: string) => {
    const otpInput = page.locator('[data-testid="otp-input"]');
    await otpInput.pressSequentially(otp, { delay: 50 });
    // Each character triggers a keyup event that moves focus to the next digit box
    await expect(otpInput).toHaveValue(otp);
  }
);

// CORRECT for a rich-text editor that does not respond to fill()
When(
  'I type the comment {string} into the rich-text editor',
  async ({ page }, comment: string) => {
    const editor = page.locator('[contenteditable="true"]').first();
    await editor.click();
    await editor.pressSequentially(comment);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.pressSequentially()` with a `delay` option is significantly slower than `locator.fill()` for long strings (e.g., a 200-character paragraph typed at 80ms/char takes 16 seconds). WHY BDD step definitions should default to `locator.fill()` and only use `pressSequentially()` when the scenario explicitly tests keystroke-dependent behaviour (autocomplete, character counters, OTP inputs, rich-text editors): using `pressSequentially()` universally to "be more realistic" inflates suite runtime without benefit for fields that do not depend on keystroke events, while using `fill()` on keystroke-dependent fields produces steps that pass in isolation but represent a scenario the application does not actually support.

---

### Pattern 108 — Cucumber.js `Before({ order: N })` Hook Ordering for Deterministic Multi-Hook Execution [official]

When a Cucumber.js project grows to include multiple `Before` hooks — one for browser launch, one for authentication, one for database seeding, one for feature-flag overrides — the order of execution matters: the auth hook must run after the browser hook (it needs `this.page`), and the seed hook must run after auth (it needs `this.currentUser`). Relying on file-load order or alphabetical hook registration is fragile. The `order` option (introduced in Cucumber.js v12.3.0 for named hooks and present in `Before`/`After` since earlier versions) provides an explicit numeric priority: lower numbers run first for `Before`, and lower numbers run last for `After`.

```typescript
// support/hooks/01-browser.ts — must run FIRST
import { Before, After } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../world';

Before({ order: 10 }, async function (this: AppWorld) {
  // Runs first — opens browser, sets this.page
  await this.openBrowser();
});

After({ order: 10 }, async function (this: AppWorld) {
  // Runs last for teardown (lowest order = last for After)
  await this.closeBrowser();
});

// support/hooks/02-auth.ts — must run AFTER browser hook
import { Before, After } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../world';

Before({ order: 20, tags: '@authenticated' }, async function (this: AppWorld) {
  // Runs second — this.page is already available from order:10
  await this.page.goto('/login');
  await this.page.fill('[name=email]', 'test@example.com');
  await this.page.fill('[name=password]', 'secret');
  await this.page.click('[type=submit]');
  await this.page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
});

// support/hooks/03-seed.ts — must run AFTER auth
import { Before } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../world';

Before({ order: 30, tags: '@seed-data' }, async function (this: AppWorld) {
  // Runs third — currentUser is already set by auth hook
  await this.seedDatabase(this.currentUser!);
});

// support/hooks/04-flags.ts — runs last in setup, first in teardown
import { Before, After } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../world';

Before(
  { order: 40, tags: '@feature-flag' },
  async function (this: AppWorld, { pickle }: ITestCaseHookParameter) {
    const flagTag = pickle.tags.find((t) => t.name.startsWith('@flag:'));
    if (flagTag) {
      const flag = flagTag.name.replace('@flag:', '');
      await this.page.addInitScript(
        ({ f }) => { (window as any).__flags = { [f]: true }; },
        { f: flag }
      );
    }
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Hook ordering with `order` numbers requires teams to agree on a numbering convention up front (e.g., infrastructure at 10-19, auth at 20-29, data at 30-39, config at 40-49) and to enforce that convention during code review — there is no built-in Cucumber.js mechanism that validates ordering correctness or warns when a hook at `order: 30` references `this.page` that is only set by a hook at `order: 10`. WHY the `order` option should be documented in a team CONTRIBUTING guide and enforced by a lint rule or comment convention rather than relying on naming or file-order conventions: Cucumber.js v12 changed the default hook registration order from file-system order to registration order within a process, so suites that previously relied on alphabetical file loading (`01-browser.ts` before `02-auth.ts`) may silently change behaviour when files are rearranged or when parallel workers load files in a different order.

---

### Pattern 109 — Playwright `page.waitForResponse()` in BDD Steps for API-Confirmation Assertions [official]

BDD scenarios that test workflows with asynchronous server-side processing (form submission, file upload, payment processing) need to assert that the application received a successful API response — not just that the UI updated. `page.waitForResponse()` intercepts network responses matching a URL glob or predicate and returns the `Response` object, letting step definitions assert on the HTTP status, response body, or response headers as part of the `Then` clause.

```typescript
// step-definitions/form-submission.steps.ts
import { When, Then } from '../fixtures';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

When(
  'I submit the contact form',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Start waiting for the response BEFORE triggering the action
    // that causes the request — avoids a race condition
    const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(
      (resp) =>
        resp.url().includes('/api/contact') && resp.request().method() === 'POST'
    );
    await page.locator('[data-testid="submit-contact"]').click();
    const response = await responsePromise;

    // Store the response on the fixture or World for the Then step
    (page as any).__lastResponse = response;
  }
);

Then(
  'the contact form submission should be accepted by the server',
  async ({ page }) => {
    const response = (page as any).__lastResponse;
    expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
    const body = await response.json();
    expect(body).toMatchObject({ success: true });
  }
);

// Alternative: use waitForResponse with URL glob pattern
When(
  'I upload the report file',
  async ({ page }) => {
    const uploadDone = page.waitForResponse('**/api/reports/upload');
    const [fileChooser] = await Promise.all([
      page.waitForEvent('filechooser'),
      page.locator('[data-testid="upload-btn"]').click(),
    ]);
    await fileChooser.setFiles('./fixtures/sample-report.pdf');
    const resp = await uploadDone;
    expect(resp.status()).toBeLessThan(400);
  }
);

Then(
  'the upload confirmation toast should appear',
  async ({ page }) => {
    await expect(
      page.locator('[data-testid="upload-toast"]')
    ).toBeVisible();
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** The `page.waitForResponse()` promise must be created *before* the action that triggers the request — if it is created after, the response may have already arrived and the promise will wait indefinitely, causing a test timeout. WHY `When` steps that combine a UI action with `waitForResponse()` should always initialise the response promise in the line immediately preceding the action call, and should document this ordering requirement with an inline comment: the race condition between promise creation and response arrival is silent in most CI environments (where the server responds slowly enough that the promise is always created first) but fails intermittently in local development against fast localhost servers, making it a hard-to-reproduce flake.

---

### Pattern 110 — Gherkin `Rule` Keyword with Per-Rule `Background` for Context-Scoped Preconditions [official]

The Gherkin `Rule` keyword (supported since Cucumber.js v7 and SpecFlow v3.9) represents a single business rule within a feature. Each `Rule` block can have its own `Background`, which runs only for scenarios under that rule — not for scenarios under other rules. This scopes setup code more precisely than a feature-level `Background`, preventing unrelated scenarios from inheriting setup they do not need and making the feature file more readable as a specification document.

```gherkin
# features/promotions/discount-rules.feature
Feature: Discount code application
  As a customer
  I want to apply discount codes at checkout
  So that I receive the correct promotional price

  Rule: Percentage-off discount codes
    Background:
      Given a 20% discount code "SAVE20" is active in the system
      And I have a product in my cart worth 100

    Scenario: Valid percentage-off code reduces total correctly
      When I apply the code "SAVE20" at checkout
      Then the order total should be 80.00
      And the discount line should show "-20.00 (SAVE20)"

    Scenario: Expired percentage-off code is rejected
      Given the code "SAVE20" expired yesterday
      When I apply the code "SAVE20" at checkout
      Then I should see the error "This discount code has expired"
      And the order total should remain 100.00

  Rule: Free-shipping discount codes
    Background:
      Given a free-shipping code "FREESHIP" is active in the system
      And I have a product in my cart worth 25

    Scenario: Free-shipping code removes shipping fee
      When I apply the code "FREESHIP" at checkout
      And I select Standard Delivery
      Then the shipping line should show "0.00"
      And the order total should be 25.00

    Scenario: Free-shipping code does not apply to next-day delivery
      When I apply the code "FREESHIP" at checkout
      And I select Next Day Delivery
      Then I should see the message "This code only applies to standard delivery"
```

```typescript
// step-definitions/promotions.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

Given(
  'a {int}% discount code {string} is active in the system',
  async function (this: AppWorld, percentage: number, code: string) {
    await this.apiClient.post('/admin/discount-codes', {
      code, type: 'percentage', value: percentage, active: true,
    });
  }
);

Given(
  'a free-shipping code {string} is active in the system',
  async function (this: AppWorld, code: string) {
    await this.apiClient.post('/admin/discount-codes', {
      code, type: 'free_shipping', active: true,
    });
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** A feature-level `Background` runs before every scenario in the file; a `Rule`-level `Background` runs only before scenarios inside its `Rule` block. Teams migrating from feature-level to rule-level `Background` may inadvertently remove setup that some scenarios still need — especially when rules share preconditions that were previously expressed once in the feature `Background`. WHY teams should audit each scenario when refactoring a feature-level `Background` into per-`Rule` `Background` blocks: Gherkin silently omits the feature-level `Background` steps from scenarios that are now under a `Rule` with its own `Background`, and no warning is emitted if a `Given` step that was previously in the shared `Background` is no longer present.

---

### Pattern 111 — Playwright `expect(page).toHaveURL()` with Regular-Expression Matching for Redirect-Agnostic BDD Navigation Assertions [official]

BDD `Then` steps that assert "the user lands on the correct page after login / checkout / form submission" frequently break when teams add query-string parameters (`?ref=email`, `?session=...`), locale prefixes (`/en-GB/dashboard`), or trailing slashes to URLs. Using an exact string match for `toHaveURL()` creates brittle steps that break on benign routing changes. Passing a `RegExp` to `toHaveURL()` lets step definitions assert on the semantically meaningful path segment while ignoring variable query strings and locale prefixes.

```typescript
// step-definitions/navigation.steps.ts
import { Then } from '../fixtures';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

// Brittle — breaks if /en-GB/ prefix is added, or ?session=abc is appended
// await expect(page).toHaveURL('https://app.example.com/dashboard');

// Resilient — asserts on the meaningful path segment only
Then(
  'I should be on the dashboard page',
  async ({ page }) => {
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard/);
  }
);

Then(
  'I should be redirected to the order confirmation page',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Matches /orders/12345/confirm, /en-US/orders/67890/confirm, etc.
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/orders\/\d+\/confirm/);
  }
);

Then(
  'I should land on the profile settings page',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Asserts the path contains /settings/profile regardless of host or
    // query string — works across staging and production base URLs
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/settings\/profile/);
  }
);

Then(
  'I should remain on the login page with an error state',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Asserts path is still /login — the query string ?error=... is ignored
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
    await expect(
      page.locator('[data-testid="auth-error"]')
    ).toBeVisible();
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Regex patterns for `toHaveURL()` can be too permissive if not anchored — `/\/dashboard/` also matches `/admin/dashboard`, `/dashboard-v2`, and `/super-dashboard`. WHY BDD navigation step definitions should use anchored regex patterns (e.g., `/\/dashboard$/` or `/\/dashboard(\?|$)/`) when the route structure has a potential for prefix or suffix collisions: a loosely anchored pattern that accidentally matches an unexpected URL produces a passing `Then` step when the user was actually redirected to an error page that shares a path segment with the intended destination, masking a real application bug.

---

### Pattern 112 — Cucumber.js `defineParameterType()` with `transformer` for Enum-Like Domain Value Step Parameters [official]

Custom parameter types let step definitions accept richly typed domain values — order statuses, user roles, payment methods — without manual parsing logic inside each step body. `defineParameterType()` registers a named type with a regex pattern and a `transformer` function that converts the matched string into the domain object or enum value. Every step definition that accepts that type receives a properly typed value without any casting.

```typescript
// support/parameter-types.ts
import { defineParameterType } from '@cucumber/cucumber';

// ---- Enum parameter type ----
type UserRole = 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer' | 'guest';

defineParameterType({
  name: 'userRole',
  regexp: /admin|editor|viewer|guest/,
  transformer(raw: string): UserRole {
    return raw as UserRole;
  },
});

// ---- Domain object parameter type ----
interface CurrencyAmount {
  amount: number;
  currency: 'GBP' | 'USD' | 'EUR';
}

defineParameterType({
  name: 'currencyAmount',
  regexp: /[GBP|USD|EUR]\d+(?:\.\d{2})?/,
  transformer(raw: string): CurrencyAmount {
    const prefixMap: Record<string, 'GBP' | 'USD' | 'EUR'> = {
      'GBP': 'GBP', 'USD': 'USD', 'EUR': 'EUR',
    };
    const currencyCode = raw.slice(0, 3) as 'GBP' | 'USD' | 'EUR';
    return {
      currency: prefixMap[currencyCode] ?? 'GBP',
      amount: parseFloat(raw.slice(3)),
    };
  },
});

// ---- Usage in step definitions ----
// step-definitions/user.steps.ts
import { Given } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

Given(
  'I am logged in as an {userRole}',
  async function (this: AppWorld, role: UserRole) {
    // role is typed as UserRole — no casting needed
    await this.loginAs(role);
  }
);

// features/checkout.feature:
//   Then the order total should be GBP49.99
//   Then the order total should be USD64.99
import { Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

Then(
  'the order total should be {currencyAmount}',
  async function (this: AppWorld, amount: CurrencyAmount) {
    // amount.currency === 'GBP', amount.amount === 49.99
    await this.assertOrderTotal(amount);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Custom parameter types with complex regexes are evaluated against every step string during Cucumber.js startup — a regex that uses catastrophic backtracking (e.g., `/(a+)+$/`) can cause the Cucumber process to hang when scanning large step libraries. WHY `defineParameterType()` regexes should be kept simple (character-class alternations rather than nested quantifiers) and should be tested in isolation with representative match and non-match strings before registering: the startup-time regex evaluation does not have a configurable timeout, so a pathological regex that worked on a small feature set can cause a CI timeout when the feature file count grows.

---

### Pattern 113 — Playwright `page.locator().filter()` for Disambiguating Duplicate Elements in BDD Step Definitions [official]

BDD step definitions that select "the second product card" or "the error message for the email field" frequently use fragile nth-index selectors (`nth(1)`) or brittle text-contains selectors. `locator.filter()` composes a parent locator with a refinement condition — `hasText`, `has`, or `hasNotText` — to select the specific element instance without hardcoding indices. This makes step definitions resilient to reordering and DOM restructuring.

```typescript
// step-definitions/product-list.steps.ts
import { When, Then } from '../fixtures';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Then(
  'the product card for {string} should show a sale badge',
  async ({ page }, productName: string) => {
    // Filter the generic card locator to the specific product by name
    const productCard = page
      .locator('[data-testid="product-card"]')
      .filter({ hasText: productName });
    await expect(productCard.locator('[data-testid="sale-badge"]')).toBeVisible();
  }
);

Then(
  'the form should show a validation error for the email field',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // Filter the generic error message locator to the one near the email field
    const emailError = page
      .locator('[data-testid="field-error"]')
      .filter({ has: page.locator('[data-field="email"]') });
    await expect(emailError).toBeVisible();
    await expect(emailError).toContainText('valid email');
  }
);

When(
  'I add {string} to my cart',
  async ({ page }, productName: string) => {
    const addButton = page
      .locator('[data-testid="add-to-cart"]')
      .filter({ has: page.locator(`text="${productName}"`) });
    await addButton.click();
  }
);

Then(
  'all out-of-stock products should show a disabled add-to-cart button',
  async ({ page }) => {
    const outOfStockCards = page
      .locator('[data-testid="product-card"]')
      .filter({ has: page.locator('[data-testid="out-of-stock-badge"]') });
    const count = await outOfStockCards.count();
    for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
      await expect(
        outOfStockCards.nth(i).locator('[data-testid="add-to-cart"]')
      ).toBeDisabled();
    }
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `locator.filter({ hasText: ... })` matches any element in the locator set whose subtree contains the given text — it is not an exact match by default. A filter of `hasText: "Pro"` will match both a "Pro Plan" card and a "Pro Max Plan" card. WHY BDD step definitions using `.filter({ hasText })` should use exact-string filters (`hasText: new RegExp('^' + escapeRegex(productName) + '$')`) when the product names in the test data have prefix/suffix relationships: failing to anchor the regex produces over-broad matches that silently select the wrong element and cause the assertion to pass against the incorrect DOM node.

---

### Pattern 114 — Cucumber.js `ITestCaseHookParameter` `willBeRetried` Flag for Retry-Aware Cleanup Logic [community]

When Cucumber.js is configured with `retry: N`, failed scenarios are re-executed up to N times. Standard `After` hooks run after every attempt — including intermediate retry attempts. If the `After` hook performs cleanup that should only run once (deleting a test record, logging to an external system, sending a Slack alert), it will trigger prematurely on retry attempts, causing data-corruption or alert spam. The `willBeRetried` flag on `ITestCaseHookParameter` lets hooks distinguish between a retry attempt (where the scenario will run again) and the final attempt (where cleanup is safe).

```typescript
// support/hooks/cleanup.ts
import { After, ITestCaseHookParameter } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../world';

After(async function (
  this: AppWorld,
  { result, willBeRetried }: ITestCaseHookParameter
) {
  // Always close the page so the next retry gets a fresh context
  await this.page?.close();

  // Only run expensive cleanup on the final attempt
  if (!willBeRetried) {
    // Delete the test-created database record regardless of pass/fail
    if (this.createdResourceId) {
      await this.apiClient.delete(`/test-resources/${this.createdResourceId}`);
      this.createdResourceId = null;
    }
  }

  // Only alert on genuine final failures — not on retried failures
  if (result?.status === 'FAILED' && !willBeRetried) {
    await this.notifySlack(
      `BDD scenario failed after ${result.duration}ms:\n${result.message}`
    );
  }
});

// separate hook: take a screenshot on every failure attempt for diagnostics
After(async function (
  this: AppWorld,
  { result, willBeRetried }: ITestCaseHookParameter
) {
  if (result?.status === 'FAILED') {
    const label = willBeRetried ? 'retry-attempt' : 'final-failure';
    const screenshot = await this.page.screenshot({ fullPage: true });
    await this.attach(screenshot, 'image/png');
    await this.log(`Screenshot captured at ${label}`);
  }
});
```

**Tradeoff.** The `willBeRetried` flag is truthy only during retry attempts that are not the final one — it is `false` on both a first-pass success and a final failed attempt. This means the flag alone does not distinguish "scenario passed on first attempt" from "scenario failed on final retry attempt". WHY `After` hooks that need to distinguish between a passing first attempt and a failing final attempt must check both `result.status` and `willBeRetried` together: `willBeRetried === false && result.status === 'FAILED'` is the final genuine failure, `willBeRetried === false && result.status === 'PASSED'` is a clean pass (which may have been a re-try success), and `willBeRetried === true` is a transient retry worth logging but not acting on.

---

### Pattern 115 — Playwright `APIRequestContext` in BDD `Given` Steps for Direct API Precondition Setup [official]

BDD scenarios that require complex data preconditions — a product with five images, a user account with a specific subscription tier, an order in "awaiting-dispatch" status — often set these up via the UI in `Given` steps. UI-driven setup is slow, fragile, and couples the precondition to the current UI state of the admin panel. Using Playwright's `request` fixture (`APIRequestContext`) in `Given` steps calls the application's REST API directly to set up the precondition state, making setup orders of magnitude faster and independent of the UI.

```typescript
// fixtures.ts — extend base test with an apiContext fixture
import { test as base, APIRequestContext } from '@playwright/test';

export const test = base.extend<{ apiContext: APIRequestContext }>({
  apiContext: async ({ playwright, baseURL }, use) => {
    const ctx = await playwright.request.newContext({
      baseURL,
      extraHTTPHeaders: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.API_TEST_TOKEN}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      },
    });
    await use(ctx);
    await ctx.dispose();
  },
});

// step-definitions/products.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then } from '../fixtures'; // uses extended test
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Given(
  'a product {string} with a price of {int} exists in the catalogue',
  async ({ apiContext }, name: string, price: number) => {
    const response = await apiContext.post('/api/products', {
      data: { name, price, active: true },
    });
    expect(response.status()).toBe(201);
  }
);

Given(
  'the order {string} is in awaiting-dispatch status',
  async ({ apiContext }, orderId: string) => {
    await apiContext.patch(`/api/orders/${orderId}`, {
      data: { status: 'awaiting_dispatch' },
    });
  }
);

When(
  'the warehouse team marks the order {string} as dispatched',
  async ({ page }, orderId: string) => {
    // The When step uses the UI — verifying the business flow
    await page.goto(`/warehouse/orders/${orderId}`);
    await page.locator('[data-testid="mark-dispatched"]').click();
  }
);

Then(
  'the customer should receive a dispatch notification email',
  async ({ apiContext }) => {
    // Assert via API on notification service state
    const resp = await apiContext.get('/api/notifications/last');
    const body = await resp.json();
    expect(body.type).toBe('dispatch_confirmation');
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Using `APIRequestContext` in `Given` steps bypasses the application's UI validation and creates data states that may be impossible to reach via normal user journeys. This is intentional for precondition setup but dangerous if misapplied to `When` steps — a `When` step that mutates state via API rather than UI is no longer testing what the user can actually do. WHY `APIRequestContext` should be restricted to `Given` steps (state setup) and `Then` steps (state verification via API) and never used in `When` steps (user actions): using the API in a `When` step short-circuits the business logic layer that the BDD scenario is intended to verify, producing a passing test that does not evidence the application's behaviour from a user's perspective.

---

### Pattern 116 — Gherkin `Scenario Outline` with `@`-Tagged `Examples` Blocks for Environment-Specific Data Variants [official]

A `Scenario Outline` can have multiple `Examples` tables, each tagged independently. This enables a single parameterised scenario to run with one data set in CI (`@smoke`) and an extended data set in regression (`@regression`), or to run different data variants for different environments (`@staging` vs `@production`), without duplicating the scenario body.

```gherkin
# features/pricing/vat-calculation.feature
Feature: VAT calculation on orders

  Scenario Outline: Order total includes correct VAT for the customer's region
    Given I am a customer from "<region>"
    And I add a product priced at <net_price> to my cart
    When I view the order summary
    Then the VAT amount should be <vat_amount>
    And the gross total should be <gross_total>

    @smoke
    Examples: UK standard rate
      | region         | net_price | vat_amount | gross_total |
      | United Kingdom | 100.00    | 20.00      | 120.00      |

    @regression
    Examples: Extended EU regions
      | region      | net_price | vat_amount | gross_total |
      | Germany     | 100.00    | 19.00      | 119.00      |
      | France      | 100.00    | 20.00      | 120.00      |
      | Italy       | 100.00    | 22.00      | 122.00      |
      | Sweden      | 100.00    | 25.00      | 125.00      |

    @smoke @regression
    Examples: Zero-rate regions
      | region   | net_price | vat_amount | gross_total |
      | Jersey   | 100.00    | 0.00       | 100.00      |
      | Guernsey | 100.00    | 0.00       | 100.00      |
```

```typescript
// step-definitions/vat.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../support/world';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

Given(
  'I am a customer from {string}',
  async function (this: AppWorld, region: string) {
    await this.setCustomerRegion(region);
  }
);

Then(
  'the VAT amount should be {float}',
  async function (this: AppWorld, vatAmount: number) {
    const displayed = await this.page
      .locator('[data-testid="vat-line"]')
      .innerText();
    expect(parseFloat(displayed.replace(/[^0-9.]/g, ''))).toBeCloseTo(vatAmount, 2);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Tagged `Examples` blocks still generate all scenario instances at `--dry-run` time — only the tag filter at execution time controls which instances run. Teams that run `--dry-run` without a tag filter will see all `Examples` instances listed, which can produce an unexpectedly long scenario inventory on large outlines with many tagged `Examples` blocks. WHY teams should document the expected tag-filter command for each `Examples` block in the feature file comment header when using multiple tagged `Examples` tables: a new team member running `cucumber-js features/` without a tag filter will execute every `Examples` instance, and if the `@regression` data set requires environment-specific credentials or slow external API calls, the unfiltered run will fail with confusing environment errors rather than a tag-not-found message.

---

### Pattern 117 — Playwright `page.addInitScript()` for Feature-Flag Override in BDD Scenario Setup [official]

BDD scenarios that test feature-flagged functionality need a way to force the feature on or off for a specific scenario without modifying the application's configuration server or database. `page.addInitScript()` injects a JavaScript snippet that runs in the browser context *before* the page script evaluates — making it the ideal injection point for overriding a client-side feature-flag evaluation function or `window.__flags` map.

```typescript
// step-definitions/feature-flags.steps.ts
import { Given } from '../fixtures';

Given(
  'the {string} feature flag is enabled for this scenario',
  async ({ page }, flagName: string) => {
    // Injected before any application JS runs — overrides the real flag service
    await page.addInitScript(
      ({ flag }) => {
        // Override the LaunchDarkly/Unleash client window shim
        Object.defineProperty(window, '__featureFlags', {
          get: () => ({ [flag]: true }),
          configurable: true,
        });
        // Also patch a common React context pattern
        (window as any).__flags = (window as any).__flags ?? {};
        (window as any).__flags[flag] = true;
      },
      { flag: flagName }
    );
  }
);

Given(
  'the {string} feature flag is disabled for this scenario',
  async ({ page }, flagName: string) => {
    await page.addInitScript(
      ({ flag }) => {
        Object.defineProperty(window, '__featureFlags', {
          get: () => ({ [flag]: false }),
          configurable: true,
        });
        (window as any).__flags = (window as any).__flags ?? {};
        (window as any).__flags[flag] = false;
      },
      { flag: flagName }
    );
    // The flag injection takes effect on the NEXT navigation
    await page.reload();
  }
);

// features/new-checkout.feature
// @flag:new-checkout-ui
// Scenario: New checkout flow shows order summary panel
//   Given the "new-checkout-ui" feature flag is enabled for this scenario
//   When I proceed to checkout
//   Then I should see the new order summary panel
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.addInitScript()` injects code that runs before the page's own scripts, but it does not persist across `page.goto()` calls by default when called after a navigation — the injected script is only applied to the *next* page load after the `addInitScript()` call. WHY `Given` steps that use `page.addInitScript()` for feature-flag overrides must always be followed by a `page.goto()` or `page.reload()` (explicitly or via a subsequent navigation step) to ensure the injected script executes on the page the scenario will test: calling `addInitScript()` after `page.goto()` has already completed means the page's own feature-flag initialisation code has already run and the override has no effect.

---

### Pattern 118 — Cucumber.js Step Definition Aliasing with Multiple Keyword Registrations on the Same Handler [official]

Gherkin scenarios often express the same precondition using both `Given` and `And` (which share the same step registry) and using slightly different phrasing depending on context — `"the user is logged in"` vs `"I am logged in"`. Rather than duplicating the step implementation, a single step handler function can be registered under multiple Cucumber keywords and multiple regex/expression patterns, keeping the step library DRY while allowing natural Gherkin prose.

```typescript
// step-definitions/auth.steps.ts
import { Given, When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { AppWorld } from '../support/world';

// Register the same function body under two phrasing variants
async function loginStep(
  this: AppWorld,
  email: string,
  password: string
): Promise<void> {
  await this.page.goto('/login');
  await this.page.fill('[name=email]', email);
  await this.page.fill('[name=password]', password);
  await this.page.click('[type=submit]');
  await this.page.waitForURL(/\/dashboard/);
}

Given('I am logged in as {string} with password {string}', loginStep);
Given('the user {string} is logged in with password {string}', loginStep);
When('I log in as {string} with password {string}', loginStep);

// Register the same assertion handler under Given and Then
async function assertLoggedOut(this: AppWorld): Promise<void> {
  await this.page.waitForURL(/\/login/);
  await this.page
    .locator('[data-testid="login-button"]')
    .waitFor({ state: 'visible' });
}

Given('I am not logged in', assertLoggedOut);
Then('I should be logged out', assertLoggedOut);
Then('I should be on the login page', assertLoggedOut);

// Register a data-table step under Given and When for flexible prose
async function setCartContents(
  this: AppWorld,
  table: import('@cucumber/cucumber').DataTable
): Promise<void> {
  for (const row of table.hashes()) {
    await this.apiClient.post('/cart/items', {
      productId: row['product_id'],
      quantity: parseInt(row['quantity'], 10),
    });
  }
}

Given('my cart contains:', setCartContents);
When('I add the following products to my cart:', setCartContents);
```

**Tradeoff.** Registering one function under multiple patterns creates a scenario where a Gherkin step change (e.g., rewording `"I am logged in"` to `"I have authenticated"`) silently stops matching the handler — Cucumber.js emits `Undefined step` instead of `Step matched but implementation missing`, and the distinction between "no step for this" and "wrong phrasing" is not obvious in the error output. WHY step definition aliasing should be audited periodically with `cucumber-js --dry-run --format json` to verify that all registered aliases are actually used in at least one feature file: unused aliases accumulate as dead code that inflates the step library's apparent coverage while providing no tested behaviour.

---

### Pattern 119 — Playwright `expect(locator).toBeInViewport()` for Scroll-Triggered BDD Behaviour Assertions [official]

BDD scenarios that test lazy-loading, infinite scroll, sticky headers, and scroll-to-reveal animations need to assert whether an element is currently within the browser's visible viewport. `expect(locator).toBeInViewport()` checks the element's intersection with the viewport using the Intersection Observer API semantics and retries until the condition is met or the timeout expires. The optional `ratio` parameter specifies the minimum fraction of the element that must be visible (0.0-1.0).

```typescript
// step-definitions/scroll.steps.ts
import { When, Then } from '../fixtures';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';

When(
  'I scroll to the bottom of the product list',
  async ({ page }) => {
    await page.evaluate(() =>
      window.scrollTo({ top: document.body.scrollHeight, behavior: 'smooth' })
    );
  }
);

Then(
  'the load-more button should become visible',
  async ({ page }) => {
    // toBeInViewport waits until at least 50% of the button is visible
    await expect(
      page.locator('[data-testid="load-more"]')
    ).toBeInViewport({ ratio: 0.5 });
  }
);

Then(
  'the sticky navigation bar should remain in the viewport after scrolling',
  async ({ page }) => {
    await page.evaluate(() => window.scrollTo(0, 500));
    await expect(
      page.locator('[data-testid="sticky-nav"]')
    ).toBeInViewport({ ratio: 1 }); // 100% of the nav must be visible
  }
);

Then(
  'the lazy-loaded product images should be visible in the viewport',
  async ({ page }) => {
    const images = page.locator('[data-testid="product-image"][loading="lazy"]');
    // Assert that at least the first lazy image has entered the viewport
    await expect(images.first()).toBeInViewport();
    // Confirm the browser has loaded the src attribute
    await expect(images.first()).toHaveAttribute('src', /.+/);
  }
);

When(
  'I scroll back to the top of the page',
  async ({ page }) => {
    await page.keyboard.press('Home');
  }
);

Then(
  'the back-to-top button should no longer be visible',
  async ({ page }) => {
    await expect(
      page.locator('[data-testid="back-to-top"]')
    ).not.toBeInViewport();
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `toBeInViewport()` with `{ ratio: 1 }` (fully visible) can fail on mobile viewport sizes or when the element is partially obscured by a fixed header — the element is technically "in the viewport" but partially overlapped. WHY BDD scenarios using `toBeInViewport({ ratio: 1 })` should be run with the same viewport dimensions as the browser configuration they are intended to test: a step that passes with `{ width: 1280, height: 720 }` may fail with a mobile viewport of `{ width: 375, height: 667 }` if the element is tall enough to overflow the smaller viewport, and the failure message `"Element is not in viewport"` does not indicate that the viewport size is the cause.

## Community Gotchas — Cycle 50

**[community] Gotcha 16 — Cucumber.js `retry` configuration retries every failed scenario including those that are deterministically broken (wrong step definition, missing page element) — teams configure `retry: 2` to handle flaky network-dependent scenarios but find that their CI suite runtime triples because every genuinely broken test now runs three times before reporting failure**: Cucumber.js `retry: N` retries any scenario whose result status is `FAILED` — it does not distinguish between a network flake (where a retry is appropriate) and a deterministic failure such as an `ElementNotFound` error or a TypeScript assertion that will never pass. WHY `retry` should always be combined with a per-scenario `@retry` tag rather than applied globally in `cucumber.js` config: using `{ retry: 2 }` globally triples the CI runtime for every broken scenario, while keeping `{ retry: 0 }` globally and using a tag-filtered retry strategy gives teams explicit opt-in control over which scenarios are worth retrying, preventing the "I tripled my CI time but fixed one flake" failure mode.

**[community] Gotcha 17 — Playwright `page.waitForSelector()` is not equivalent to `locator.waitFor()` in the context of BDD step definitions that navigate across pages — `waitForSelector()` resolves as soon as the selector exists in the DOM but does not retry if the element is removed and re-added (e.g., during a React re-render), while `locator.waitFor()` retries continuously and respects the action timeout, causing step definitions written with `waitForSelector()` to pass intermittently depending on render timing**: `page.waitForSelector()` returns a `JSHandle` when the selector first appears and is considered legacy since Playwright v1.16 — it does not benefit from the auto-retry semantics of the Locator API. Teams migrating from Puppeteer or older Playwright versions frequently carry over `waitForSelector()` patterns into step definitions, where the selector appears briefly during SSR hydration and then re-renders, causing the handle to become stale. WHY all Playwright step definitions written after Playwright v1.16 should use `locator.waitFor({ state: 'visible' })` instead of `page.waitForSelector()`: the Locator API retries the selector evaluation on every action and assertion call, making it resilient to transient DOM mutations during React/Vue hydration, while `waitForSelector()` captures a one-time snapshot and returns a stale `ElementHandle` that will throw `ElementHandle is not attached to the DOM` on subsequent action calls.

**[community] Gotcha 18 — Cucumber.js parallel execution (`--parallel N`) does not share `World` instances across workers — teams assume that a `World` property set in a `Before` hook in worker 1 will be visible to a step running in worker 2 for the same scenario, but each worker has its own `World` instance and there is no cross-worker shared state**: In Cucumber.js parallel mode, each worker process is an independent Node.js process with its own `World` constructor instantiation per scenario. There is no IPC mechanism that synchronises `World` properties across workers; each scenario's `World` lives entirely within the worker that executes it. Teams who attempt to use a module-level singleton (e.g., `let sharedBrowser: Browser` at the top of `world.ts`) to share a browser instance across workers observe that the singleton is initialised once per worker process, not once globally, resulting in N browser instances for N workers. WHY cross-scenario shared state in Cucumber.js parallel mode must use an external store (a shared file, a Redis key, a SQLite database) rather than module-level variables or `World` properties: module-level singletons in Node.js are process-local, not cross-process, so any data that multiple parallel workers need to share must be externalised to a medium that all worker processes can read from and write to atomically.

**[community] Gotcha 19 — Playwright `page.screenshot({ path: '...' })` in Cucumber.js `After` hooks writes to the path relative to `process.cwd()`, which in parallel Cucumber.js workers is the project root — but when tests run in a monorepo where `cucumber-js` is invoked from a subdirectory, `process.cwd()` resolves to the subdirectory, causing screenshot paths to be written outside the expected output directory and `--format html` attachment paths to become broken relative links in the report**: `page.screenshot({ path: 'screenshots/failure.png' })` resolves `'screenshots/failure.png'` against `process.cwd()` at the time of the `After` hook — if Cucumber.js is launched from `packages/web-app/` in a monorepo, screenshots write to `packages/web-app/screenshots/` rather than the project root `screenshots/` directory, but the HTML report's attachment references are generated relative to the report's own output directory (which is the project root), producing broken `src` paths in the report. WHY `After` hook screenshot paths should always be constructed using `path.resolve(__dirname, '../../screenshots', filename)` with an absolute anchor rather than a bare relative path: using an absolute path derived from the hook file's own location (`__dirname`) is invariant to the working directory from which Cucumber.js is launched, ensuring screenshots are always written to the same location regardless of monorepo invocation context.

**[community] Gotcha 20 — `expect(locator).toHaveText()` in Playwright BDD `Then` steps fails with a cryptic mismatch when the element contains non-breaking spaces, zero-width joiners, or locale-specific quotation marks rendered by the browser's CSS `content` pseudo-element — the failure message shows visually identical strings that differ only in invisible Unicode code points, making the mismatch undetectable without explicit Unicode inspection**: Browsers render typographic characters — `&nbsp;` as a non-breaking space, CSS `content: "\201C"` as a curly left-quotation-mark — as part of the element's `innerText`. `toHaveText()` by default uses a string equality check against the element's `textContent`, which includes these invisible characters. A `Then` step asserting `"Order confirmed"` will fail if the page renders `"Order confirmed"` with a non-breaking space between words, producing a Playwright diff that shows `Expected: "Order confirmed"` vs `Actual: "Order confirmed"` with no visible difference. WHY BDD `Then` steps that assert on displayed text should use `toContainText()` instead of `toHaveText()` when the text comes from a Gherkin feature file that team members type manually: `toContainText()` performs a substring match and is insensitive to surrounding whitespace characters, while `toHaveText()` performs a full-string match that includes typographic Unicode characters the step author cannot see in the feature file editor.

## Cycle 51 — 2026-05-14

### Pattern 120 — Playwright `test.extend()` Custom BDD Fixture with Setup/Teardown Lifecycle

Custom Playwright fixtures declared with `test.extend()` give BDD step definitions a structured setup/teardown lifecycle that mirrors the Cucumber `Before`/`After` hook pair but integrates directly into the Playwright fixture dependency graph. The fixture's `await use(value)` call demarcates the setup phase (above it) from the teardown phase (below it), eliminating the need for manual state tracking across hooks.

```typescript
// fixtures/authenticated-user.ts
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test';

type AuthFixtures = {
  authenticatedPage: { page: import('@playwright/test').Page; userId: string };
};

export const test = base.extend<AuthFixtures>({
  authenticatedPage: async ({ page, request }, use) => {
    // Setup: create a user via API, set auth cookie
    const resp = await request.post('/api/test/users', {
      data: { role: 'standard', email: `user-${Date.now()}@test.example` },
    });
    const { id: userId, token } = await resp.json();
    await page.context().addCookies([
      { name: 'auth_token', value: token, domain: 'localhost', path: '/' },
    ]);
    await page.goto('/dashboard');

    await use({ page, userId }); // ← step definitions run here

    // Teardown: delete the ephemeral test user
    await request.delete(`/api/test/users/${userId}`);
  },
});

// steps/dashboard-steps.ts
import { createBdd } from 'playwright-bdd';
import { test } from '../fixtures/authenticated-user';

const { Given, Then } = createBdd(test);

Given('I am logged in as a standard user', async ({ authenticatedPage }) => {
  await expect(authenticatedPage.page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' }))
    .toBeVisible();
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Fixture-based setup produces shorter, more composable `Given` steps than Cucumber `Before` hooks, because the fixture dependency graph guarantees execution order and prevents the "hook fires but the World property is undefined" failure mode. The downside is that playwright-bdd is required to bind fixtures to `Given`/`When`/`Then` functions; vanilla Cucumber.js does not have the Playwright fixture model and must use `setWorldConstructor` + `Before` hooks instead.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 121 — Playwright Worker-Scoped Fixtures for Shared Browser State Across BDD Scenarios

Worker-scoped fixtures (`{ scope: 'worker' }`) are set up once per Playwright worker process and shared across all scenarios assigned to that worker, making them ideal for expensive BDD preconditions such as OAuth login flows, database seeding, or browser-level storage state that should not repeat per-scenario. The teardown (code after `await use()`) runs when the worker exits, not between scenarios.

```typescript
// fixtures/worker-session.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import * as path from 'path';
import * as fs from 'fs/promises';

type WorkerFixtures = {
  workerStorageState: string; // path to a saved storageState JSON file
};

export const test = base.extend<{}, WorkerFixtures>({
  workerStorageState: [
    async ({ browser }, use, workerInfo) => {
      const storageFile = path.resolve(
        __dirname,
        `../tmp/storage-worker-${workerInfo.workerIndex}.json`
      );

      // Perform login only if no cached storage state exists
      const contextForLogin = await browser.newContext();
      const page = await contextForLogin.newPage();
      await page.goto('/login');
      await page.getByLabel('Email').fill(`worker${workerInfo.workerIndex}@test.example`);
      await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.TEST_USER_PASSWORD!);
      await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
      await page.waitForURL('/dashboard');
      await contextForLogin.storageState({ path: storageFile });
      await contextForLogin.close();

      await use(storageFile); // all tests in this worker share this storage state

      await fs.rm(storageFile, { force: true }); // cleanup on worker exit
    },
    { scope: 'worker' },
  ],

  // Override the page fixture to use the worker's storage state
  page: async ({ browser, workerStorageState }, use) => {
    const ctx = await browser.newContext({ storageState: workerStorageState });
    const pg = await ctx.newPage();
    await use(pg);
    await ctx.close();
  },
});
```

**Tradeoff.** Worker-scoped storage state dramatically reduces login overhead in large BDD suites — a 200-scenario suite with 4 workers performs 4 logins instead of 200. The risk is scenario pollution: if a scenario mutates the authenticated user's profile (e.g., changes the email address), subsequent scenarios in the same worker inherit that mutation. BDD suites using worker-scoped sessions must treat the authenticated identity as read-only within scenarios, or must explicitly reset state in `After` hooks using the API.

**Tag:** [official]

### Pattern 122 — Playwright `expect.soft()` for Multi-Assertion BDD `Then` Steps

`expect.soft()` allows a `Then` step to evaluate multiple assertions without aborting on the first failure, collecting all failures before the scenario is marked as failed. This is particularly useful in BDD `Then` steps that assert page state across multiple UI elements — for example, a "checkout confirmation page" step that validates order number, item list, and total price simultaneously.

```typescript
// steps/order-confirmation-steps.ts
import { Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { ICustomWorld } from '../support/world';

interface OrderSummary {
  orderNumber: string;
  itemCount: number;
  totalPrice: string;
}

Then(
  'the order confirmation page should display all order details',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, dataTable: import('@cucumber/cucumber').DataTable) {
    const expected = dataTable.rowsHash() as unknown as OrderSummary;
    const { page } = this;

    // Soft assertions: collect all failures before surfacing them
    await expect.soft(
      page.getByTestId('order-number')
    ).toHaveText(expected.orderNumber);

    await expect.soft(
      page.getByTestId('item-count')
    ).toHaveText(`${expected.itemCount} item${Number(expected.itemCount) !== 1 ? 's' : ''}`);

    await expect.soft(
      page.getByTestId('order-total')
    ).toHaveText(expected.totalPrice);

    await expect.soft(
      page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Order Confirmed' })
    ).toBeVisible();

    // Surface all collected soft-assertion failures at once
    expect(test.info().errors).toHaveLength(0);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `expect.soft()` produces failure messages that list all mismatches together, making triage faster for `Then` steps with many assertions. However, the Playwright documentation notes that soft assertions only work with the Playwright test runner — they are not natively available in plain Cucumber.js without the playwright-bdd bridge or a `@playwright/test` test runner wrapper. Teams using vanilla Cucumber.js must implement their own error-collection array in `World` and throw an aggregated error at the end of the step.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 123 — Playwright `page.route()` in BDD `Given` Steps for Deterministic API Mocking

`page.route()` intercepts network requests matching a URL pattern and fulfills them with controlled responses, allowing BDD `Given` steps to establish deterministic API state without a running backend. This is the recommended approach for BDD scenarios that test UI behaviour under specific API conditions (empty state, error state, partial data) that are difficult or slow to reproduce against a live server.

```typescript
// steps/product-listing-steps.ts
import { Given, Before } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { ICustomWorld } from '../support/world';

// Mock an empty product catalogue
Given(
  'the product catalogue is empty',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld) {
    await this.page.route('**/api/v1/products**', async (route) => {
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 200,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify({ items: [], total: 0, page: 1 }),
      });
    });
    await this.page.goto('/products');
  }
);

// Mock a server error on product load
Given(
  'the product service is unavailable',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld) {
    await this.page.route('**/api/v1/products**', async (route) => {
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 503,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify({ error: 'Service temporarily unavailable' }),
      });
    });
    await this.page.goto('/products');
  }
);

// Partial response: mock a specific product by ID
Given(
  'a product with ID {string} exists with the name {string}',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, productId: string, productName: string) {
    await this.page.route(`**/api/v1/products/${productId}`, async (route) => {
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 200,
        contentType: 'application/json',
        body: JSON.stringify({
          id: productId,
          name: productName,
          price: 29.99,
          inStock: true,
        }),
      });
    });
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Route-based mocking in `Given` steps produces fast, stable, parallelisable BDD scenarios with no network dependency. The cost is maintenance of mock payloads — when the real API response shape evolves, mock responses must be updated separately, and a mock that does not match the live API structure can cause tests to pass while the real integration is broken. Teams should validate mock shapes against a JSON Schema or OpenAPI contract in CI to prevent mock drift.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 124 — Playwright `page.evaluate()` for localStorage and sessionStorage Precondition Setup in BDD `Given` Steps

`page.evaluate()` executes JavaScript directly in the browser context, making it the correct mechanism for seeding `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` before a scenario's first navigation — a common BDD precondition for features that depend on client-side persisted state (e.g., onboarding completion flags, feature toggles stored client-side, or previously viewed items). The critical constraint is that `page.evaluate()` must be called after `page.goto()` has established an origin, because storage is origin-scoped.

```typescript
// steps/onboarding-steps.ts
import { Given } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { ICustomWorld } from '../support/world';

Given(
  'the user has previously completed the onboarding wizard',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld) {
    // Navigate to origin first so localStorage is scoped correctly
    await this.page.goto('/');

    await this.page.evaluate(() => {
      localStorage.setItem('onboarding_complete', 'true');
      localStorage.setItem('onboarding_completed_at', new Date().toISOString());
    });

    // Navigate to the target page now that storage state is established
    await this.page.goto('/dashboard');
  }
);

Given(
  'the user has {int} items in their recently viewed list',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, itemCount: number) {
    await this.page.goto('/');

    const recentItems = Array.from({ length: itemCount }, (_, i) => ({
      id: `product-${i + 1}`,
      name: `Product ${i + 1}`,
      viewedAt: new Date(Date.now() - i * 60_000).toISOString(),
    }));

    // Pass the value as an argument — do not close over test variables directly
    await this.page.evaluate((items) => {
      localStorage.setItem('recently_viewed', JSON.stringify(items));
    }, recentItems);

    await this.page.goto('/products');
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `page.evaluate()` with explicit argument passing (the second parameter) is the only safe way to transfer test-side data into browser-side scripts — variables referenced directly inside the function body are not accessible because the function executes in the browser context, not the Node.js test process. Teams frequently hit `ReferenceError: myVariable is not defined` when they forget this separation, which is why the Playwright documentation emphasises: "If you want to pass something from the Node.js environment to the browser, use the argument parameter."

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 125 — Cucumber.js `AfterStep` Hook for Per-Step Screenshot Evidence Trail

The `AfterStep` hook fires after every individual Gherkin step (not just after a whole scenario), giving teams the ability to capture a screenshot after each step and attach it to the scenario report. This creates a visual evidence trail for long multi-step BDD scenarios where pinpointing the exact step that caused a visual regression is otherwise difficult.

```typescript
// support/step-evidence.ts
import { AfterStep, ITestStepHookParameter, attach, Status } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { ICustomWorld } from './world';

AfterStep(async function (
  this: ICustomWorld,
  { result, pickleStep }: ITestStepHookParameter
) {
  // Only capture screenshots on failed or warning steps to avoid report bloat
  if (result?.status === Status.FAILED || result?.status === Status.PENDING) {
    const screenshot = await this.page.screenshot({ fullPage: false });
    await attach(screenshot, 'image/png');
  }
});

// For exhaustive evidence mode (e.g., audit runs), capture all steps
AfterStep({ tags: '@evidence' }, async function (
  this: ICustomWorld,
  { pickleStep }: ITestStepHookParameter
) {
  const stepTitle = pickleStep.text.replace(/[^a-z0-9]/gi, '-').toLowerCase();
  const screenshot = await this.page.screenshot({ fullPage: false });
  // Attach with a descriptive name visible in the HTML report
  await attach(screenshot, 'image/png');
  // Also attach the step name as a text note for traceability
  await attach(`Step: ${pickleStep.text}`, 'text/plain');
});
```

**Tradeoff.** `AfterStep` screenshots create dense, navigable visual evidence in the Cucumber HTML report but add measurable latency — each screenshot call (even async) adds 20–80 ms per step depending on page complexity and viewport size. For a scenario with 20 steps, this is 400–1600 ms of additional overhead. The `@evidence` tag gate in the second hook above limits the overhead to scenarios where evidence is explicitly requested, rather than applying it to every step in every scenario. Avoid using `{ fullPage: true }` in AfterStep hooks on pages with lazy-loaded content, as the full-page screenshot waits for all lazy elements to render and can add seconds of overhead.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 126 — Playwright `getByRole()` with `name` Option as the Primary BDD Step Locator

`getByRole(role, { name })` is the highest-fidelity BDD locator strategy because it matches elements exactly the way a screen reader or assistive technology would identify them — by their ARIA role and accessible name. Using role-based locators in step definitions produces tests that break when accessibility regressions occur (role removed, name changed) while remaining resilient to CSS class renames, DOM restructuring, and test ID changes.

```typescript
// steps/form-interaction-steps.ts
import { When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { ICustomWorld } from '../support/world';

When(
  'I click the {string} button',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, buttonName: string) {
    // getByRole('button', { name }) matches the accessible name:
    //   - aria-label attribute
    //   - aria-labelledby reference
    //   - button text content
    //   - title attribute (fallback)
    await this.page
      .getByRole('button', { name: buttonName })
      .click();
  }
);

When(
  'I fill in the {string} field with {string}',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, fieldLabel: string, value: string) {
    // getByRole('textbox', { name }) matches via associated <label> or aria-label
    await this.page
      .getByRole('textbox', { name: fieldLabel })
      .fill(value);
  }
);

Then(
  'the {string} navigation link should be highlighted',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, linkName: string) {
    // 'exact: false' allows partial name matching for links with icons
    await expect(
      this.page.getByRole('link', { name: linkName, exact: false })
    ).toHaveAttribute('aria-current', 'page');
  }
);

Then(
  'the {string} region should contain the text {string}',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, regionName: string, expectedText: string) {
    await expect(
      this.page.getByRole('region', { name: regionName })
    ).toContainText(expectedText);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** `getByRole()` locators are tightly coupled to the page's accessibility tree, which is their strength and their limitation: a button rendered as a `<div role="button">` with an accessible name set via `aria-label` works correctly, but a `<div class="btn">` with no ARIA semantics will not be found. Teams must ensure the application marks up interactive elements correctly, making `getByRole()` an effective driver of accessibility compliance in the codebase — every BDD step that uses it is implicitly an accessibility regression check.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 127 — Cucumber.js `BeforeAll` / `AfterAll` for Suite-Level Database Seeding

`BeforeAll` and `AfterAll` hooks run once per Cucumber.js worker process — not once per scenario — making them suitable for expensive suite-level setup such as database migration execution, static fixture seeding, or external service configuration that is identical for every scenario in a worker. Unlike `Before`, `BeforeAll` does not receive a `World` instance (it runs at the worker level, before any scenario's `World` is instantiated), so it communicates seeded data to scenarios via module-level variables or environment variables.

```typescript
// support/db-hooks.ts
import { BeforeAll, AfterAll, Before } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { Pool } from 'pg';

let dbPool: Pool;
let seedTenantId: string;

BeforeAll({ name: 'database-setup', order: 10 }, async () => {
  dbPool = new Pool({
    connectionString: process.env.TEST_DATABASE_URL,
    max: 5,
  });

  // Run migrations against the test database
  await dbPool.query(`
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tenants (
      id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
      name TEXT NOT NULL,
      created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
    )
  `);

  // Seed a reference tenant used by all read-only scenarios
  const { rows } = await dbPool.query<{ id: string }>(
    `INSERT INTO tenants (name) VALUES ('Acme Corp') RETURNING id`
  );
  seedTenantId = rows[0].id;

  // Make the pool and seed ID available to Before hooks via module export
});

AfterAll({ name: 'database-teardown', order: 10 }, async () => {
  await dbPool.query(`DELETE FROM tenants WHERE id = $1`, [seedTenantId]);
  await dbPool.end();
});

// Module-level accessor for Before hooks and step definitions
export function getDbPool(): Pool { return dbPool; }
export function getSeedTenantId(): string { return seedTenantId; }
```

**Tradeoff.** `BeforeAll` is a correct fit for setup that is both expensive and identical across scenarios — running it once per worker rather than once per scenario saves time proportional to the number of scenarios. The hazard is state leakage: if any scenario mutates the seeded data (e.g., deletes the seed tenant), subsequent scenarios in the same worker will fail in ways that are difficult to diagnose because the `BeforeAll` only runs once. Suite-level seeded data should be treated as read-only fixtures; mutable data should be created in per-scenario `Before` hooks.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 128 — Playwright `page.locator().filter()` Chained with `getByRole()` for Unambiguous BDD Step Locators

When a page renders repeated component instances (e.g., a list of product cards, each containing a "Add to cart" button), `getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })` returns multiple elements and subsequent actions throw a strict-mode error. The correct resolution is to chain `getByRole()` with `.filter({ hasText })` or `.filter({ has })` to narrow to the specific component instance described in the Gherkin step, rather than using a numeric index (`.nth(0)`) which is position-dependent.

```typescript
// steps/product-card-steps.ts
import { When, Then } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { ICustomWorld } from '../support/world';

When(
  'I add {string} to my cart from the product listing',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, productName: string) {
    // Find the product card whose heading matches productName,
    // then locate the "Add to cart" button within that card.
    const productCard = this.page
      .getByRole('article')
      .filter({ has: this.page.getByRole('heading', { name: productName }) });

    await productCard
      .getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })
      .click();
  }
);

Then(
  'the {string} product card should show {string} in stock',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, productName: string, stockLabel: string) {
    const productCard = this.page
      .getByRole('article')
      .filter({ has: this.page.getByRole('heading', { name: productName }) });

    await expect(
      productCard.getByTestId('stock-label')
    ).toHaveText(stockLabel);
  }
);

When(
  'I remove {string} from the cart summary',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, itemName: string) {
    // Use hasText on the row-level container to scope the remove button
    const cartRow = this.page
      .getByRole('row')
      .filter({ hasText: itemName });

    await cartRow
      .getByRole('button', { name: /remove/i })
      .click();
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** Filtering by semantic content (`hasText`, `has: getByRole(...)`) keeps step locators aligned with the user-visible page structure — the step reads "find the product card for X, then click its Add to cart button", mirroring how a human tester would navigate. The risk is over-specificity: if the product name appears in multiple elements within the same card (heading and image alt text), the `hasText` filter may match more elements than expected. Using `has: page.getByRole('heading', { name })` is more precise than `hasText` for structural disambiguation because it matches only elements that contain a heading with the exact name.

**Tag:** [official]

---

### Pattern 129 — Playwright `expect(page).toHaveTitle()` and `toHaveURL()` as BDD Navigation Confirmation Steps

`expect(page).toHaveTitle()` and `expect(page).toHaveURL()` are auto-retrying assertions that wait for the page title or URL to match before continuing — making them the canonical way to confirm navigation in BDD `Then` steps without explicit `waitForURL()` calls. Both accept strings (exact match) or regular expressions (partial/pattern match), and both default to the action timeout, preventing flaky timing-dependent navigation assertions.

```typescript
// steps/navigation-steps.ts
import { Then, When } from '@cucumber/cucumber';
import { expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { ICustomWorld } from '../support/world';

When(
  'I navigate to the {string} page',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, pageName: string) {
    const routes: Record<string, string> = {
      'home': '/',
      'products': '/products',
      'account settings': '/account/settings',
      'checkout': '/checkout',
    };
    const path = routes[pageName.toLowerCase()];
    if (!path) throw new Error(`Unknown page: "${pageName}"`);
    await this.page.goto(path);
  }
);

Then(
  'I should be on the {string} page',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld, pageName: string) {
    const expectations: Record<string, { title: RegExp; url: RegExp }> = {
      'dashboard':  { title: /Dashboard/, url: /\/dashboard/ },
      'login':      { title: /Sign In/,   url: /\/login/ },
      'checkout':   { title: /Checkout/,  url: /\/checkout/ },
      'order confirmation': { title: /Order Confirmed/, url: /\/orders\/[a-z0-9-]+\/confirmation/ },
    };
    const exp = expectations[pageName.toLowerCase()];
    if (!exp) throw new Error(`Unknown page expectation: "${pageName}"`);

    await expect(this.page).toHaveTitle(exp.title);
    await expect(this.page).toHaveURL(exp.url);
  }
);

Then(
  'I should be redirected to the login page',
  async function (this: ICustomWorld) {
    // Regex URL match handles both /login and /login?redirect=/... variants
    await expect(this.page).toHaveURL(/\/login/);
  }
);
```

**Tradeoff.** The auto-retry semantics of `toHaveTitle()` and `toHaveURL()` eliminate the most common source of navigation flakiness in BDD suites — the race between the click action returning and the browser completing the navigation. The tradeoff is that assertion failures do not distinguish between "page never navigated" and "page navigated but to a different URL than expected"; both produce the same timeout-after-N-seconds failure. Teams should set `actionTimeout` explicitly in their Playwright config rather than relying on the default 30-second timeout to keep failed navigation steps from bloating CI run times.

**Tag:** [official]
